blocks.h: 1. What IMO is, and the organs that do the work

blocks.p: The International Maritime Organization is the specialised agency of the United Nations responsible for the safety and security of shipping and for the prevention of pollution from ships. It is a regulator that owns no ships, inspects nothing and enforces nothing directly: it produces instruments which flag States give force to in their own law and which port States then check. Its architecture follows that purpose exactly - a two-tier governing structure of an Assembly and a Council, five main committees that do the technical work, seven sub-committees that prepare it, and a permanent Secretariat headed by the Secretary-General.

The division worth stating at the outset, because it organises the rest of the answer: the governing organs decide policy, budget and membership; the committees produce the regulation that reaches a ship. A candidate who describes only the Assembly and Council has described the constitution and none of the output.

blocks.h: 2. The Assembly - the governing body

ul: The highest governing body. All Member States sit in it, each with one vote.
Meets in regular session once every two years. The 33rd Assembly is the operative cycle at this sitting; its resolutions were adopted on 6 December 2023.
Approves the work programme, votes the budget and determines the financial arrangements of the Organization.
Elects the Council. The Council serving at this sitting was elected at the 33rd Assembly for the 2024-2025 biennium and is in the second year of that term.
Receives the reports of the Council and of the committees, and adopts Assembly resolutions - recommendations, guidelines and codes, carrying the A. prefix.
Approves the appointment of the Secretary-General made by the Council.

blocks.h: 3. The Council - the executive organ

ul: 40 Members, elected by the Assembly for a two-year term, in three categories: (a) ten States with the largest interest in providing international shipping services; (b) ten States with the largest interest in international seaborne trade; (c) twenty States elected to secure representation of all major geographic areas.

Between Assembly sessions it performs all the functions of the Assembly - with one reserved exception: the function of making recommendations to Governments on maritime safety and pollution prevention, which the Assembly keeps to itself.
Supervises the work of the Organization and co-ordinates the activities of its organs.
Considers the draft work programme and budget and submits them to the Assembly with its comments and recommendations.
Appoints the Secretary-General, subject to the approval of the Assembly. The present Secretary-General took office on 1 January 2024 and has been in post for thirteen months at this sitting.

⚠ An amendment would enlarge the Council to 52 Members - resolution A.1152(32), adopted in December 2021. It amends the IMO Convention itself and therefore requires acceptance by two thirds of Members. It is NOT in force at this sitting: the correct figure to write in February 2025 is 40.

blocks.h: 4. The five main committees and what each owns

rows: Maritime Safety Committee (MSC)

The senior technical body. Navigational safety, construction and equipment, manning from a safety standpoint, carriage of dangerous goods, casualty investigation, search and rescue, and maritime security. Adopts amendments to SOLAS and to the codes made mandatory under it
Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC)
Prevention and control of pollution from ships - MARPOL and all six Annexes, ballast water, anti-fouling, recycling, and the greenhouse-gas and energy-efficiency measures. Adopts amendments to MARPOL
Legal Committee
Any legal matter within the scope of the Organization - in particular the liability and compensation conventions, and the legal aspects of new technology
Technical Cooperation Committee
Implementation of the Organization's technical assistance and capacity-building work, particularly for developing States
Facilitation Committee
Elimination of unnecessary formalities and administrative burden in international shipping - the FAL Convention and the single-window regime

blocks.p: All five are open to all Member States. The two that matter most to an engineer are MSC and MEPC, because they are the organs that adopt amendments to the mandatory instruments - and they do so by tacit acceptance, which is why a MARPOL or SOLAS amendment can enter into force without any State ratifying anything.

blocks.h: 5. The seven sub-committees, and the role they perform

ul: HTW - Human Element, Training and Watchkeeping
III - Implementation of IMO Instruments
NCSR - Navigation, Communications and Search and Rescue
PPR - Pollution Prevention and Response
SDC - Ship Design and Construction
SSE - Ship Systems and Equipment
CCC - Carriage of Cargoes and Containers

blocks.p: Their role is preparatory and technical, and the reason for it is practical. A committee sits for about a week and cannot itself draft detailed regulation, so it remits the work to the sub-committee holding the relevant expertise. The sub-committee develops the draft text, guidelines or unified interpretation, works through the technical argument with the flag States, classification societies and industry observers who attend, and reports back to its parent committee - MSC, MEPC, or both where the subject straddles them.

A sub-committee adopts nothing. It prepares; the parent committee approves; the committee or the Assembly adopts. That separation is what keeps technical depth and treaty-making authority in different hands, and it is the specific point the last sentence of limb (a) is asking for.

blocks.h: 6. What a convention is

blocks.p: A convention is a formal, legally binding treaty between States. It is negotiated and adopted at a diplomatic conference or by the Assembly; it is then opened for signature and for ratification, acceptance, approval or accession; and it enters into force only when the conditions written into the convention itself are satisfied - characteristically a stated number of Contracting States representing a stated share of world gross tonnage.
Three consequences follow, and they are what separate a convention from everything else in limb (b):

ol: It binds only the States that have become party to it. A convention in force is not law everywhere; it is law in the States that have accepted it and, through them, on their ships.
It has no effect on a ship until the flag State enacts it domestically and issues the certificates. IMO does not legislate for ships; States do.
Adoption, entry into force and application are three different dates, and confusing them is the single most common error in this subject.

blocks.p: Example: the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974 (SOLAS).

blocks.h: 7. Protocol, Code and Resolution - what distinguishes each, with examples

rows: Convention
A binding treaty between States, entering into force on its own stated conditions and binding only its parties
SOLAS 1974; the STCW Convention 1978
Protocol

A separate treaty instrument that amends, supplements or replaces part of a parent convention, used where the change is too large or too structural for the ordinary amendment procedure. It has its own signature, ratification and entry-into-force conditions, so a State can be party to the convention and not to the protocol

The 1978 and 1997 Protocols to MARPOL - the 1997 Protocol is what introduced Annex VI. The 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and to the Load Lines Convention, which introduced the harmonized system of survey and certification
Code

A detailed technical instrument. Of itself it is recommendatory; it becomes mandatory only when a convention makes it so. Mandatory status is therefore a property of the hook, not of the document - and it can be partial

The ISM Code, adopted by resolution A.741(18) and made mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX. Contrast the 2008 Intact Stability Code, whose Part A is mandatory and whose Part B is recommendatory - one document, two statuses
Resolution

The formal decision of the Assembly or of a committee. It is the vehicle by which an instrument is adopted or guidance issued - so a resolution can be either mandatory or recommendatory, and which it is depends entirely on what it carries

MEPC.328(76), adopting the revised MARPOL Annex VI - mandatory, because MARPOL makes it so, and in force 1 November 2023. Contrast A.1184(33), revised guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations - recommendatory guidance

blocks.p: The organising idea, and the mark limb (b) is really testing: a convention and a protocol are treaty instruments that States accept one by one; a code and a resolution are outputs of the Organization whose legal force is borrowed from whatever convention points at them. Ask of any instrument what makes this binding? - and if the answer is not "a convention says so", it is guidance.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Two limbs at 8 marks each, so two visible regions and roughly equal length. Limb (a) has four named objects - Assembly, Council, main committees, sub-committees - and a marker will look for four. Giving each its own heading, and answering the sub-committee sentence as a separate question about role rather than as a list of acronyms, is worth more than any amount of extra prose about what IMO does. Limb (b) prints four instrument types and demands an example of each: a table is the fastest way to score it, and the four examples are half the marks.

blocks.h: The one idea that unlocks limb (b)

blocks.p: Legal force in this system is borrowed, not intrinsic. A Code is a technical document with no more legal effect than a textbook until a Convention says it is mandatory. A Resolution is a container - it can carry a mandatory amendment or a recommendation, and its number tells you nothing about which. Once a candidate can say that in one sentence, the distinctions stop needing memorisation, because they follow.

blocks.h: The tacit acceptance point, and why it is worth a line

blocks.p: Amendments to SOLAS and MARPOL enter into force by tacit acceptance: MSC or MEPC adopts an amendment, a date is set by which a stated proportion of Parties may object, and if the objections do not come the amendment is deemed accepted and enters into force on a later stated date. This is why the committees, not the Assembly, are where regulation is actually made - and it explains the three-date sequence adopted / deemed accepted / in force that examiners test repeatedly.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Describing IMO's purposes at length and never naming the organs. The stem says structure.
Omitting the sub-committee question entirely. It is the last sentence of limb (a) and it is asked separately for a reason.
Saying a sub-committee adopts or approves regulation. It prepares and reports; the parent committee approves; the committee or Assembly adopts.
Writing that the Council has 52 members. The enlargement under A.1152(32) is an amendment to the IMO Convention that was not in force at this sitting.
Giving four instrument types and no examples, when the stem says "give at least one example of each".
Saying a Code is always mandatory, or that a Resolution is always recommendatory. Both are false and both are examiner favourites.
Confusing a Protocol with an amendment. A protocol is a separate treaty a State accepts separately; an amendment adopted by tacit acceptance is not.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Asking how many members the Council has and how they are chosen, expecting the three categories and their 10 / 10 / 20 split.
Asking who appoints the Secretary-General. The Council appoints, subject to Assembly approval - not the Assembly alone.
Asking what the Council cannot do between Assembly sessions. It cannot make recommendations to Governments on maritime safety and pollution prevention; that is reserved to the Assembly.
Asking how MARPOL Annex VI came into existence, expecting the 1997 Protocol rather than an amendment.
Asking for an instrument that is partly mandatory, expecting the 2008 IS Code - Part A mandatory, Part B recommendatory.
Asking how often the Assembly meets. Once every two years in regular session.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which committee would adopt an amendment to the IGF Code, and which sub-committee would have prepared it?
A new SOLAS amendment is adopted today. Walk me through to the day it applies to your ship.
Your flag State has not ratified a convention. Does it apply to your ship in a port State that has?
Name an IMO instrument that is mandatory in part and recommendatory in part.
What is the difference between a resolution number beginning A. and one beginning MSC.?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: For limb (a), go top down and get narrower: ASSEMBLY - COUNCIL - COMMITTEES - SUB-COMMITTEES, and attach one fact to each: all members, every two years; forty, three categories, two years; five, and MSC and MEPC adopt; seven, and they prepare but never adopt. For limb (b), go hardest law to softest: CONVENTION - PROTOCOL - CODE - RESOLUTION, and ask of each what makes it binding?

ul: Convention on the International Maritime Organization, 1948, as amended - the constitution: Assembly, Council, Committees, Secretariat.
Resolution A.1152(32) - Council enlargement 40 to 52; not in force at this sitting.
SOLAS 1974 and the 1988 Protocol - convention and protocol examples.
MARPOL 73/78 and the 1997 Protocol - the protocol that introduced Annex VI.
Resolution A.741(18) - the ISM Code; SOLAS chapter IX - the hook that makes it mandatory.
Resolution MSC.267(85) - the 2008 IS Code, Part A mandatory and Part B recommendatory.
Resolution MEPC.328(76) - the revised MARPOL Annex VI, in force 1 November 2023.
Resolution A.1184(33) - revised guidelines on ISM implementation by Administrations, recommendatory.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: The IMO Convention itself is not held by the MIW corpus and was not read. The organs, their functions and the Council's three categories are stated from the Convention's architecture as authoritative secondary, and no Article number is asserted - which is deliberate, because an invented Article reference is worse than none.

Resolution A.1152(32) is the one live boundary and it is flagged. It was adopted in December 2021 and requires acceptance by two thirds of Members. It was not in force at February 2024, when the exact-stem MIW answer for that sitting was written, and it was re-checked and found still not in force for February 2025. It is flagged for a currency check because it is precisely the kind of fact that changes without any announcement reaching a ship.

The Secretary-General's date of taking office - 1 January 2024 - rests on the earlier MIW record and is not corpus-verified. It is stated as a tenure rather than as a recent event, which is the correction the twelve-month gap between the two sittings requires and the reason a sitting-relative sentence is never copied forward.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A two-limb question in two different registers. Limb (a) is INSTITUTIONAL and asks for the structure of IMO with FOUR named objects - Assembly, Council, main committees, sub-committees - and then asks a fifth, separate question about the ROLE sub-committees perform in supporting the committees. Limb (b) is CONCEPTUAL and asks for a definition of a convention followed by the differences between four instrument types, each with an example. The examiner is testing whether the candidate understands that legal force in this system is borrowed from the convention that points at an instrument.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, set as 8 + 8. Two equal limbs, so two equal regions. Within limb (a) the four organs and the sub-committee role question split the eight marks; within limb (b) the definition takes about a third and the four instrument types with their examples take the rest.

Then a convention defined as a binding treaty entering into force on its own conditions and binding only its parties, and Protocol, Code and Resolution distinguished from it with at least one example of each.

questions.understand_first: This question is two questions wearing one number, and they reward different things. Limb (a) is a map: who sits where, who decides what, and - the part most candidates drop - what the sub-committees are actually for. The answer to that last part is one idea: a sub-committee prepares and never adopts. It does the technical drafting a week-long committee has no time for, hands the text back up, and the committee or the Assembly does the adopting. That separation is deliberate: it keeps technical depth and treaty-making authority in different hands. Limb (b) is a hierarchy of legal force, and it has one organising idea too: force is borrowed, not intrinsic. A Convention binds because States accept it. A Protocol is a second treaty they accept separately. A Code is only a technical document until a convention says it is mandatory - which is why the 2008 IS Code can be mandatory in Part A and recommendatory in Part B. A Resolution is a container, and whether it is binding depends entirely on what is inside it. Hold those two ideas - prepare versus adopt, and borrowed force - and both limbs write themselves.

steps.title: The five main committees and what each owns
points: MSC - navigational safety, construction and equipment, manning for safety, dangerous goods, casualties, search and rescue, security
MEPC - all pollution prevention from ships, MARPOL and its Annexes, ballast water, anti-fouling, recycling, greenhouse gas
Legal Committee - legal matters within the Organization's scope, especially liability and compensation
Technical Cooperation Committee - technical assistance and capacity building
Facilitation Committee - removal of administrative burden, the FAL Convention
All five open to all Member States; MSC and MEPC are the two that adopt amendments to mandatory instruments, by tacit acceptance

steps.title: The seven sub-committees, and the role they perform
points: HTW, III, NCSR, PPR, SDC, SSE and CCC
Role is preparatory and technical - a committee sits about a week and remits detailed drafting to the sub-committee holding the expertise
The sub-committee develops draft text, guidelines and unified interpretations and reports back to its parent committee
A sub-committee adopts nothing: it prepares, the parent committee approves, the committee or Assembly adopts
That separation keeps technical depth and treaty-making authority in different hands

steps.title: What a convention is
points: A formal, legally binding treaty between States
Adopted at a diplomatic conference or by the Assembly, opened for signature, then ratification, acceptance, approval or accession
Enters into force only on the conditions written into the convention itself - typically a number of Contracting States and a share of world tonnage
Binds only the States party to it; reaches a ship only through the flag State's domestic law
Adoption, entry into force and application are three different dates
Example: SOLAS 1974

steps.title: Protocol, Code and Resolution - what distinguishes each, with examples
points: Protocol - a separate treaty amending or supplementing a parent convention, with its own ratification and entry into force. Example: the 1997 Protocol to MARPOL, which introduced Annex VI; the 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and Load Lines

Code - a detailed technical instrument, recommendatory of itself, mandatory only when a convention makes it so. Example: the ISM Code, mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX; the 2008 IS Code is mandatory in Part A and recommendatory in Part B

Resolution - the formal decision of the Assembly or a committee, and the vehicle by which an instrument is adopted or guidance issued; it can be either mandatory or recommendatory. Example: MEPC.328(76) adopting the revised MARPOL Annex VI, mandatory; A.1184(33) revised ISM implementation guidelines, recommendatory
The organising idea: legal force is borrowed from the convention that points at the instrument, never intrinsic to it

questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) top down and narrowing: ASSEMBLY (2) - COUNCIL (3) - COMMITTEES (4) - SUB-COMMITTEES (5), with one number on each: all members and every two years; forty in three categories; five, and two of them adopt; seven, and none of them adopts. Limb (b) hardest law to softest: CONVENTION (6) - PROTOCOL - CODE - RESOLUTION (7), asking each the same question - what makes this binding?

quick_revision.recall_15s: IMO = UN specialised agency for safety, security and pollution prevention. Assembly - all Members, meets every two years, budget and work programme, elects the Council. Council - 40 Members, two-year term, 10 / 10 / 20 in three categories; acts for the Assembly between sessions except recommendations to Governments; appoints the Secretary-General subject to Assembly approval. Five main committees - MSC, MEPC, Legal, Technical Cooperation, Facilitation; MSC and MEPC adopt amendments by tacit acceptance. Seven sub-committees - HTW, III, NCSR, PPR, SDC, SSE, CCC - they prepare and never adopt. Convention = binding treaty, in force on its own conditions, binds only its parties. Protocol = separate treaty amending a convention (1997 Protocol gave MARPOL Annex VI). Code = technical, mandatory only when a convention says so (ISM via SOLAS IX). Resolution = the vehicle, mandatory or recommendatory depending on content (MEPC.328(76) mandatory; A.1184(33) guidance).
critical_numbers: Assembly meets in regular session once every two years; the 33rd Assembly is operative at this sitting
Council: 40 Members in three categories of 10, 10 and 20, elected for a two-year term - resolution A.1152(32) would make it 52 but is not in force
Five main committees and seven sub-committees
The Council serving at this sitting was elected at the 33rd Assembly for the 2024-2025 biennium
quick_revision.critical_regulation: The Convention on the International Maritime Organization for the organs, read with SOLAS chapter IX as the worked example of a Convention conferring mandatory force on a Code - the pairing that carries limb (b)'s central idea that legal force is borrowed
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing that a Code is mandatory or that a Resolution is recommendatory as though either were a property of the document. Neither is: a Code is mandatory only where a Convention makes it so - and the 2008 IS Code is mandatory in Part A and recommendatory in Part B - while a Resolution takes its force from whatever it carries. Second trap: saying a sub-committee adopts anything. It prepares and reports; the parent committee approves; the committee or Assembly adopts.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the IMO structure and instruments question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What IMO is and its organs. 2 The Assembly. 3 The Council. 4 The five main committees. 5 The seven sub-committees and their role. 6 What a convention is. 7 Protocol, Code and Resolution with examples. Sections 1-5 are limb (a), 6-7 limb (b).
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (a) names four objects and then asks a fifth question about role; limb (b) needs a definition and then a four-way comparison with examples.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many Members does the IMO Council have, and how are they chosen?
retrieval_cards.answer: 40 Members, elected by the Assembly for a two-year term in three categories: ten States with the largest interest in providing international shipping services, ten with the largest interest in international seaborne trade, and twenty elected to secure representation of all major geographic areas. Resolution A.1152(32) would enlarge it to 52 but was not in force at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: The three categories and the 10/10/20 split are the marks; writing 52 is wrong for this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What role do the sub-committees perform, and what can they not do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Preparatory and technical. A parent committee sits for about a week and remits detailed work to the sub-committee with the relevant expertise, which develops draft text, guidelines and unified interpretations and reports back. A sub-committee adopts nothing - it prepares, the parent committee approves, and the committee or the Assembly adopts.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the last sentence of limb (a) and it is asked separately, so it must be answered separately.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a convention, and state what follows from the definition.
retrieval_cards.answer: A formal, legally binding treaty between States, adopted at a diplomatic conference or by the Assembly, opened for signature and then ratification, acceptance, approval or accession, entering into force only on the conditions written into it - typically a number of Contracting States representing a share of world tonnage. It binds only its parties, reaches a ship only through the flag State's own law, and its adoption, entry into force and application are three different dates.
retrieval_cards.why: The definition alone is one mark; the three consequences are where the rest of them are.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a Code differ from a Convention, and what makes a Code mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: A Convention is a treaty States accept individually. A Code is a detailed technical instrument with no legal force of its own; it becomes mandatory only when a convention makes it so. The ISM Code is mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX. Mandatory status can be partial - the 2008 Intact Stability Code is mandatory in Part A and recommendatory in Part B.
retrieval_cards.why: Legal force in this system is borrowed from the convention that points at the instrument, never intrinsic to it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is a Resolution mandatory or recommendatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: Either. A resolution is the formal decision of the Assembly or of a committee and is the vehicle by which an instrument is adopted or guidance issued, so its force depends entirely on what it carries. MEPC.328(76) adopting the revised MARPOL Annex VI is mandatory because MARPOL makes it so; A.1184(33), revised guidelines on ISM implementation by Administrations, is recommendatory.
retrieval_cards.why: Treating a resolution as one or the other is the commonest error in limb (b), and one example of each settles it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a Protocol, and give an example of what one achieved.
retrieval_cards.answer: A separate treaty instrument that amends, supplements or modifies a parent convention, used where the change is too large or structural for the ordinary amendment procedure. It has its own signature, ratification and entry-into-force conditions, so a State can be party to the convention and not to the protocol. The 1997 Protocol to MARPOL introduced Annex VI; the 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and to the Load Lines Convention introduced the harmonized system of survey and certification.
retrieval_cards.why: A protocol is a separate treaty accepted separately - not the same thing as an amendment adopted by tacit acceptance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain tacit acceptance and why it matters for where regulation is made.
retrieval_cards.answer: MSC or MEPC adopts an amendment to SOLAS or MARPOL and sets a date by which a stated proportion of Parties may object. If the objections do not come, the amendment is deemed accepted and enters into force on a later stated date. Because no State has to ratify anything, the committees rather than the Assembly are where binding regulation is actually made - and it produces the three-date sequence adopted, deemed accepted, in force.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why MSC and MEPC matter more to an engineer than the Assembly, and it is the mechanism behind every amendment status question.

QP2502 Q1 - the sub-committee (HTW) that prepares this work, and the tacit acceptance route that dates it

blocks.h: 1. What the human element is, and why STCW is where it is addressed

blocks.p: The human element is the whole of the human contribution to the safe, secure and clean operation of a ship - competence, health, alertness, communication, decision-making, leadership, culture and the organisational conditions a company creates around all of them. IMO's own position, in resolution A.947(23), is that it is a complex, multi-dimensional issue affecting safety, security and environmental protection across the entire spectrum of shipboard and shore-side activity.

STCW is the instrument that regulates it directly, and it does so in a particular way that is worth naming at the outset: SOLAS regulates the ship, MARPOL regulates the discharge, and STCW regulates the person. Every mechanism below is a variation on one method - define a competence, require it to be demonstrated, and require the conditions under which a person can exercise it.

blocks.h: 2. The competence-based architecture - the mechanism STCW actually uses

blocks.p: The single most important structural fact about STCW is that it is competence-based, not time-based. Part A of the Code is mandatory and sets out, for every function and level, a table with four columns:

ol: the competence itself;
the knowledge, understanding and proficiency (KUP) underpinning it;
the methods for demonstrating competence - approved training, service, simulator, workshop skills;
the criteria for evaluating it.

blocks.p: That fourth column is the human-element mechanism in miniature: it forces an assessor to judge observable performance rather than accept a certificate of attendance. Part B is guidance and is recommendatory.

blocks.h: 3. Chapter I - the controls on the person and on the company

ul: Regulation I/6 - training and assessment. Those who train, assess and supervise must themselves be qualified for the task.

Regulation I/8 - quality standards. Every Party must run a quality standards system covering training, assessment and certification, independently evaluated at intervals. This is what stops the competence tables becoming a paper exercise.
Regulation I/9 - medical standards. Fitness for duty begins with medical fitness, including eyesight and hearing.
Regulation I/11 - revalidation. Certificates are revalidated at intervals not exceeding five years on evidence of continued professional competence - the recognition that competence decays.

Regulation I/14 - responsibilities of companies. The one every engineer should be able to quote: the company must ensure seafarers are certificated and assigned in accordance with the Convention, that documentation is held, that seafarers receive ship-specific familiarization before being assigned duties, and that the ship's complement can co-ordinate its activities in an emergency. It places the human element on the employer, not only on the seafarer.

Chapter VI - safety familiarization, basic training, personal survival, fire fighting, first aid and personal safety and social responsibilities: the behavioural and communication floor for everyone on board.

blocks.h: 4. Chapter VIII - fitness for duty, rest and the alcohol limit

blocks.p: Regulation VIII/1 and Code section A-VIII/1 address the human element at its most physiological. Administrations must require, and take account of, the danger of fatigue, and must enforce:

ul: a minimum of 10 hours of rest in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period;
rest divided into no more than two periods, one of which is at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rest periods;
musters and drills conducted so as to minimise disturbance of rest periods;
posted watch schedules and records of daily hours of rest, so that compliance is monitorable rather than asserted;

a blood alcohol limit of 0.05 %, or 0.25 mg/l in breath, for masters, officers and other seafarers on designated safety, security and marine-environmental duties, together with drug and alcohol abuse prevention.

blocks.p: These limits are deliberately aligned with the ILO's Maritime Labour Convention and are enforced in practice through both. Section 9 below returns to that.

blocks.h: 5. Chapters VIII and III - watchkeeping principles and resource management

blocks.p: Regulation VIII/2 and Code section A-VIII/2 set the principles to be observed in keeping a watch. For the engine department these are explicitly human-element provisions: the chief engineer officer, in consultation with the master, determines the watch composition having regard to the ship's machinery, the mode of operation, and - expressly - the fitness for duty of the personnel available; watchkeepers must be familiar with the machinery and its controls, and a periodically unattended machinery space is treated as a mode requiring its own arrangements rather than as an absence of watchkeeping.

The 2010 Manila amendments added the competences that make the human element examinable rather than merely aspirational. Tables A-III/1 and A-III/2 now require engine-room resource management at operational level and use of leadership and managerial skills at management level - allocation and prioritisation of resources, effective communication, assertiveness, obtaining and maintaining situational awareness, consideration of team experience, workload and task management, and decision-making techniques. That is crew resource management under another name, made a certificated competence.

MSC.486(103) and MSC.487(103), in force 1 January 2023, are a current example of the same mechanism keeping pace with technology - a defined high-voltage threshold and formal recognition of the electro-technical officer in the operational-level definition.

blocks.h: 6. What is adopted and NOT yet in force - the mark most candidates miss

blocks.p: ⚠ Resolution MSC.560(108) introduces mandatory minimum training on the prevention of harassment, bullying and sexual assault into STCW Code table A-VI/1-4. It was adopted in 2024 and it enters into force on 1 January 2026. At this sitting it is adopted but NOT in force. Writing that STCW requires this training is wrong; writing that it will require it from 1 January 2026 is right, and shows the examiner exactly the distinction being tested.
The comprehensive review of STCW being taken forward through the HTW Sub-Committee is likewise in progress and not adopted. Nothing from it is law and nothing from it may be cited as such.

blocks.h: 7. The IMO fatigue guidance - what it is, and what it is not

blocks.p: The current IMO instrument is the Guidelines on fatigue, MSC.1/Circ.1598, approved by the Maritime Safety Committee at its 100th session and issued in 2019. It superseded MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001, and the revision was substantial rather than cosmetic: the science of sleep, circadian disruption and sleep debt had moved on by nearly two decades.

Its status must be stated before its content. It is a circular - recommendatory guidance, not law. It creates no obligation of its own. What makes fatigue management mandatory is the combination of STCW A-VIII/1, MLC Standard A2.3 and the ISM Code; the circular tells the industry how to discharge those duties intelligently. An answer that presents the Guidelines as a requirement has misdescribed the whole regime.

The Guidelines are addressed not to one actor but to several - the seafarer, the master and senior officers, the company and its shore-side management, the Administration, and those who design ships and organise work on board - on the explicit reasoning that fatigue cannot be managed by the person suffering it.

blocks.h: 8. Causes and effects - what the guidance asks the industry to recognise

rows: Insufficient and fragmented sleep
The dominant cause. A six-on / six-off watch system can satisfy the rest-hour rules and still make a consolidated sleep period impossible, so sleep debt accumulates over a voyage
Circadian disruption
Night watches, rotating schedules and repeated time-zone change put the work period against the body clock's lowest alertness, characteristically in the early hours
Workload and port turnaround
Intense port periods, surveys, inspections, bunkering and repairs concentrated into short stays, with the administrative burden falling on the same senior officers
Environmental stressors
Noise, vibration, ship motion, heat and humidity in machinery spaces - each degrades sleep quality even where sleep time is nominally available
Manning and organisation
Reduced complements, short-sea trading, unfamiliar routines, poor handovers, and non-work stressors such as fatigue from travel to join
Health and lifestyle
Diet, hydration, exercise, medical conditions including sleep apnoea, and the effect of alcohol and some medication on sleep quality

blocks.p: The effects are cognitive before they are physical, which is why fatigue is dangerous and hard to self-detect: reduced vigilance and situational awareness, slowed reaction, impaired judgement and risk assessment, memory lapses, degraded communication and teamwork, mood change - and, at the extreme, uncontrollable micro-sleeps. The fatigued person's own assessment of their capability is itself impaired.

blocks.h: 9. Mitigation and management - the three levels, and the statutory backstop

blocks.p: Company and shore-side - where the leverage actually is.

ul: Treat fatigue as an identified risk within the safety management system under the ISM Code, with controls, monitoring and review - element 6 (resources and personnel) and element 7 (shipboard operations) are the natural hooks.

Set realistic manning. The Minimum Safe Manning Document issued under SOLAS regulation V/14, following the principles in resolution A.1047(27), is a floor and not a target - and the assessment behind it is supposed to account for the actual workload.
Plan voyages, port calls, surveys and inspections so that they do not systematically collide with rest, and reduce the administrative burden placed on senior officers.
Maintain a non-punitive reporting culture so that fatigue and near-misses are reported rather than concealed - a punitive culture destroys the data the system depends on.

blocks.p: On board - what the Chief Engineer controls.

ul: Design watch and work patterns to protect at least one consolidated sleep period, rather than merely to satisfy the arithmetic of the rest-hour table.
Monitor the rest-hour records as data, not as a filing task. Persistent use of the exception provisions is a signal that the manning or the plan is wrong.

Schedule planned maintenance and drills to minimise rest disturbance, and manage the unattended-machinery-space call-out pattern deliberately - repeated night call-outs are a fatigue mechanism in themselves.
Use proper handovers, task rotation, controlled napping where the company policy permits it, and adequate rest before high-workload periods.
Set the example. A department in which the senior engineer visibly works through rest periods will not report fatigue.

blocks.p: Design and habitability. Accommodation location and insulation, noise - the Code on Noise Levels On Board Ships, resolution MSC.337(91), mandatory through SOLAS II-1/3-12 - vibration, lighting, ventilation, bunk quality and the layout of alarms and controls all determine whether the rest hours a seafarer is given are rest hours they can actually use.

The statutory backstop, stated precisely. Under MLC Standard A2.3 a Member must fix either a maximum of 14 hours of work in any 24-hour period and 72 hours in any 7-day period, or a minimum of 10 hours of rest in any 24 and 77 in any 7 days. Rest may be in no more than two periods, one at least 6 hours, with the interval between consecutive periods not exceeding 14 hours. Drills must be conducted so as to minimise the disturbance of rest periods and not induce fatigue. Where a seafarer is on call - the Standard names the unattended machinery space expressly - they must receive adequate compensatory rest if the normal rest period is disturbed by call-outs. A table of shipboard working arrangements is posted in the working language and in English, and records of daily hours are kept, copied to the seafarer and endorsed by the master. Exceptions are permitted only through authorised or registered collective agreements, and nothing in the Standard removes the master's authority to require work necessary for the immediate safety of the ship, persons on board or cargo, or to assist others in distress at sea.

The 2022 amendments to the MLC Code entered into force on 23 December 2024 - two months before this sitting - and are the latest set in force. The amendments approved at the 113th Session in June 2025 are later than this sitting and are not in force.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Two limbs at 8 marks each. Limb A fails most often through vagueness - a page about how important people are, with no regulation number in it. The fix is to organise it by chapter: I, VI, VIII and III, in that order, each with what it actually requires. Limb B fails through the opposite problem - a list of causes and a list of cures with no instrument named. The fix is to open limb B by identifying MSC.1/Circ.1598 and stating that it is guidance, then to give causes, effects and mitigation at three levels, and to close on the mandatory instruments that make any of it enforceable.

blocks.h: The single distinction that carries limb B

blocks.p: The IMO fatigue Guidelines are not law and the rest-hour limits are. A circular recommends; STCW A-VIII/1, MLC Standard A2.3 and the ISM Code oblige. Say that in one sentence early and the rest of the limb reads as an informed answer rather than a description of a pamphlet. It is also the honest position: MSC.1/Circ.1598 creates no duty on anyone.

blocks.h: Why the rest-hour rules are necessary but not sufficient

blocks.p: The most valuable single idea in this whole subject is that a schedule can be fully compliant and still be fatiguing. Six-on / six-off satisfies 10 hours in 24 and 77 in 7 - two six-hour blocks is exactly the maximum permitted division - and yet it can deny a consolidated sleep period for weeks. The rules set a floor on quantity; fatigue is driven by quality, timing and continuity. A candidate who states that, and then says the Guidelines exist precisely because compliance is not the same as alertness, has understood the topic rather than memorised it.

blocks.h: The company, not the seafarer, is the duty-bearer that matters

blocks.p: STCW regulation I/14 puts responsibility on the company; the ISM Code puts the system on the company; the MLC puts the hours obligation on the Member and the shipowner; and the IMO Guidelines are addressed to shore management as much as to the seafarer. The common thread is that fatigue is an organisational output, not a personal failing - and the fatigued individual is the one least able to assess it. Saying so is worth more than another paragraph of symptoms.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Writing limb A with no chapter or regulation numbers. Chapter I, VI, VIII and the chapter III competence tables are the skeleton.
Omitting regulation I/14. The company's responsibilities are the human-element provision most directly examinable at management level.
Presenting MSC.1/Circ.1598 as mandatory. It is recommendatory guidance.
Stating that STCW requires training on prevention of harassment and bullying. MSC.560(108) enters into force on 1 January 2026 and is not in force at this sitting.
Quoting only the 10 and 77 figures and omitting the two-period division, the six-hour block and the fourteen-hour interval - which is where most real non-compliance sits.
Forgetting the on-call compensatory rest provision, which is the one that bites hardest on an unattended machinery space and is therefore the most relevant of all to an engineer.
Treating the Minimum Safe Manning Document as a target rather than a floor.
Confusing the instruments: STCW and the fatigue Guidelines are IMO; the MLC is ILO.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Asking for the maximum interval between consecutive rest periods, expecting 14 hours - a figure that is easy to confuse with the 14-hour maximum work period in the MLC's alternative limb.
Asking whether a six-on / six-off system complies. It can; that is precisely why the question is asked.
Asking who the IMO fatigue Guidelines are addressed to, expecting more than "the seafarer".
Asking what STCW requires of the company, expecting regulation I/14 rather than a certificate list.
Asking for the blood alcohol limit - 0.05 %, or 0.25 mg/l in breath.
Asking what happens to rest when the ship is on UMS and the duty engineer is called out repeatedly. Adequate compensatory rest is required.
Asking whether the master can override the rest hours - yes, for the immediate safety of ship, persons or cargo, or to assist others in distress.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your third engineer's rest-hour record shows repeated use of the exception provision. What do you do?
How would you demonstrate to a port State control officer that fatigue is managed in your SMS?
What is engine-room resource management, and where is it required?
Your ship is UMS and the duty engineer was called out three times last night. What are your obligations?

Name an amendment to STCW that has been adopted but is not yet in force.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb A by chapter number, ascending: I - the company and the certificate controls; VI - the safety and behavioural floor; VIII - fitness, rest and watchkeeping; III - the resource-management and leadership competences. Limb B in three moves: NAME IT (MSC.1/Circ.1598, guidance not law) - CAUSES AND EFFECTS (sleep, circadian, workload, environment; cognitive before physical) - THREE LEVELS (company, ship, design), closing on the mandatory backstop: STCW A-VIII/1, MLC A2.3, ISM.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: The MLC figures in this answer were read; the STCW numbers were not. That asymmetry is stated rather than smoothed over. The MIW corpus holds the ILO consolidated Maritime Labour Convention including the 2022 amendments - whose own recorded rights position is that the instrument text is public domain - and Standard A2.3 was read directly. The STCW 2017 consolidated edition is held by path only and is recorded as not text-verified, so every STCW regulation, section and table number here is authoritative secondary.

MSC.1/Circ.1598 is not held and was not read. Its identity, its approval at MSC 100, its supersession of MSC/Circ.1014 and its multi-actor approach are authoritative secondary. Its internal module structure is deliberately not enumerated - listing the contents of a document that was not read is the precise failure the production protocol forbids, and nothing in the mark scheme requires it.

Two instruments moved in opposite directions across this sitting and both are flagged. The MLC 2022 amendments entered into force on 23 December 2024, two months before; MSC.560(108) does not enter into force until 1 January 2026, eleven months after. The MLC amendments approved at the 113th Session in June 2025 and the HTW comprehensive review of STCW are both post-sitting and are excluded. Five later MIW answers exist in this question's family, from June 2025 to April 2026; none was consulted for content, and the only donor used is the April 2024 one, which is earlier than this sitting.

notes: THE DONOR DIRECTION WAS CHOSEN, NOT ACCEPTED. The family has six built members and five of them are LATER sittings. QP2404-Q7 (April 2024) is the only earlier one and is the adopted donor. QP2506-Q8 (June 2025), QP2508-Q4 (August 2025), QP2601-Q9 (January 2026), QP2602-Q4 (February 2026) and QP2604-Q9 (April 2026) are named forward-contamination sweep targets and none was consulted for content.

ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE - MSC.560(108). Mandatory minimum training on prevention of harassment, bullying and sexual assault, STCW Code table A-VI/1-4, adopted 2024, ENTERS INTO FORCE 1 JANUARY 2026 - eleven months AFTER this sitting. The answer states it as a future requirement and never as a current one. Corpus-verified from the STCW instrument log.

RECENTLY IN FORCE - MLC 2022 AMENDMENTS. In force 23 December 2024, two months BEFORE this sitting. They are the latest set in force and the answer may and does rely on the Convention as so amended. The 2025 amendments approved at the 113th Session in June 2025 are POST-SITTING and are excluded; the corpus segregates them under not-yet-in-force.

IN FORCE AND USED - MSC.486(103) and MSC.487(103), the high-voltage definition and electro-technical officer recognition, entered into force 1 January 2023 and are part of the operative Code at this sitting.
IN PROGRESS, NOT LAW. The HTW comprehensive review of STCW is recorded by the corpus instrument log as in progress and not adopted. Nothing from it appears in this answer.
NO ASSEMBLY BOUNDARY BITES ON THE STCW CONTENT. A.947(23) is a 23rd Assembly instrument and A.1047(27) a 27th; both long precede this sitting. Any A.12xx(34) edition is post-sitting and none appears.
NO INDIAN STATUTE IS ENGAGED, so the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 / 2025 boundary does not bite on this question.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs that look like one topic and test two different things. Limb A is INSTRUMENT-STRUCTURAL: how does one named Convention and its Code act on the human element - and the expected answer is a set of mechanisms with chapter and regulation numbers, not an essay on the importance of people. Limb B is GUIDANCE AND MANAGEMENT: identify the IMO fatigue guidance, state what it is and is not, and set out causes, effects and mitigation. The examiner is testing whether the candidate can separate recommendatory guidance from mandatory limits, and whether they know that a compliant rest schedule can still be a fatiguing one.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, set as 8 + 8. Two equal limbs and therefore two equal regions. Within limb A the four chapters share the marks; within limb B the identification and status of the guidance is worth as much as any single list, and mitigation carries the most because it is where the management-level judgement shows.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For limb A: the competence-based Part A tables with their four columns; chapter I controls including regulation I/14 company responsibilities; chapter VI; chapter VIII fitness for duty with the rest-hour figures and the alcohol limit; the A-VIII/2 watchkeeping principles including the chief engineer's determination of watch composition; and the Manila-amendment resource-management and leadership competences in tables A-III/1 and A-III/2. For limb B: MSC.1/Circ.1598 named and correctly classed as recommendatory; causes and effects; and mitigation at company, shipboard and design level anchored to the mandatory instruments - STCW A-VIII/1, MLC Standard A2.3 and the ISM Code.
primary_source_plan: True Source corpus MLC-2006 holdings - Standard A2.3 read directly for the hours, the division rule, the on-call provision, the records and the master's override
True Source corpus STCW instrument log and _base-and-amendments for the amendment chain and its entry-into-force dates, in particular MSC.486/487(103) and MSC.560(108)
STCW Convention and Code 2017 edition as amended for the regulation, section and table numbers - authoritative secondary, base edition not text-verified
MSC.1/Circ.1598 by identity and status only - not held, not read, contents not enumerated
QP2502_TEMPORAL_AND_DONOR_ANCHOR.md section 4.1 for the two instruments that move across this sitting
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - the STCW human-element architecture has been stable since the 2010 Manila amendments, but two dated items sit close to this sitting on opposite sides: the MLC 2022 amendments came into force two months before it and MSC.560(108) comes into force eleven months after it. A comprehensive STCW review is also in progress, so this question's answer will need re-anchoring for any later sitting.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW for the instruments, MEDIUM for the reader. STCW and the fatigue Guidelines are IMO instruments and the MLC is an ILO one amended by a Special Tripartite Committee under Article XIII, entirely outside the IMO tacit-acceptance process - conflating the two is the jurisdictional error available here. No Indian statute is engaged.
technical_ambiguities: The stem writes 'Human Element issue' as though it were a single defined issue. It is a field rather than an issue, and the answer says so once without labouring it.

'The IMO guidance on fatigue' is singular. There is one current instrument - MSC.1/Circ.1598 - but the mandatory rest limits sit in STCW and the MLC, which are not guidance. The answer names the guidance, then names what actually obliges.

The rest-hour limits appear in both STCW A-VIII/1 and MLC Standard A2.3 in deliberately aligned but not identically drafted form. The MLC's alternative maximum-work limb (14 and 72) has no direct STCW counterpart and is easy to quote as though it were one, so the answer attributes each figure to its own instrument.
'Fatigue mitigation and management' invites a list of tips. The marks are in the three levels and in the point that the leverage sits ashore, not with the fatigued individual.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Nine numbered sections. Sections 1 to 6 are limb A: what the human element is and why STCW is the instrument, the competence-based mechanism, then chapters I, VIII and the watchkeeping and resource-management competences, closing on what is adopted and not yet in force. Sections 7 to 9 are limb B: identify the guidance and state its status, causes and effects in a table with the cognitive-first point, then mitigation at three levels closing on the mandatory backstop with the MLC figures stated precisely.

questions.understand_first: Two limbs, and the trap is that they look like the same question twice. Limb A is about an instrument and wants mechanisms with numbers on them. STCW addresses the human element by defining competences and requiring them to be demonstrated - Part A's tables have a column headed criteria for evaluating competence, which is the whole idea in three words - and by regulating the conditions under which a person can use that competence: medical fitness, revalidation, rest, sobriety and watchkeeping. The provision most candidates forget is regulation I/14, which puts the duty on the company. Limb B is about guidance, and its first mark is a status mark: MSC.1/Circ.1598 is recommendatory - it is not law. What obliges is STCW A-VIII/1, MLC Standard A2.3 and the ISM Code. Hold one further idea and limb B writes itself: a schedule can comply with every rest-hour rule and still be fatiguing, because the rules govern quantity while fatigue is driven by timing, continuity and quality of sleep. Six-on / six-off is the standing proof. That is why guidance exists at all, and why the leverage sits with the company ashore rather than with the person who is too tired to notice.

steps.title: What the human element is, and why STCW is where it is addressed
points: The whole human contribution - competence, health, alertness, communication, decision-making, leadership, culture and the organisational conditions around them
IMO's position in resolution A.947(23): a complex multi-dimensional issue affecting safety, security and environmental protection
SOLAS regulates the ship, MARPOL the discharge, STCW the person
One method throughout: define a competence, require it to be demonstrated, regulate the conditions for exercising it

steps.title: The competence-based architecture - the mechanism STCW actually uses
points: STCW is competence-based, not time-based
Part A is mandatory; each table gives competence, knowledge/understanding/proficiency, methods for demonstrating, and criteria for evaluating
The evaluation column forces judgement of observable performance rather than acceptance of attendance
Part B is recommendatory guidance

steps.title: Chapter I - the controls on the person and on the company
points: I/6 training and assessment; those who train and assess must be qualified for it
I/8 quality standards systems, independently evaluated - what stops the competence tables becoming a paper exercise
I/9 medical standards; I/11 revalidation at intervals not exceeding five years on continued professional competence
I/14 responsibilities of companies - certification, assignment, documentation, ship-specific familiarization, ability to co-ordinate in an emergency
Chapter VI - familiarization, basic training, and personal safety and social responsibilities

steps.title: Chapter VIII - fitness for duty, rest and the alcohol limit
points: Regulation VIII/1 and section A-VIII/1 - Administrations must take account of the danger of fatigue
Minimum 10 hours rest in any 24 and 77 in any 7 days
No more than two rest periods, one at least 6 hours, interval not exceeding 14 hours
Musters and drills conducted to minimise disturbance of rest
Posted watch schedules and records of daily hours of rest
Blood alcohol limit 0.05 %, or 0.25 mg/l in breath, with drug and alcohol abuse prevention

steps.title: Chapters VIII and III - watchkeeping principles and resource management
points: Regulation VIII/2 and section A-VIII/2 - principles to be observed in keeping a watch
The chief engineer officer, in consultation with the master, determines watch composition having regard to machinery, mode of operation and fitness for duty
A periodically unattended machinery space is a mode with its own arrangements, not an absence of watchkeeping
The 2010 Manila amendments added engine-room resource management to table A-III/1 and use of leadership and managerial skills to table A-III/2
Those competences cover resource allocation, communication, assertiveness, situational awareness, workload management and decision-making - crew resource management made certificable
MSC.486(103) and MSC.487(103), in force 1 January 2023, added the high-voltage definition and recognition of the electro-technical officer

steps.title: What is adopted and NOT yet in force - the mark most candidates miss
points: MSC.560(108) makes training on prevention of harassment, bullying and sexual assault mandatory in table A-VI/1-4
It was adopted in 2024 and enters into force on 1 January 2026 - after this sitting
Write that STCW WILL require it from that date, never that it does require it
The HTW comprehensive review of STCW is in progress and not adopted; nothing from it is law

steps.title: The IMO fatigue guidance - what it is, and what it is not
points: MSC.1/Circ.1598, Guidelines on fatigue, approved at MSC 100 and issued in 2019, superseding MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001
It is a circular - recommendatory guidance, creating no obligation of its own
What obliges is STCW A-VIII/1, MLC Standard A2.3 and the ISM Code; the Guidelines say how to discharge those duties
Addressed to several actors - seafarer, master and senior officers, company and shore management, Administration, and ship designers - because fatigue cannot be managed by the person suffering it

steps.title: Causes and effects - what the guidance asks the industry to recognise
points: Insufficient and fragmented sleep is the dominant cause; a compliant watch system can still deny a consolidated sleep period
Circadian disruption from night watches, rotating schedules and time-zone change
Workload and port turnaround, surveys, inspections and administrative burden concentrated on senior officers
Environmental stressors - noise, vibration, motion, heat and humidity - degrade sleep quality even where sleep time exists
Manning, short-sea trading, poor handovers, health and lifestyle factors

Effects are cognitive before physical: reduced vigilance and situational awareness, slowed reaction, impaired judgement, memory lapses, degraded communication, micro-sleeps - and self-assessment is itself impaired

steps.title: Mitigation and management - the three levels, and the statutory backstop
points: Company: fatigue as an identified risk in the SMS under the ISM Code, elements 6 and 7; realistic manning with the Minimum Safe Manning Document under SOLAS V/14 and A.1047(27) treated as a floor; voyage and port planning; reduced administrative burden; non-punitive reporting

Shipboard: protect a consolidated sleep period rather than satisfy arithmetic; read rest-hour records as data; schedule maintenance and drills to minimise disturbance; manage the UMS call-out pattern; proper handovers and controlled napping; set the example
Design: accommodation, noise under MSC.337(91) and SOLAS II-1/3-12, vibration, lighting, ventilation and alarm layout determine whether rest hours are usable

Statutory backstop under MLC Standard A2.3: either maximum 14 hours work in 24 and 72 in 7, or minimum 10 hours rest in 24 and 77 in 7; no more than two rest periods, one at least 6 hours, interval not exceeding 14 hours; drills to minimise disturbance; adequate compensatory rest for on-call seafarers, the unattended machinery space named expressly; posted table and daily records endorsed by the master; exceptions only by authorised collective agreement; and the master's overriding authority for immediate safety
The 2022 MLC amendments entered into force 23 December 2024 and are the latest set in force; the 2025 amendments are later than this sitting

questions.memory_cue: Limb A by CHAPTER NUMBER ASCENDING - ONE the company and the certificate controls (3), SIX the safety floor (3), EIGHT fitness, rest and watchkeeping (4, 5), THREE the resource-management competences (5) - then the one that is NOT YET LAW (6). Limb B in three moves: NAME IT AND CLASS IT (7), CAUSES AND EFFECTS (8), THREE LEVELS PLUS THE BACKSTOP (9).

quick_revision.recall_15s: STCW addresses the human element by competence, not time. Part A tables: competence, KUP, methods of demonstrating, criteria for evaluating. Ch I - I/6 training, I/8 quality standards, I/9 medical, I/11 revalidation every 5 years, I/14 company responsibilities and ship-specific familiarization. Ch VI - basic training and PSSR. Ch VIII - A-VIII/1 fitness for duty: 10 h rest in 24, 77 h in 7, no more than two periods, one at least 6 h, interval not over 14 h, records posted, alcohol 0.05 %. A-VIII/2 watchkeeping - the chief engineer sets watch composition having regard to fitness for duty. Ch III tables A-III/1 and A-III/2 - engine-room resource management and leadership and managerial skills (Manila 2010). MSC.560(108) harassment training - in force 1 Jan 2026, NOT yet. Fatigue: MSC.1/Circ.1598 (2019), GUIDANCE not law, superseded MSC/Circ.1014. Mandatory backstop = STCW A-VIII/1 + MLC A2.3 + ISM. MLC A2.3: 14/72 work OR 10/77 rest; on-call in a UMS space gets compensatory rest. Key idea: a compliant schedule can still be fatiguing.
critical_numbers: Rest: minimum 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period - in both STCW A-VIII/1 and MLC Standard A2.3
Rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rest periods
MLC Standard A2.3 alternative limb: maximum 14 hours of work in any 24-hour period and 72 hours in any 7-day period
Blood alcohol limit 0.05 %, or 0.25 mg/l in breath
Certificates revalidated at intervals not exceeding five years
MSC.560(108) enters into force 1 January 2026 - after this sitting; the MLC 2022 amendments entered into force 23 December 2024, before it
quick_revision.critical_regulation: STCW Code section A-VIII/1 read with MLC 2006 Standard A2.3 - the deliberately aligned mandatory rest regime that makes fatigue management enforceable, as against MSC.1/Circ.1598, which is recommendatory guidance and obliges no one
quick_revision.major_trap: Presenting MSC.1/Circ.1598 as mandatory. It is a circular and it creates no duty; what obliges is STCW A-VIII/1, MLC Standard A2.3 and the ISM Code. Second trap, and the one that costs a whole mark at this sitting: writing that STCW requires training on the prevention of harassment and bullying. MSC.560(108) enters into force on 1 January 2026 and is adopted but not in force here. Third: assuming a rest-hour-compliant schedule cannot be fatiguing - six-on / six-off satisfies 10 in 24 and 77 in 7 and can still deny a consolidated sleep period.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the human element and fatigue question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the human element is and why STCW. 2 The competence-based mechanism. 3 Chapter I controls and the company. 4 Chapter VIII fitness for duty. 5 Watchkeeping and resource management. 6 Adopted but not in force. 7 Name the fatigue guidance and class it. 8 Causes and effects. 9 Mitigation at three levels plus the statutory backstop. Sections 1-6 are limb A, 7-9 limb B.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb A is organised by chapter number so nothing is dropped; limb B opens on status because the first mark there is a status mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the STCW and MLC rest-hour limits in full.
retrieval_cards.answer: Minimum 10 hours of rest in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. Rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which is at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive rest periods must not exceed 14 hours. The MLC allows a Member to fix the alternative instead: maximum 14 hours of work in any 24 and 72 hours in any 7 days.
retrieval_cards.why: Most candidates give 10 and 77 and stop. The division rule and the 14-hour interval are where real non-compliance sits.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does STCW regulation I/14 require, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: It places responsibility on the company: to ensure seafarers are certificated and assigned in accordance with the Convention, that the required documentation is held, that seafarers receive ship-specific familiarization before being assigned duties, and that the ship's complement can co-ordinate its activities in an emergency. It matters because it puts the human element on the employer, not only on the seafarer.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the human-element provision most directly examinable at management level and the one most often omitted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the IMO guidance on fatigue mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. MSC.1/Circ.1598, the Guidelines on fatigue issued in 2019, is a circular and is recommendatory - it creates no obligation of its own. What is mandatory is STCW section A-VIII/1, MLC Standard A2.3 and the ISM Code; the Guidelines explain how to discharge those duties intelligently.
retrieval_cards.why: The first mark in limb B is a status mark, and presenting guidance as law misdescribes the whole regime.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can a fully rest-hour-compliant watch system still be fatiguing?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the rules govern the quantity of rest and fatigue is driven by its timing, continuity and quality. Six-on / six-off gives two six-hour rest blocks, which is exactly the maximum division permitted, and satisfies 10 hours in 24 and 77 in 7 - while denying any consolidated sleep period, so sleep debt accumulates across a voyage.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the single idea that separates an informed answer from a compliance checklist, and it explains why the Guidelines exist at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship is UMS and the duty engineer is called out repeatedly at night. What does the regime require?
retrieval_cards.answer: MLC Standard A2.3 provides expressly that where a seafarer is on call, such as when a machinery space is unattended, they must have an adequate compensatory rest period if the normal rest period is disturbed by call-outs. As Chief Engineer you would also treat the call-out pattern as a fatigue signal, review it as data rather than paperwork, and address the underlying defect or manning cause through the safety management system.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the rest provision most specific to an engineer, and it is named in the Standard rather than inferred.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is engine-room resource management and where is it required?
retrieval_cards.answer: The non-technical competence of using all available resources - people, equipment and information - effectively: allocation and prioritisation of resources, effective communication, assertiveness, obtaining and maintaining situational awareness, consideration of team experience, and workload and decision-making management. It was introduced by the 2010 Manila amendments into STCW Code table A-III/1, with use of leadership and managerial skills at management level in table A-III/2.
retrieval_cards.why: It is crew resource management made a certificated competence, and it is the clearest example of STCW addressing the human element directly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name a human-element STCW amendment that is adopted but not in force at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution MSC.560(108), which makes training on the prevention of harassment, bullying and sexual assault a mandatory minimum requirement in STCW Code table A-VI/1-4. It was adopted in 2024 and enters into force on 1 January 2026. At February 2025 it is adopted and not in force, so it must be described as a future requirement.
retrieval_cards.why: Adopted, accepted and in force are three different things, and this is the live example on this paper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which fatigue instruments are IMO and which are ILO?
retrieval_cards.answer: STCW and MSC.1/Circ.1598 are IMO instruments. The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006, including Standard A2.3, is an ILO instrument, adopted by the International Labour Conference and amended by the Special Tripartite Committee under Article XIII - a process entirely separate from IMO's tacit acceptance. The ISM Code is IMO, mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX.
retrieval_cards.why: The rest-hour limits are deliberately aligned across two organisations, which makes it easy to attribute a figure to the wrong one.

questions.short_title: Integrated Safety Management System and the ISM Code
questions.text_verbatim: a) Explain the concept of the Integrated Safety Management System (ISMS) and its significance in maritime operations. How does ISMS ensure compliance with the international Safety Management (ISM) Code? (10) b) Discuss the key elements of ISMS that align with the ISM Code to enhance safety, environmental protection, and operational efficiency on board ship. (6)

subparts.text: Explain the concept of the Integrated Safety Management System (ISMS), its significance in maritime operations, and how it ensures compliance with the ISM Code.
Discuss the key elements of ISMS that align with the ISM Code to enhance safety, environmental protection and operational efficiency on board ship.

decomposition: What the printed term ISMS is, and what it is not - the ISM Code creates a safety management system, not an 'integrated' one
The ISM Code itself - instrument, hook, objectives and functional requirements
What integration actually means in practice, and the systems an SMS is integrated with
Why integration matters operationally - the significance the stem asks for
How the arrangement ensures ISM compliance - the certification and verification chain that tests it
The key elements that align with the Code, mapped to safety

The same elements mapped to operational efficiency
reuse_evidence: DERIVED TIER C AGAINST THE POST-QP2501 CORPUS (21 papers contributing donors, 189 built answers of 252). No family member exists for this stem, solved or unsolved: build_families returns a family size of one.
