No certificate, no pass or fail, no power to detain - just a report published to charterers with the operator's response beside it. But a poor record ends the ship's employment. SIRE inspects the ship; TMSA assesses the office. Current generation SIRE 2.0 - risk-based, question pool, hardware / process / human element, digital and photographic, crew must demonstrate. Process: screen - Pre-Inspection Questionnaire - inspector assigned - opening meeting - documents - physical inspection - crew demonstration - closing meeting - report published - operator comments with root cause and corrective action. Chief Engineer, three tenses. BEFORE: no leaks, dry bilges, insulation intact and oil-free, critical equipment list and standby testing, inert gas system (deck seal, PV breaker, O2 analysers, alarms and trips), pump room gas detection, 15 ppm alarm and no bypass, sludge reconciles with the ORB, emergency generator and fire pump run, quick-closing valves and dampers operated, steering changeover, PMS with no unexplained overdue jobs, and close out the last report. DURING: accompany, produce records promptly, never conceal or falsify. AFTER: root cause, corrective action, into the SMS under ISM 9 and 12, verify closure.
critical_numbers: There is no pass mark and no certificate - the output is a report and the charterer's decision
SIRE is the ship-level programme and TMSA the company-level one - two instruments, two subjects
ISM element 10 requires critical equipment and systems to be identified and standby arrangements regularly tested
The 15 ppm oily-water separating equipment must have a working alarm and automatic stopping device and no bypass, and the sludge account must reconcile with Oil Record Book Part I
quick_revision.critical_regulation: There is no regulation - and that is the point. Vetting rests on OCIMF industry programmes and on contract, while the statutory anchors an inspector actually tests against are the ISM Code elements 9, 10 and 12, MARPOL Annex I record-keeping and the SOLAS chapter II-2 machinery-space fire-safety and inert gas requirements
quick_revision.major_trap: Describing vetting as a statutory inspection, or saying a ship passes or fails it. There is no certificate, no pass, no fail and no power to detain - only a published report and a commercial decision. Second trap, and the one the examiner is really probing: what to do about a defect you already know about. A defect that is recorded, risk-assessed and being managed is an ordinary finding; the same defect concealed, or a record tidied before the visit, is a finding about integrity and the ship does not recover from it. Third: naming SIRE and forgetting TMSA, which is what turns a description of a visit into an understanding of the system.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the tanker vetting question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What vetting is - commercial not statutory. 2 Purpose. 3 The instruments: SIRE, TMSA, CDI, ISGOTT. 4 The process in sequence. 5 Chief Engineer before. 6 Chief Engineer during. 7 Chief Engineer after. 8 Relationship to the statutory regime and what to avoid. Sections 1-4 answer purpose and process; 5-7 answer the Chief Engineer's role in three tenses.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem names two tasks, so the answer splits evenly; before/during/after guarantees the after stage - root cause and corrective action - actually gets written.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a vetting inspection differ from a port State control inspection?
retrieval_cards.answer: Port State control is statutory: a State acting under conventions given force in national law, producing deficiencies and the power to detain. Vetting is commercial: an industry programme run for charterers and terminals, producing a report with no certificate, no pass or fail and no power to detain. The vetting standards frequently sit above the convention minimum, and a poor vetting record can end the ship's employment even though it cannot stop her sailing.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the distinction the whole question turns on, and answering vetting from a PSC template inverts it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between SIRE and TMSA?
retrieval_cards.answer: SIRE is the ship-level inspection programme - an accredited inspector examines the individual ship and the report is published to subscribing charterers. TMSA is the company-level self assessment, in which the operator assesses its own shore management against elements at staged levels of maturity and charterers review it alongside the ship's reports. SIRE looks at the ship; TMSA looks at the office.
retrieval_cards.why: The industry learnt that the shore organisation predicts performance better than one well-presented visit, which is why both exist.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the Chief Engineer do about the inert gas system before a vetting inspection?
retrieval_cards.answer: Check the deck water seal level and operation; confirm the pressure-vacuum breaker is correctly charged; check the non-return and deck isolation arrangements; confirm the oxygen analysers are calibrated with records available; test and record the low- and high-oxygen alarms, the low-pressure alarm and the automatic trips; and check scrubber and blower condition.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the most tanker-specific machinery item in the question and the one most often omitted from a generic engine-room answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The inspector is due tomorrow and you have a known machinery defect. What do you do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Nothing that hides it. Ensure the defect is properly recorded in the planned maintenance system and the defect list, that a risk assessment and interim controls are in place, that it has been reported to the company, and that a repair plan with parts and a date exists. Then show it. A recorded, risk-assessed, managed defect is an ordinary finding; a concealed one is a finding about integrity and the ship does not recover from it.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the judgement the examiner is really probing, and it is the same answer under ISM as under vetting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must the operator do after the report is issued, and what part does the Chief Engineer play?
retrieval_cards.answer: The operator must comment on each observation, stating the root cause and the corrective action, and those comments are published alongside the report. The Chief Engineer supplies the real root cause for machinery observations rather than a restatement of the finding, proposes corrective and preventive action with an owner and a date, routes it through the safety management system under ISM elements 9 and 12, verifies that closure is real and effective, and checks whether the finding applies to sister ships.
retrieval_cards.why: Charterers read the response as evidence about the office, so a thin response damages the operator more than the observation did.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is a repeat observation so damaging?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it says the previous corrective action was cosmetic. A single observation is a defect; the same observation twice is evidence that the management system did not correct it, which is a finding about the operator rather than about the ship - and that is precisely what a charterer is screening for.
retrieval_cards.why: Closing out the previous report is the highest-value single item of preparation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can a modern vetting inspection not be rehearsed?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the questions are drawn from a pool rather than a fixed list, so no two inspections are the same; each is examined for its hardware, its process and its human element, so working equipment with no procedure or an untrained operator still produces a finding; the record is photographic; and the crew are asked to demonstrate rather than describe. The only viable preparation is continuous readiness.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why the correct posture is a ship always ready because always maintained - which is what the ISM Code requires anyway.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which pollution-prevention items will an inspector examine in the engine room, and why is this area different?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 15 ppm oily-water separating equipment with a functioning alarm and automatic stopping device and no bypass of any kind, the incinerator, the sewage plant, the ballast water management equipment, and whether the sludge and bilge account reconciles with Oil Record Book Part I. This area is different because an observation here is not merely commercial - it is evidence of a potential MARPOL offence.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the one part of the engineer's scope where a vetting finding can have criminal rather than commercial consequences.

blocks.h: 1. What admiralty law is, and the feature that makes it different

blocks.p: Admiralty law is the body of law by which a court determines maritime claims and exercises a jurisdiction over vessels themselves. Its defining feature - the one that separates it from every other kind of civil litigation - is the action in rem: the claim is brought against the ship, and the ship can be arrested and, if necessary, sold by the court to satisfy the claim.

The commercial reason for this is straightforward. A shipowner may be a single-ship company registered in a jurisdiction the claimant will never reach, its directors unknown and its assets nil. The one asset that is certainly present, identifiable and valuable is the ship - and she is only present for as long as the cargo takes to discharge. An in rem jurisdiction lets a claimant obtain security from the asset in the few days it is within reach, which is why arrest, and not judgment, is the practical objective of most admiralty proceedings.

blocks.h: 2. The statute in force, and what it replaced

blocks.p: The governing statute is the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - Act 22 of 2017, dated 9 August 2017 and brought into force on 1 April 2018. Its long title states its purpose exactly: to consolidate the laws relating to admiralty jurisdiction, legal proceedings in connection with vessels, their arrest, detention, sale and other matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

What it replaced was colonial and fragmented. Section 17(1) repeals the application in India of the Admiralty Court Act, 1840, the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty (India) Act, 1891, and the provisions of the Letters Patent, 1865 so far as they applied to the admiralty jurisdiction of the Bombay, Calcutta and Madras High Courts. Until 2018, in other words, an Indian admiralty claim was governed by nineteenth-century English statutes, and only three High Courts could hear one.

Section 17 also preserves continuity: proceedings pending immediately before commencement continue, but are adjudicated under the 2017 Act, and things done under the repealed enactments are deemed done under the corresponding provisions of the new one.

blocks.h: 3. The scope of the jurisdiction - which courts, what waters, what vessels

ul: Which courts (section 2(1)(e)). The jurisdiction is High Court jurisdiction, and the Act names them: Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, Karnataka, Gujarat, Orissa and Kerala, and the High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad for Telangana and Andhra Pradesh - or any other High Court as may be notified by the Central Government. That last clause is what allows the list to grow. The extension from three chartered High Courts to a notifiable list of coastal High Courts is one of the Act's principal achievements.

What waters (section 3). Jurisdiction over all maritime claims vests in the respective High Courts and is exercisable over the waters up to and including the territorial waters of their respective jurisdictions. The proviso matters: the Central Government may, by notification, extend that jurisdiction up to the limit defined in section 2 of the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976.

What vessels (section 2(1)(l)). 'Vessel' is defined broadly - any ship, boat, sailing vessel or other description of vessel used or constructed for use in navigation by water, whether propelled or not, and expressly including a barge, lighter or other floating vessel, a hovercraft and an off-shore industry mobile unit. The breadth is deliberate: it captures the craft that would otherwise fall outside a narrow definition of 'ship'.
Against whom (sections 5 and 6). The Act provides for both action in rem, by arrest of the vessel, and action in personam against the person liable - so a claimant is not confined to one route.

blocks.h: 4. What may be claimed - maritime claims, and the maritime liens

blocks.p: Section 4 enumerates the maritime claims over which a High Court may exercise jurisdiction. It is a long, closed list, and its coverage is the practical measure of the Act's scope. It includes disputes over possession or ownership of a vessel and between co-owners over her employment or earnings; mortgages and charges; loss or damage caused by the operation of a vessel; loss of life or personal injury in direct connection with her operation; loss of or damage to goods; agreements for the carriage of goods or passengers and for the use or hire of a vessel, whether in a charterparty or otherwise; salvage, including special compensation where the vessel or her cargo threatened damage to the environment; towage and pilotage; goods, materials, provisions, bunker fuel, equipment including containers, and services supplied to the vessel for her operation, management, preservation or maintenance; her construction, repair, conversion or equipping; port, harbour, canal, dock and light dues; claims by the master or crew for wages, repatriation cost and social insurance contributions - and this one is expressed notwithstanding sections 150 and 151 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; disbursements made on behalf of the vessel; particular and general average; disputes over a contract for the sale of the vessel; and insurance premium, including mutual insurance calls.
A maritime lien is a narrower and far more powerful thing. Section 9 recognises five, and gives their inter se priority in this order:

ol: wages and other sums due to the master, officers and other members of the complement, including repatriation costs and social insurance contributions;
loss of life or personal injury, on land or water, in direct connection with the operation of the vessel;
salvage, including special compensation;
port, canal and other waterway dues, pilotage dues and other statutory dues related to the vessel;
claims in tort arising out of loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel, other than loss or damage to cargo and containers carried on her.

blocks.p: Two features of the lien are what make it formidable, and both are examinable. First, it attaches to the vessel and follows her: section 9(2) provides that it continues notwithstanding any change of ownership, of registration or of flag - so a buyer takes the ship with the lien on her. Second, it is time-limited: it is extinguished after one year unless the vessel has been arrested or seized within that period and the arrest has led to a forced sale by the High Court - except for a wage claim, where the period is two years from the date the sum falls due. The period runs continuously from discharge from the vessel for a wage claim and from when the claim arises for the others, with time spent under arrest excluded.

No maritime lien attaches for oil pollution or hazardous and noxious substance damage compensable under other law, or for damage from the radioactive properties of nuclear fuel or waste - section 9(4). And section 10 sets the order of priority of claims overall: first claims secured by a maritime lien, then registered mortgages and charges of the same nature, then all other claims - claims within a category ranking equally, and salvage claims ranking in inverse order of time, the later salvor first.

blocks.h: 5. Arrest, security and the protections against its abuse

ul: Arrest in rem (section 5(1)). The High Court may order the arrest of a vessel within its jurisdiction to provide security against a maritime claim, where it has reason to believe that the person who owned her when the claim arose is liable and still owns her; or that the demise charterer at that time is liable and is now the demise charterer or the owner; or that the claim is based on a mortgage or similar charge; or that it relates to ownership or possession; or that it is against the owner, demise charterer, manager or operator and is secured by a maritime lien under section 9.

Sister-ship arrest (section 5(2)). Another vessel may be arrested in lieu of the one against which the claim is made - except for a claim under section 4(1)(a), a dispute about possession or ownership, which is inherently ship-specific.

In personam and its restrictions (sections 6 and 7). The High Court may proceed in personam, but section 7 restricts that route where the claim arises from a collision, from a manoeuvre or its omission, or from non-compliance with the collision regulations made under section 285 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - requiring, among other conditions, that the cause of action arise wholly or in part in India.

Protection against wrongful arrest (section 11). This is the counterweight and it is real. As a condition of arrest or of maintaining one, the court may require the claimant to give an unconditional undertaking or security for loss or damage the defendant may suffer - expressly including where the arrest was wrongful or unjustified or where excessive security was demanded. The person providing security may apply to have it reduced, modified or cancelled.

Abandonment (section 11(3)). If the owner or demise charterer abandons the vessel after arrest, the High Court shall cause her to be auctioned and the proceeds dealt with, within forty-five days of arrest or abandonment - extendable by a further thirty days for reasons recorded in writing. A practical provision: an abandoned ship deteriorates, incurs port dues and endangers her crew.

Clean title (section 8). Rights vest on a court sale free of prior claims, which is what makes the court's sale worth anything to a buyer - and therefore what makes the security worth anything to the claimant.

Procedure and appeal. The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 applies so far as not inconsistent (section 12); an appeal lies from any judgment, decree, final or interim order of a single Judge to a Division Bench of the same High Court (section 14); and the Supreme Court may transfer proceedings (section 15).

blocks.h: 6. The significance - why the Act matters

ul: It ended reliance on repealed colonial English statutes. Indian admiralty jurisdiction had rested on nineteenth-century Acts that England itself had long replaced, supplemented by judicial development. The 2017 Act supplies a modern statutory basis.
It widened access from three High Courts to a notifiable list of coastal High Courts, so a claimant is no longer confined to Bombay, Calcutta or Madras and can proceed where the ship actually is.

It codified maritime claims and maritime liens, with a stated priority order and stated limitation periods. Financiers, insurers, bunker suppliers, crew and salvors can now assess where they stand before they are owed money rather than afterwards.

It aligned Indian law with the international pattern - the structure of the claims list, the liens and the arrest regime follows the model of the modern international arrest and maritime-lien conventions, which makes Indian practice legible to foreign parties even though the alignment is by drafting rather than by treaty.
It balanced the claimant's remedy against the owner's protection. Arrest is commercially devastating, and section 11's wrongful-arrest security is what keeps it a remedy rather than a weapon.

It strengthens India as a maritime forum. A predictable arrest jurisdiction across the coast supports ship finance, repair, bunkering and supply, because a supplier who can arrest is a supplier who will extend credit.

For a ship's officer it is directly practical. Wages carry the first maritime lien and a two-year period rather than one - so an unpaid crew has the strongest claim in the queue, ahead even of the mortgagee bank.

blocks.h: 7. Assessors - what section 13 actually provides

blocks.p: Section 13 is headed 'Assistance of assessors', and it has two subsections. It is short, and reading it closely is the whole of limb (b).

ul: Section 13(1). Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the Central Government shall appoint by notification a list of assessors with such qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters, the nature of the duties to be performed by them, the fees to be paid to them and other ancillary or incidental matters for the purposes of the Act, in the manner as may be prescribed.
Section 13(2). The appointment of assessors shall not be construed as a bar to the examination of expert witnesses by any of the parties in any admiralty proceeding.

blocks.p: ⚠ Three things follow, and the first is the one the question is really testing.

ol: The Act does not state the qualifications. It requires that the assessors have qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters, and it leaves what those qualifications are to be fixed 'in the manner as may be prescribed'. Section 2(1)(j) defines 'prescribed' as prescribed by rules made by the Central Government under this Act, and the rule-making power is in section 16. The Act creates the mechanism and delegates the criteria. A candidate who recites a list of qualifications as though the statute contained one is describing delegated legislation that the statute does not print.

The appointment is central, not case-by-case. It is the Central Government that appoints, by notification, a list - a standing panel from which a court can draw - rather than each High Court appointing its own expert in each case.

The assessor does not displace the expert witness. Subsection (2) exists precisely to prevent the argument that, an assessor having been appointed, a party may not call its own expert. Both routes remain open.

blocks.h: 8. The role of assessors in practice, and how they differ from expert witnesses

blocks.p: An admiralty case turns on questions a judge cannot be expected to have lived: whether a manoeuvre was good seamanship, whether a machinery failure was the result of a defect or of misoperation, whether a salvage service was reasonably rendered, whether cargo damage was caused by a failure of care or by inherent vice, what a vessel is worth. An assessor is a technical adviser to the court, appointed so that the court can engage with such matters properly.

blocks.p: Section 13(2) settles the question the table might otherwise raise: both may feature in the same case. The assessor helps the court to understand and to weigh the technical evidence; the parties remain free to call their own experts to give it.

The concept is not new to Indian law or to admiralty. It is the statutory descendant of the practice by which admiralty courts have long sat with nautical advisers, and it has a domestic analogue in the assessors who sit with courts in shipping-casualty inquiries. What the 2017 Act does is put the admiralty version on a modern statutory footing with a centrally notified panel.

blocks.h: 9. Qualifications - what the Act says, and what it therefore contemplates

blocks.p: The honest and complete answer to the qualifications half of limb (b) has three parts, and giving all three is worth more than a confident invented list.

ol: What the Act requires. That the person appointed has qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters. That is the statutory standard, and it is the only one section 13 states.

Where the detail lives. In rules made by the Central Government under section 16, because section 13(1) fixes the qualifications, the nature of duties, the fees and ancillary matters 'in the manner as may be prescribed' and section 2(1)(j) defines 'prescribed' accordingly. The criteria are delegated legislation, not statute.

What the section contemplates. Given a standard expressed as qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters, the panel it contemplates is drawn from those whose professional standing rests on exactly that - master mariners and chief engineer officers with command or charge experience; naval architects and marine engineers; marine surveyors; specialists in salvage, towage, pilotage and port operations; those experienced in marine insurance, average adjusting and ship valuation; and lawyers and academics of standing in maritime law. Seniority, professional certification and demonstrable independence are the natural components of any such rule.

blocks.p: State the third part as what the section contemplates, not as what it enacts. That distinction - between the statutory standard, the delegated detail and the professional reality - is precisely the legal literacy a management-level examination is looking for, and it is also the only defensible position: the rules were not read, and inventing their contents would be worse than saying where they live.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Two limbs at 8 marks each. Limb (a) says scope and significance - two different demands, and most candidates answer only the first. Scope is which courts, what waters, what vessels, what claims; significance is why the 2017 Act mattered, and it needs its own visible section or it will not be written. Limb (b) says role and qualifications, and the qualifications half is where the answer is either precise or invented. Six sections for limb (a) and three for limb (b) is the right weighting, because limb (b)'s substance is concentrated in one short statutory section that has to be read carefully rather than at length.

blocks.h: The finding that carries limb (b)

blocks.p: Section 13 does not state any qualification. It requires the Central Government to appoint by notification a list of assessors with such qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters - and the nature of their duties, their fees and ancillary matters - 'in the manner as may be prescribed'. Section 2(1)(j) defines 'prescribed' as prescribed by rules made by the Central Government, and section 16 is the rule-making power. So the Act creates the mechanism and delegates the criteria. A candidate who writes a confident list of statutory qualifications is describing rules the statute does not print. The right answer is: here is the statutory standard, here is where the detail lives, and here is the professional population the standard contemplates.

blocks.h: In rem is the whole point

blocks.p: If one idea is carried away from this topic it should be that admiralty exists to solve a security problem, not a liability problem. A single-ship company may be unreachable, but the ship is present, identifiable and valuable - and only for as long as she is discharging. That is why arrest, rather than judgment, is the practical objective, why the maritime lien follows the ship through a change of ownership, registration and flag, and why section 8's clean title on a court sale matters: without it the sale realises nothing and the security is worthless.

blocks.h: Why the wages lien should matter to a candidate personally

blocks.p: Section 9 puts wages first among the five maritime liens - ahead of salvage, ahead of statutory dues, and, through section 10, ahead of the registered mortgage. And the wage lien alone runs for two years rather than one, from the date the sum falls due, with the master's, officers' and crew's repatriation costs and social insurance contributions included. An unpaid crew on an abandoned ship therefore holds the strongest claim in the queue. It is one of the few places where an examination answer describes something an officer may one day rely on.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Answering only scope and never significance. Two words in the stem, two demands.
Inventing a statutory list of assessor qualifications. Section 13 states none - it delegates them.

Confusing an assessor with an expert witness. An assessor advises the court and gives no evidence; an expert is called by a party, testifies on oath and is cross-examined. Section 13(2) preserves both.
Saying an assessor decides the technical issue. The judge decides everything.
Confusing a maritime claim with a maritime lien. Section 4 lists many claims; section 9 recognises five liens, and only the liens follow the ship and outrank the mortgage.
Saying the jurisdiction extends to the EEZ as of right. Section 3 gives territorial waters; the extension is by Central Government notification under the proviso.
Forgetting the protections in section 11 - security for wrongful or unjustified arrest, and the forty-five-day auction on abandonment.
Naming only Bombay, Calcutta and Madras. That is the position the Act repealed.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Asking who appoints assessors, expecting the Central Government by notification, not the High Court.
Asking whether an assessor can be cross-examined. No - they are not a witness.
Asking whether appointing an assessor stops a party calling its own expert. No - section 13(2).
Asking for the five maritime liens in order, and the limitation period, expecting one year, two for wages.
Asking what happens to a maritime lien when the ship is sold and re-flagged. It continues.
Asking which ranks higher, a maritime lien or a registered mortgage. The lien - section 10.
Asking which statutes the 2017 Act repealed, expecting the colonial Acts of 1840, 1861, 1890 and 1891 and the Letters Patent of 1865.
Asking whether a sister ship can be arrested for an ownership dispute. No - the proviso to section 5(2) excludes a section 4(1)(a) claim.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your ship is arrested in Kochi for unpaid bunkers supplied to a previous owner. Is the claim good against her?
The crew have not been paid for four months and the owner has disappeared. What is their position?
Which High Court would hear a claim arising off Paradip, and how far out does its jurisdiction run?
Who advises the judge on whether the engine failure was a defect or misoperation?
The arrest turns out to have been unjustified. What can the owner recover, and under which section?
The owner abandons the vessel after arrest. What must the court do, and in what time?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb (a) is four questions and a consequence: WHICH COURT - WHAT WATER - WHAT VESSEL - WHAT CLAIM, then ARREST, then WHY IT MATTERS. Attach one number to each: nine-plus notifiable High Courts; territorial waters, extendable by notification to the 1976 Act limits; a broad 'vessel' including barges, hovercraft and offshore units; section 4's long claims list and section 9's five liens; one year, two for wages; forty-five days on abandonment. Limb (b) is THREE PARTS TO THE QUALIFICATION ANSWER: what the Act says, where the detail lives, what it contemplates - plus the assessor / expert-witness contrast.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 (Act 22 of 2017), dated 9 August 2017, in force 1 April 2018.
Section 2(1)(e) - the High Courts; 2(1)(j) 'prescribed'; 2(1)(k) territorial waters; 2(1)(l) 'vessel'.

Section 3 - admiralty jurisdiction over waters up to and including territorial waters, extendable by Central Government notification to the limits under the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976.
Section 4 - maritime claims; the crew-wages limb expressed notwithstanding sections 150 and 151 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
Section 5 - arrest of vessel in rem, and sister-ship arrest with the ownership-claim proviso.
Sections 6 and 7 - jurisdiction in personam and its restrictions in collision cases, referring to section 285 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
Section 8 - vesting of rights on sale of vessels.
Section 9 - the five maritime liens, their inter se priority, survival of change of ownership, registration or flag, and the one-year and two-year extinction periods.
Section 10 - order of priority: maritime liens, then registered mortgages and charges, then all other claims.
Section 11 - protection of owner and crew: security for wrongful or unjustified arrest, and auction within forty-five days on abandonment, extendable by thirty.
Section 12 - the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 applies so far as not inconsistent.
Section 13 - assistance of assessors: the notified list, the delegated qualifications, and the preservation of party expert witnesses.
Section 14 - appeal to a Division Bench; section 15 - transfer by the Supreme Court; section 16 - power to make rules.

Section 17 - repeal of the Admiralty Court Acts 1840 and 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty (India) Act 1891 and the relevant Letters Patent, 1865 provisions.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence limits

blocks.p: ⭐ This is the best-evidenced question on the paper. The MIW corpus holds the official India Code text of Act 22 of 2017 and it was read directly this session. Sections 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14 and 17 are primary verified - the section numbers, the five liens and their order, the one-year and two-year periods, the forty-five-day auction provision and the exact structure of section 13 all come from the page rather than from recollection.

What was NOT read is the delegated legislation, and that is exactly where limb (b)'s qualification detail lives. The rules made under section 16 are not held by the corpus and were not read, so no qualification list is asserted as statutory anywhere in this answer. The professional categories in section 9 of the answer are given expressly as what the statutory standard contemplates, not as what any rule prescribes.

Two limitations are carried forward rather than closed. The corpus records open verification RQ-34 - whether the Act has been amended since 2017 - and it is not closed here; the text read is the India Code base text. And section 2(1)(e) as printed names the High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad for both Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, a court subsequently bifurcated, so the enumeration is reproduced as printed and the Act's own closing words - or any other High Court, as may be notified - are what carry the position forward. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is not held by the corpus, so its sections 150, 151 and 285 are named here only because the 2017 Act names them, and nothing about their content is asserted.

notes: THE GOVERNING STATUTE WAS IN FORCE THROUGHOUT. The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 came into force on 1 April 2018, nearly seven years before this sitting, and nothing in the Indian statute wave of 2025 touches admiralty jurisdiction.

THE 2025 INDIAN STATUTES ARE POST-SITTING AND NONE OF THEM IS ENGAGED. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and the Coastal Shipping Act, 2025 received assent in August 2025 - both after this paper, and neither amends the 2017 Act. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the operative merchant shipping statute at this sitting, and it is the 1958 Act whose sections 150, 151 and 285 the 2017 Act cross-refers to.

THE REPEALS IN SECTION 17 ARE OF COLONIAL STATUTES AND ARE HISTORIC. The Admiralty Court Acts of 1840 and 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty (India) Act 1891 and the relevant Letters Patent 1865 provisions ceased to apply on 1 April 2018. No answer on this paper may describe them as current.

AN OPEN CORPUS VERIFICATION IS CARRIED FORWARD, NOT CLOSED. RQ-34 records that whether the Act has been amended since 2017 is unverified. The text read is the India Code base text of Act 22 of 2017 and the answer states nothing that depends on an amendment.

ONE ENUMERATION IS OF HISTORICAL FORM AND IS REPRODUCED AS PRINTED. Section 2(1)(e) names the High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad for both Telangana and Andhra Pradesh; that court was later bifurcated. The Act's own closing words - or any other High Court as may be notified by the Central Government - carry the position forward, and the answer relies on those rather than on the enumeration.

NO DONOR, SO NO DONOR CONTAMINATION. QP2504-Q5 (April 2025) is the only family relation, it is unsolved, it is a different task, and it is a LATER sitting. The direction runs the other way: this answer becomes its donor.
NO IMO INSTRUMENT AND NO ASSEMBLY BOUNDARY IS ENGAGED by this question.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A two-limb Indian-law question. Limb (a) asks for the SCOPE and the SIGNIFICANCE of Indian admiralty law in regulating maritime disputes and jurisdiction over vessels - two demands, of which significance is the one usually omitted. Limb (b) asks for the ROLE of assessors and the QUALIFICATIONS required for their appointment 'under Indian maritime regulations'. The examiner is testing statutory literacy rather than recall: whether the candidate knows that the governing statute is the 2017 Act and what it replaced, and - the concealed test - whether they notice that the Act does not state the assessors' qualifications at all but delegates them to rules.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, set as 8 + 8. Two equal limbs, so two equal regions. Limb (a) covers a whole statute and needs several short sections; limb (b) rests on one two-subsection provision, so its length comes from reading that provision closely and from the assessor-versus-expert contrast rather than from breadth.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For limb (a): admiralty as an in rem jurisdiction whose object is security; the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 in force 1 April 2018 and the colonial statutes it repealed; jurisdiction vested in the named High Courts over waters up to and including territorial waters, extendable by notification; the broad definition of vessel; the maritime claims list; the five maritime liens with their priority and limitation periods; arrest, sister-ship arrest, and the section 11 protections; and then the significance - consolidation, wider access, codified priorities, alignment with the international pattern, and India as a maritime forum. For limb (b): section 13's notified list appointed by the Central Government, the delegation of qualifications to rules, section 13(2) preserving party expert witnesses, and a clear statement of the assessor's advisory, non-evidential, non-deciding role.
primary_source_plan: True Source corpus Admiralty-Act-2017 official India Code text, read directly - sections 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14 and 17
Section 13 read word by word, with section 2(1)(j) for the meaning of 'prescribed' and section 16 for the rule-making power
The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 sections named by the 2017 Act itself - by reference only, since the 1958 Act is not held
QP2502_TEMPORAL_AND_DONOR_ANCHOR.md section 4.3 for the temporal position and the section 13 finding
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - the Act has been in force since 1 April 2018 and none of the 2025 Indian statutes touches admiralty jurisdiction. Two residual items are recorded rather than closed: the corpus's open verification RQ-34 on post-2017 amendments, and the fact that the rules made under section 16, where the assessor qualifications actually live, were not read.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW as to which law applies - this is an Indian statute question and the statute is unambiguous. The real risk is INTERNAL to Indian law: mistaking delegated legislation for statute in limb (b), or treating the repealed colonial enactments as still operative. Both are addressed expressly.
technical_ambiguities: The stem says 'under Indian maritime regulations' rather than 'under the Act'. That wording is, if anything, more accurate than the candidate might expect, because the qualifications genuinely do live in delegated rules rather than in the statute - and the answer says so.

'Indian Admiralty Law' is not confined to the 2017 Act in principle, since the Code of Civil Procedure applies and the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is cross-referred. The answer treats the 2017 Act as the governing statute and names the others where the Act itself names them.
Section 2(1)(e) as printed lists a High Court that has since been bifurcated. Reproduced as printed, with the Act's own notification clause relied on to carry the position forward.
The definition of 'vessel' in section 2(1)(l) is reproduced only so far as it was read on the page; its closing limb is not completed and nothing is attributed to it that was not read.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Nine numbered sections. Sections 1 to 6 are limb (a): what admiralty law is and why in rem exists, the statute and what it repealed, the scope of jurisdiction across courts, waters and vessels, the claims and the five liens, arrest and the protections against its abuse, and a separate section on significance. Sections 7 to 9 are limb (b): what section 13 actually provides with the three consequences drawn out, the assessor-versus-expert-witness contrast as a table, and a three-part answer to the qualifications question distinguishing what the Act says, where the detail lives and what the standard contemplates.

questions.understand_first: Admiralty law exists to solve a security problem, and holding that in mind makes the whole question fall out. A shipowner may be a single-ship company in a jurisdiction the claimant will never reach, with unknown directors and no assets - but the ship is right there, identifiable, valuable, and present only until the cargo is discharged. So admiralty allows an action in rem, against the ship herself: arrest her, obtain security, and if necessary have the court sell her with clean title. That is why arrest, not judgment, is the practical objective, and why the maritime lien follows the ship through a change of owner, registration and flag. In India the governing statute is the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, in force 1 April 2018, which swept away the nineteenth-century colonial Acts under which only three High Courts could hear such a claim. Then limb (b), where the real test is hidden. Section 13 does not tell you what an assessor must be. It requires the Central Government to appoint by notification a list of assessors with such qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters - and the nature of their duties and their fees - 'in the manner as may be prescribed', which section 2(1)(j) defines as by rules made by the Central Government. The statute creates the mechanism and delegates the criteria. Say that, then say what the standard contemplates, and you have answered a question most candidates will answer by invention. And keep the assessor distinct from the expert witness: an assessor advises the court and gives no evidence; an expert is called by a party, testifies on oath and is cross-examined. Section 13(2) exists to make clear that having one does not exclude the other.

steps.title: What admiralty law is, and the feature that makes it different
points: The body of law determining maritime claims and exercising jurisdiction over vessels themselves
Its defining feature is the action in rem - the claim is against the ship, which can be arrested and sold by the court
The commercial reason: a single-ship company may be unreachable, but the ship is present, identifiable and valuable - and only briefly
So arrest for security, not judgment, is the practical objective of most admiralty proceedings

steps.title: The statute in force, and what it replaced
points: The governing statute is the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - Act 22 of 2017, dated 9 August 2017, in force 1 April 2018
Long title: to consolidate the laws relating to admiralty jurisdiction, proceedings in connection with vessels, their arrest, detention and sale

Section 17 repealed the application in India of the Admiralty Court Acts 1840 and 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty (India) Act 1891 and the relevant Letters Patent 1865 provisions
Pending proceedings continue but are adjudicated under the 2017 Act; things done under the repealed enactments are deemed done under it

steps.title: The scope of the jurisdiction - which courts, what waters, what vessels
points: Section 2(1)(e) - Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, Karnataka, Gujarat, Orissa, Kerala and Hyderabad for Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, or any other High Court notified by the Central Government
The extension from three chartered High Courts to a notifiable list of coastal High Courts is a principal achievement of the Act

Section 3 - jurisdiction over waters up to and including the territorial waters of the respective jurisdictions, with a proviso allowing extension by notification to the limits under the 1976 Maritime Zones Act
Section 2(1)(l) - 'vessel' defined broadly, propelled or not, expressly including a barge, lighter, hovercraft and off-shore industry mobile unit
Sections 5 and 6 - both in rem by arrest and in personam against the person liable

steps.title: What may be claimed - maritime claims, and the maritime liens
points: Section 4 enumerates the maritime claims - ownership and possession, co-owner disputes, mortgages, damage by operation, loss of life or injury, cargo loss, carriage and hire agreements, salvage, towage, pilotage, supplies and bunkers, construction and repair, port and canal dues, crew wages, disbursements, average, sale disputes and insurance premium including mutual calls

Section 9 recognises five maritime liens in priority order: wages including repatriation and social insurance; loss of life or personal injury; salvage; port, canal, waterway and pilotage dues; and tort from operation other than cargo damage
The lien continues notwithstanding any change of ownership, registration or flag
Extinguished after one year unless arrest or seizure has led to a forced sale - two years for a wage claim, running continuously with time under arrest excluded
No lien for oil or HNS damage compensable under other law, or for nuclear radioactivity - section 9(4)
Section 10 - priority: maritime liens first, then registered mortgages and charges, then all other claims; equal ranking within a category; salvage claims in inverse order of time

steps.title: Arrest, security and the protections against its abuse
points: Section 5(1) - arrest of a vessel within jurisdiction for security, on the five stated grounds including a claim secured by a maritime lien
Section 5(2) - sister-ship arrest, excluding a possession or ownership claim under section 4(1)(a)
Sections 6 and 7 - in personam, restricted in collision, manoeuvre and collision-regulation cases referring to section 285 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958
Section 11 - the court may require the claimant to give an unconditional undertaking or security for loss from wrongful or unjustified arrest or excessive security demanded
Section 11(3) - on abandonment after arrest the court shall auction the vessel within forty-five days, extendable by thirty for recorded reasons
Section 8 - clean title on a court sale, which is what makes the security worth anything
Section 12 CPC applies; section 14 appeal to a Division Bench; section 15 transfer by the Supreme Court

steps.title: The significance - why the Act matters
points: Ended reliance on repealed nineteenth-century colonial English statutes
Widened access from three High Courts to a notifiable list of coastal High Courts, so a claimant can proceed where the ship is
Codified maritime claims and liens with stated priority and limitation periods, so financiers, insurers, suppliers, crew and salvors know where they stand in advance
Aligned Indian law with the international arrest and maritime-lien pattern by drafting, making Indian practice legible to foreign parties
Balanced remedy against protection - section 11 keeps arrest a remedy rather than a weapon
Strengthens India as a maritime forum, supporting finance, repair, bunkering and supply
Directly practical for an officer: wages carry the first lien and a two-year period, ahead even of the mortgagee bank

steps.title: Assessors - what section 13 actually provides
points: Section 13(1) - notwithstanding any other law, the Central Government shall appoint by notification a list of assessors with such qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters, the nature of their duties, their fees and ancillary matters, in the manner as may be prescribed
Section 13(2) - appointment of assessors is no bar to the examination of expert witnesses by any party
First consequence: the Act states NO qualification - it delegates, 'prescribed' being defined by section 2(1)(j) as by rules made by the Central Government under the rule-making power in section 16
Second consequence: appointment is central and by notification of a standing list, not case-by-case by each High Court
Third consequence: the assessor does not displace the party's own expert

steps.title: The role of assessors in practice, and how they differ from expert witnesses
points: Admiralty cases turn on good seamanship, machinery failure causation, salvage reasonableness, cargo care and valuation - matters a judge cannot be expected to have lived
An assessor is a technical adviser to the court, appointed so the court can engage with those matters properly
Assessor: appointed by the Central Government to a notified list, owes duty to the court, advises, gives no evidence on oath, is not cross-examined, decides nothing
Expert witness: called by a party, gives evidence on oath, is cross-examined
Section 13(2) means both may feature in the same case - the assessor helps the court weigh the evidence the experts give
The statutory descendant of the long admiralty practice of sitting with nautical advisers, with a domestic analogue in shipping-casualty inquiry assessors

steps.title: Qualifications - what the Act says, and what it therefore contemplates
points: What the Act requires: qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters - the only standard section 13 states

Where the detail lives: rules made by the Central Government under section 16, because section 13(1) fixes the matter 'in the manner as may be prescribed' and section 2(1)(j) defines 'prescribed' accordingly. The criteria are delegated legislation, not statute

What the standard contemplates: master mariners and chief engineer officers with command or charge experience; naval architects and marine engineers; marine surveyors; salvage, towage, pilotage and port specialists; marine insurance, average adjusting and valuation practitioners; and maritime lawyers and academics of standing
Seniority, professional certification and demonstrable independence are the natural components of any such rule
State the third part as what the section contemplates, never as what it enacts - which is both the honest position and the legal literacy being tested

questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) as four questions then a consequence - WHICH COURT, WHAT WATER, WHAT VESSEL, WHAT CLAIM (3, 4), then ARREST AND ITS CHECKS (5), then WHY IT MATTERS (6), on the foundation that admiralty is about SECURITY, NOT JUDGMENT (1, 2). Limb (b) as three parts to the qualification answer - what the Act SAYS, where the detail LIVES, what it CONTEMPLATES (7, 9) - with the assessor and the expert witness kept apart (8).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Admiralty is about SECURITY, not judgment - the action in rem against the ship, because the owner may be unreachable and the ship is not. Statute: Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 (Act 22 of 2017, 9 Aug 2017), in force 1 April 2018; s.17 repealed the colonial Acts of 1840, 1861, 1890, 1891 and the Letters Patent 1865. s.3 - jurisdiction in the High Courts over waters up to and including territorial waters, extendable by Central Government notification to the 1976 Maritime Zones Act limits. s.2(1)(e) - Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, Karnataka, Gujarat, Orissa, Kerala, Hyderabad, or any other notified. s.4 - the maritime claims list. s.9 - FIVE maritime liens in order: wages; death or personal injury; salvage; port/canal/pilotage dues; tort other than cargo damage. Lien survives change of owner, registration and flag; extinguished after 1 year - 2 years for wages. s.10 - liens, then registered mortgages, then all other claims. s.5 arrest and sister-ship arrest; s.11 security for wrongful arrest and auction within 45 days on abandonment; s.8 clean title. s.13 ASSESSORS: the Central Government appoints by notification a list, with qualifications 'as may be prescribed' - the Act states NO qualification, it delegates (s.2(1)(j), rules under s.16). s.13(2) - no bar to a party's own expert witness. An assessor advises the court, gives no evidence, is not cross-examined and decides nothing.
critical_numbers: Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - Act 22 of 2017, dated 9 August 2017, in force 1 April 2018
Section 9 recognises FIVE maritime liens, wages ranking first
A maritime lien is extinguished after one year - two years for a wage claim - unless arrest or seizure has led to a forced sale
Section 10 priority: maritime liens, then registered mortgages and charges, then all other claims
Section 11(3): on abandonment after arrest the vessel is auctioned within forty-five days, extendable by thirty for reasons recorded in writing

Section 17 repealed the Admiralty Court Acts 1840 and 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty (India) Act 1891 and the relevant Letters Patent, 1865 provisions
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Section 13 of the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, read with section 2(1)(j) and section 16 - the provision that appoints assessors by central notification and delegates their qualifications to rules rather than stating them, which is the finding limb (b) turns on
quick_revision.major_trap: Inventing a statutory list of assessor qualifications. Section 13 states none. It requires the Central Government to appoint by notification a list of assessors with such qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters 'in the manner as may be prescribed' - and 'prescribed' means by rules made by the Central Government under section 2(1)(j) and section 16. The Act creates the mechanism and delegates the criteria. Second trap: confusing an assessor with an expert witness - the assessor advises the court, gives no evidence and is not cross-examined, while an expert is called by a party and testifies on oath; section 13(2) preserves both. Third: confusing a maritime claim with a maritime lien - section 4 lists many claims, section 9 recognises only five liens, and only a lien follows the ship and outranks the registered mortgage.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Indian admiralty law and assessors question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What admiralty law is and why in rem exists. 2 The 2017 Act and what it repealed. 3 Scope - courts, waters, vessels. 4 Maritime claims and the five liens. 5 Arrest and the protections against abuse. 6 Significance. 7 What section 13 actually provides. 8 Assessor versus expert witness. 9 Qualifications in three parts. Sections 1-6 are limb (a), 7-9 limb (b).
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (a) says scope AND significance, so significance gets its own section or it never gets written; limb (b) rests on one short provision read closely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does section 13 of the Admiralty Act, 2017 provide about assessors?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 13(1) requires the Central Government, notwithstanding any other law, to appoint by notification a list of assessors with such qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters, the nature of the duties to be performed by them, the fees to be paid and other ancillary matters, in the manner as may be prescribed. Section 13(2) provides that the appointment of assessors shall not be construed as a bar to the examination of expert witnesses by any of the parties.
retrieval_cards.why: The whole of limb (b) is in these two subsections, and the second is the one candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What qualifications does the Admiralty Act, 2017 require of an assessor?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Act states none. It requires qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters, and leaves what those are to be fixed 'in the manner as may be prescribed' - 'prescribed' meaning by rules made by the Central Government under section 2(1)(j), the rule-making power being section 16. The criteria are delegated legislation, not statute. The right answer states the statutory standard, says where the detail lives, and then says what the standard contemplates.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the concealed test in limb (b), and a confident invented list is the wrong answer however plausible it sounds.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an assessor differ from an expert witness?
retrieval_cards.answer: An assessor is appointed by the Central Government to a notified list, owes their duty to the court, advises it on technical maritime matters, gives no evidence on oath, is not cross-examined and decides nothing. An expert witness is called by a party, gives evidence on oath and is subject to cross-examination. Section 13(2) makes clear that appointing an assessor is no bar to a party examining its own expert, so both may feature in the same case.
retrieval_cards.why: The assessor helps the court weigh evidence; the expert supplies it. Collapsing the two is the standard error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the five maritime liens in order of priority, with their limitation period.
retrieval_cards.answer: One, wages and other sums due to the master, officers and crew including repatriation costs and social insurance contributions. Two, loss of life or personal injury in direct connection with the vessel's operation. Three, salvage including special compensation. Four, port, canal and other waterway dues and pilotage dues. Five, tort claims from loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel, other than to cargo and containers. Each is extinguished after one year - two years for wages - unless arrest or seizure has led to a forced sale.
retrieval_cards.why: Section 9 is the most examinable provision in the Act, and wages ranking first is the fact with the most practical consequence for a seafarer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between a maritime claim and a maritime lien?
retrieval_cards.answer: A maritime claim is any of the many heads of claim listed in section 4 over which a High Court may exercise admiralty jurisdiction. A maritime lien is one of only five claims recognised by section 9, and it is far stronger: it attaches to the vessel and continues notwithstanding any change of ownership, registration or flag, and under section 10 it ranks ahead of registered mortgages and all other claims.
retrieval_cards.why: Only the lien follows the ship and outranks the bank, which is why the distinction decides who gets paid.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How far does Indian admiralty jurisdiction extend geographically?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 3 vests it in the respective High Courts, exercisable over the waters up to and including the territorial waters of their respective jurisdictions. The proviso allows the Central Government, by notification, to extend it up to the limit defined in section 2 of the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying the jurisdiction reaches the EEZ as of right is wrong - the extension requires a notification.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What protection does an owner have against a wrongful arrest?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 11 allows the High Court, as a condition of arrest or of maintaining one, to require the claimant to give an unconditional undertaking to pay damages or such security as the court determines for loss the defendant may suffer - expressly including where the arrest was wrongful or unjustified or where excessive security was demanded. The person providing security may apply to have it reduced, modified or cancelled.
retrieval_cards.why: Arrest is commercially devastating, and section 11 is what keeps it a remedy rather than a weapon.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does the law allow a claim against the ship herself?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the owner may be a single-ship company in an unreachable jurisdiction with no assets, while the ship is present, identifiable and valuable - and only for as long as she is discharging. An action in rem lets a claimant obtain security from the asset in the days it is within reach, which is why arrest rather than judgment is the practical objective, why a maritime lien survives a change of owner and flag, and why section 8's clean title on a court sale matters.
retrieval_cards.why: The security rationale explains every other feature of the jurisdiction and is the fastest way into the whole topic.

questions.short_title: EEDI Verification of a New Ship
questions.text_verbatim: For the purpose of verification of Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) of a new ship, explain: - a) The content of EEDI Technical File (5) b) The scope of preliminary EEDI verification at design stage (5) c) Final verification of attained EEDI at sea trial stage (6)

The scope of preliminary EEDI verification at design stage.
Final verification of attained EEDI at sea trial stage.

Who does what - the duty-bearer allocation, and the trap inside it

The content of the EEDI Technical File - the speed prediction and the calculation itself
The scope of preliminary verification at the design stage

questions.verification_status: Authored fresh against the True Source corpus's frozen canonical records for MARPOL Annex VI, which is CITATION-READY and frozen. Regulations 22, 24 and 5 were read as canonical records this session and the regulatory architecture in this answer is P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED from them: regulation 22 as the attained-EEDI provision with its three paragraphs, the ship-specificity and technical-file requirements and the seven-month reporting duty; regulation 24 as the required EEDI with its Table 1 reduction factors and Table 2 reference-line parameters; and regulation 5.4 as the survey provision that carries the initial survey verifying the attained EEDI.
