blocks.h: 1. Where the duty comes from, and why verification is in two stages

blocks.p: The Energy Efficiency Design Index is a measure of the CO2 emitted per unit of transport work that a ship's design will produce - grammes of CO2 per tonne-mile. It is a design index: it is fixed by what the ship is, not by how she is operated.
The obligation sits in MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4, in the revised Annex adopted by resolution MEPC.328(76) and in force since 1 November 2023:

ul: Regulation 22 - Attained EEDI. An attained EEDI shall be calculated for new ships, for new ships that have undergone a major conversion, and for new or existing ships whose conversion is so extensive that the Administration regards the ship as newly constructed - in each case where the ship falls into one of the ship-type categories the regulation lists. The attained EEDI shall be ship-specific, shall be accompanied by the EEDI technical file containing the information necessary for the calculation and showing the process of the calculation, and shall be verified on the basis of that file.

Regulation 24 - Required EEDI. The attained EEDI must not exceed the required EEDI, which is the applicable reference line value reduced by a reduction factor. Table 1 gives the reduction factor by ship type, size band and phase; Table 2 gives the parameters from which the reference line is computed.

Regulation 5.4 - Surveys. Ships to which chapter 4 applies are subject to an initial survey verifying the attained EEDI and the SEEMP, a survey after a major conversion of a new ship, and a discretionary initial survey where the conversion is so extensive that the ship is regarded as newly constructed.

Regulation 19 - Application. Chapter 4 admits ships of 400 gross tonnage and above, excludes ships trading solely domestically and unpropelled ships and platforms, and expressly disapplies regulations 22 to 25 to ships with non-conventional propulsion.

blocks.p: Why two stages? Because the index depends on the ship's speed at 75 % of rated engine power, and at the design stage that speed is a prediction from tank tests. It cannot be known until the ship exists and runs. So the file is verified once on the prediction - which is what permits construction and trials to proceed on an agreed basis - and again on the measurement, after which it becomes final. The whole two-stage architecture exists to resolve one unknown quantity.

blocks.h: 2. Who does what - and the trap inside it

rows: Shipbuilder / shipowner
Calculates the attained EEDI, prepares the EEDI technical file, submits it, conducts the sea trial, and revises the file after the trial
The verifier - the Administration, or any organization duly authorized by it
Verifies the attained EEDI on the basis of the EEDI technical file, attends the sea trial, and confirms the final value
The Administration alone
Forms the opinion that a converted ship is to be regarded as newly constructed. This one is not delegable to an authorized organization
The Administration or its authorized organization
Reports the required and attained EEDI values and relevant information to the Organization, within seven months of completion of the regulation 5.4 survey
The Organization
Develops the guidelines for the calculation and for the reporting, and receives the reports. Regulation 22 imposes no duty on it

blocks.p: ⚠ The trap, and it is a precise one: the Administration does NOT calculate the attained EEDI, and it does NOT approve it. It VERIFIES it. The value is calculated by the shipbuilder and evidenced by the technical file; the verifier's function is to satisfy itself that the calculation is correct and that the file supports it. Writing that the Administration calculates or approves an attained EEDI misstates the whole allocation of duty.

A second point worth making because it surprises candidates: regulation 22 imposes no duty on any ship, owner or company at all. The duties it creates fall on the Administration. The obligation to have a compliant design bites through regulation 24 and through survey and certification, not through regulation 22.

blocks.h: 3. The EEDI Technical File - ship, machinery and capacity data

blocks.p: The Annex does not define the EEDI technical file. Regulation 22.1 makes it the evidential basis of verification and requires that it contain the information necessary for the calculation and show the process of the calculation, but the contents themselves come from the Organization's guidelines. What the file must in practice carry is this:

ul: Ship particulars - name, IMO number, flag, port of registry, classification society and class notations; ship type and the regulation 2.2 category into which she falls; shipyard, hull number, and the contract, keel-laying and delivery dates that determine whether she is a 'new ship' and which EEDI phase applies to her.

Capacity - the deadweight at the summer load draught for most types, or the gross tonnage for passenger and ro-ro passenger ships, with the basis on which it is derived, together with the lightweight, displacement and the summer load line draught.

Main engine data - maker, type and number of engines; the rated power (MCR) and rated speed; and the specific fuel consumption at the EEDI power point, taken from the engine's NOx Technical File test report so that it is a certified figure rather than a claimed one. Where a shaft limitation or overridable power limitation is fitted, its arrangement and value.
Auxiliary engine data - maker, type, rated power and specific fuel consumption, again from the NOx Technical File.

The electrical power table and the derivation of the auxiliary power used in the calculation - the sea-going electrical load, and for a ship with a significant non-propulsion load such as a reefer or a tanker with cargo pumps, the basis on which it is established.
Fuel data - the fuel type or types and the corresponding carbon conversion factor; and for a dual-fuel ship, the treatment of each fuel and of pilot fuel.
Shaft generator or shaft motor arrangements, where fitted, and how they enter the calculation.

blocks.h: 4. The EEDI Technical File - speed, correction factors and the calculation

ul: The reference speed. The ship speed at 75 % of the rated installed power, in the maximum design load condition, in deep water and calm weather with no wind and no waves - together with the evidence for it: the tank test report, the model-ship correlation, the power-speed curve, and the identity and quality-system status of the towing tank. At the design stage this speed is an estimate, and saying so is part of the file.

The correction factors and their justification. Each factor claimed must be supported, not merely stated - the factors for ship-specific design elements, for ice class and other technical or regulatory capacity limitation, for cubic capacity where volume rather than weight limits the ship, for general cargo ships fitted with cranes, for shaft motors, and the weather factor representing speed reduction in representative sea conditions where it is claimed.

Innovative energy efficiency technology. Where waste heat recovery, wind assistance, solar, air lubrication or a similar technology is credited, the file must describe it and evidence the power saved or generated - separated into technologies that reduce the propulsion power required and those that generate electrical power - with the test or measurement basis for the claim. This is the most closely examined part of any file, because it is where an unsupported claim would directly reduce the attained value.

The calculation itself. Every input value, each with its source; the process of the calculation set out so that it can be followed and reproduced - which regulation 22.1 requires in terms; and the resulting attained EEDI.
The required EEDI for the ship, computed under regulation 24 from her type, size band and phase, and the comparison showing that the attained value does not exceed it.
The description of the sea trial - the intended trial condition, the measurement arrangements and the procedure by which the measured speed will be corrected to the reference condition.

blocks.p: Note what is deliberately not reproduced here. Regulation 22.2 refers the entire method of calculation out to Organization guidelines, and regulation 22 prints no formula, no coefficient, no reference-line value and no reduction factor of its own. The structure of the calculation and the inputs it needs can be stated with confidence; the equation belongs to the guidelines.

blocks.h: 5. Preliminary verification at the design stage - what it is and when

ul: When. At the design stage, before construction is complete and before delivery - as the first part of the initial survey under regulation 5.4.

What is submitted. The shipowner or shipbuilder submits the EEDI technical file with its supporting documentation - the tank test report and power curve, the NOx Technical File extracts for main and auxiliary engines, the capacity and load-line documentation, the electrical load table, and the evidence for any correction factor or innovative technology claimed.
To whom. To the verifier - the Administration or an organization duly authorized by it, in practice the recognised organization acting for the flag State.

The object. To establish, before the ship exists in her final form, that the design as specified will comply - so that a non-compliance is found on paper, where it can be corrected by design change, rather than at the trial, where it cannot.

blocks.h: 6. What the verifier interrogates - and why it is only preliminary

ul: Applicability and phase. Is the ship within chapter 4 at all - 400 gross tonnage and above, not solely domestic, not unpropelled, and not of non-conventional propulsion, which regulation 19.3 takes outside regulations 22 to 25 entirely? Which regulation 2.2 category is she, and which phase do her contract, keel and delivery dates place her in?

The required EEDI. Recomputed independently under regulation 24 - the correct reference line from Table 2 for her type and capacity, and the correct reduction factor from Table 1 for her type, size band and phase.
The calculation method. Checked against the current calculation guidelines, including that the correct edition has been used.

Each input value. Capacity against the load line and stability information; rated power against the engine documentation and any power limitation arrangement; specific fuel consumption against the NOx Technical File, not against a maker's brochure; the carbon factor against the fuel; the auxiliary power against a defensible electrical load table.

The speed prediction. The tank test and the power curve from which the estimated reference speed is derived - the test conditions, the model scale, the extrapolation method, and whether the tank operates under a recognised quality system. The verifier may witness the model test or call for additional data, and this is the item most often queried, because the index is highly sensitive to speed.
Correction factors and innovative technology. Each claim examined against its justification; an unsupported factor is removed and the attained value recalculated.
The trial plan. That the proposed sea-trial condition, measurement arrangements and correction procedure will actually produce a usable reference speed.

Outcome. The verifier confirms the preliminary verification of the attained EEDI on the technical file. It is preliminary for one reason only: the reference speed is still a prediction. Every other input is already final.

blocks.h: 7. The sea trial - conduct, measurement and correction

ul: Attendance. The trial is conducted by the shipbuilder in the presence of the verifier, who examines the conduct of the trial as well as its result.

Condition. The ship should be at the EEDI reference load condition, or at a condition close enough to it that the result can be corrected back; the actual draught, trim and displacement are measured and recorded, and the hull and propeller condition confirmed as clean.

Environment recorded - wind speed and direction, sea state and swell, water depth, current, and water temperature and density. Trials are run in deep water where possible, because a shallow-water correction is large and uncertain.

Measurement. Speed and shaft power are measured over a set of runs at several power settings spanning the EEDI power point. Runs are made as double runs on reciprocal courses at each setting, so that the effect of current cancels in the mean. Shaft power is taken from a calibrated torsion meter, and speed over ground from satellite positioning, with the run length and steady-state period long enough to be meaningful.

Correction to the reference condition. The measured results are corrected by the recognised international speed-power trial analysis procedure for wind, waves, current, shallow water, water temperature and density, and any deviation of displacement and trim from the reference condition. The output is a corrected power-speed curve, from which the speed at 75 % of rated power is read.

Series ships. Where a ship is one of a series and is not separately trialled, the guidelines permit the lead ship's trial result to be used, provided the ships are demonstrably identical in the relevant respects and the reliance is justified in the file.

blocks.h: 8. Final verification - revision, comparison and certification

ol: Compare measured with predicted. The corrected reference speed from the trial is compared with the estimated speed used in the technical file.

Revise the technical file. ⚠ If they differ - and they generally do - the technical file must be revised. The reference speed is replaced with the measured, corrected value and the attained EEDI is recalculated. Every other input remains as verified at the design stage, so the revision is confined to the one quantity the trial existed to establish.

Verify the trial itself. The verifier examines the trial procedure, the measured data and the corrections applied - not merely the resulting number. A correctly reported result from a badly conducted trial is not verifiable.

Confirm compliance. The verifier confirms that the final attained EEDI does not exceed the required EEDI computed under regulation 24. If it does exceed it, the ship does not comply: the remedy is a design or operational change - a power limitation, a modification, or credited technology - and re-verification. There is no tolerance to be argued.

Certification. With the initial survey under regulation 5.4 complete, the International Energy Efficiency Certificate is issued under regulation 6, and the verified EEDI technical file is retained on board with it as the evidence supporting the certificate.

Reporting. For a ship also subject to regulation 24, the Administration or its authorized organization reports the required and attained EEDI values and relevant information to the Organization, by electronic communication, within seven months of completion of the regulation 5.4 survey.

blocks.p: The design is then fixed. The attained EEDI does not change with operation - a fouled hull or a slow-steaming voyage does not alter it. What changes with operation is the carbon intensity indicator, and confusing the two is the commonest error in this whole subject.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Three limbs at 5 + 5 + 6, so three visible regions with the last slightly the largest - and the answer opens with two short framing sections before them, because a marker who can see that the candidate knows where the duty comes from and who does what reads everything after it more generously. Limb (a) is a content list and is best given as two grouped lists rather than one long one - data about the ship, then the speed and the calculation. Limb (b) needs the timing and the object stated before the checklist, or it reads as a random set of checks. Limb (c) carries the most marks and has a natural sequence - trial, correction, revision, comparison, certificate - so it is written as a sequence.

blocks.h: The idea that makes the whole question simple

blocks.p: There are two verification stages because there is exactly one unknown. Every input to the index - capacity, rated power, specific fuel consumption from the NOx Technical File, carbon factor, auxiliary load - is known on paper at the design stage. The one quantity that cannot be known until the ship exists and runs is her speed at 75 % of rated power, which at design is a prediction from a tank test. So the file is verified once on the prediction and again on the measurement. Say that in one sentence and limbs (b) and (c) organise themselves: preliminary verification checks everything and accepts one estimate; final verification replaces that estimate with a measurement and recalculates.

blocks.h: Verify, not calculate, and not approve

blocks.p: The regulation allocates duties precisely and an examiner can test it in one question. The shipbuilder calculates; the verifier verifies. Regulation 22.1 requires the attained EEDI to be verified based on the EEDI technical file, either by the Administration or by any organization duly authorized by it - and the Administration neither calculates the value nor approves it. The one function that is not delegable is the Administration's opinion that a converted ship is to be regarded as newly constructed, which is what brings a converted ship into the calculation cohort at all.

blocks.h: Why the sea trial is a measurement problem, not a formality

blocks.p: The index is highly sensitive to speed, so the credibility of the whole scheme rests on the trial being properly conducted and properly corrected. That is why the answer names the mechanics: double runs on reciprocal courses so that current cancels in the mean; deep water, because shallow-water correction is large and uncertain; measured draught, trim and displacement so the result can be corrected back to the reference condition; a calibrated torsion meter for shaft power; and correction for wind, waves, current, depth, water density and temperature by the recognised analysis procedure. An engineer who can explain why reciprocal runs are used has demonstrated more than one who lists the corrections.

blocks.h: EEDI, EEXI and CII - keep them apart

blocks.p: EEDI is design and applies to new ships and to ships so converted that they count as new. EEXI is the same style of index applied once to existing ships. CII is operational and is recalculated every year from actual fuel consumed and distance sailed. Only the CII changes with how the ship is run - a fouled hull, a slower speed or a longer ballast leg move the CII and do not touch the attained EEDI at all. Mixing them is the commonest error in the topic and is easy for an examiner to expose in one follow-up.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Saying the Administration calculates or approves the attained EEDI. It verifies it, on the basis of the technical file.
Treating the EEDI as something that changes with operation. That is the CII.
Omitting the NOx Technical File as the source of specific fuel consumption, and quoting a maker's brochure figure instead.
Describing preliminary verification as a formality. It is where every input except speed is fixed.
Forgetting that the technical file must be revised after the trial and the attained EEDI recalculated.
Omitting the correction of trial results to the reference condition, or the reason for reciprocal double runs.
Failing to say that the attained EEDI must be compared against the required EEDI under regulation 24, and that exceeding it is non-compliance with no tolerance.
Forgetting the International Energy Efficiency Certificate at the end, and that the verified file is retained on board.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Asking who verifies the attained EEDI and whether the Administration may delegate it. It may - to any organization duly authorized by it - except the opinion that a converted ship is newly constructed.
Asking why the trial uses reciprocal runs, expecting the cancellation of current.
Asking what happens if the measured speed is lower than predicted. The file is revised, the attained EEDI recalculated, and if it now exceeds the required value the ship does not comply.
Asking where the specific fuel consumption comes from.
Asking what document the ship keeps on board afterwards, expecting the IEEC and the verified technical file.
Asking whether EEDI applies to an existing ship. Only through EEXI - or through a conversion so extensive that the Administration regards her as newly constructed.
Asking whether a ship with non-conventional propulsion must have an attained EEDI. Regulation 19.3 disapplies regulations 22 to 25 to her.
Asking what a weather factor or an innovative technology credit must be supported by.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your new ship's trial speed comes in 0.3 knots below the tank prediction. What happens next?
How would you evidence a waste heat recovery credit in the technical file?
Why is the trial run in deep water?
Your ship has a shaft power limitation fitted. How does that affect the attained EEDI?
What is the difference between the attained EEDI, the EEXI and the CII?
Who reports the attained EEDI to IMO, and within what period?

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: MARPOL Annex VI, revised Annex adopted by resolution MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2023.
Regulation 19 - application of chapter 4: 400 gross tonnage and above; exclusions; and regulation 19.3 disapplying regulations 22 to 25 to ships with non-conventional propulsion.

Regulation 22 - attained EEDI: the calculation cohort, ship-specificity, the EEDI technical file, verification by the Administration or an organization duly authorized by it, the reference of the calculation method to Organization guidelines, and the seven-month reporting duty.

Regulation 24 - required EEDI: the attained value must not exceed the reference line value reduced by the applicable factor, with Table 1 for reduction factors by type, size band and phase and Table 2 for the reference-line parameters.
Regulation 5.4 - surveys for chapter 4 ships, including the initial survey verifying the attained EEDI and the SEEMP, and the major-conversion surveys.
Regulation 6 - issue or endorsement of the International Energy Efficiency Certificate.
The Organization's guidelines on the method of calculation of the attained EEDI, and on survey and certification of the EEDI - to which regulation 22.2 refers the whole method.
The NOx Technical File - the certified source of engine specific fuel consumption and rated power data.
The recognised international procedure for speed-power trial analysis - double runs on reciprocal courses and correction to the reference condition.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: One sentence holds the whole question: everything is known on paper except the speed, so verify twice. Then three limbs in order. FILE (3, 4) - ship, engines, capacity, speed evidence, factors, calculation. DESIGN (5, 6) - submit, check applicability and phase, recompute the required value, check every input, interrogate the tank test, accept one estimate. TRIAL (7, 8) - run it, correct it, revise the file, recalculate, compare, certify, report.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence limits

blocks.p: ⭐ The regulatory architecture here is primary-verified and the procedural detail is not, and the line between them is worth understanding. The MIW corpus holds MARPOL Annex VI as frozen canonical records, promoted to citation-ready and frozen, and regulations 22, 24 and 5 were read as those records this session. The cohort, the ship-specificity and technical-file requirements, the verification allocation, the seven-month reporting duty, the structure of regulation 24 and the content of regulation 5.4 all come from them. The corpus's export policy is facts-and-pointers-only, so identity, structure, duty-bearers and numerics are used and no body text is reproduced.

The Annex is silent on the two things this question is mostly about, and the corpus record says so in terms. First, 'EEDI technical file' is undefined anywhere in MARPOL Annex VI, even though regulation 22.1 makes it the evidential basis of verification - so every item of file content listed in the answer is authoritative secondary, drawn from the Organization's guidelines, which the corpus does not hold and which were not read. Second, regulation 22.2 refers the entire calculation method out to those guidelines and the regulation itself prints no formula, no coefficient, no reference line and no reduction factor. The corpus record states that it can say an attained EEDI must be calculated and cannot state the equation. This answer respects that boundary exactly: it explains the structure and the inputs and does not reproduce the formula.

No numeric value from regulation 24's tables is asserted. No reduction factor, phase date, size-band threshold or reference-line parameter appears anywhere in this answer, because each varies by ship type and size band and no single figure would be true generally. The answer states the structure and directs the reader to the tables. Likewise the speed-power trial correction procedure is described by effect: no standard document is held and no standard designation, revision or coefficient is asserted.

Temporally this question is clean. The corpus's amendment sweep records that no resolution in the held in-force chain operates on regulation 22 - it is one of the Annex's unamended units and the base text of MEPC.328(76) is the current text. MEPC.385(81), deemed accepted in the sitting month itself, operates on regulations 2, 13, 14, 18 and 27 and appendices I and IX, and touches nothing in this answer; it is in any event not in force until 1 August 2025. The IMO Net-Zero Framework is post-sitting and is excluded, and the two later MIW answers that legitimately carry it were not consulted.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A three-limb technical-regulatory question about the VERIFICATION of the EEDI rather than about its calculation. Limb (a) asks what the EEDI Technical File contains; limb (b) asks the scope of preliminary verification at design stage; limb (c) asks about final verification at sea trial. The examiner is testing whether the candidate understands WHY verification is in two stages - that everything is known on paper except the ship's speed - and whether they know the duty allocation, in particular that the Administration verifies rather than calculates or approves. The engineering content the question really rewards is the sea trial: measurement, correction to the reference condition, and revision of the file.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, set as 5 + 5 + 6. Three limbs, three regions, with the sea-trial limb slightly the largest - which is correct, because it contains the real engineering. Two short framing sections precede the limbs: where the duty comes from, and who does what. They cost little and they set up all three limbs.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For (a): ship and machinery particulars, capacity, rated power and specific fuel consumption from the NOx Technical File, carbon factor, auxiliary power, the estimated reference speed with its tank-test and power-curve basis, the correction factors with their justification, innovative technology claims with evidence, the calculation process itself, and the comparison against the required EEDI. For (b): submission of the file to the Administration or its authorized organization before delivery, checking of applicability, category and phase, independent recomputation of the required EEDI, checking of every input against its source, and close interrogation of the tank test - concluding with the point that it is preliminary only because the speed is a prediction. For (c): trial in the presence of the verifier at or near the reference condition, double runs on reciprocal courses, measurement of speed and shaft power, correction for wind, waves, current, depth, density and displacement, revision of the technical file with the measured speed, recalculation of the attained EEDI, confirmation against the required EEDI, and issue of the IEEC.

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW for the regulation and MEDIUM for the method. Regulation 22 is unamended and regulation 24's structure is stable, so the architecture in this answer does not go stale. But regulation 22.2 refers the whole calculation method out to Organization guidelines that sit OUTSIDE the Annex and can be revised without any amendment to the regulation - so the operative method is time-variable while the regulation is not. The mitigation is that no formula, coefficient, reduction factor or phase date is asserted anywhere.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW - MARPOL Annex VI is international and operates through the flag Administration and its authorized organizations. No Indian statute is engaged. The one allocation risk is internal rather than jurisdictional: attributing the calculation or an approval to the Administration when the regulation gives it only a verification function.
technical_ambiguities: The stem says 'verification of EEDI of a new ship', but regulation 22 also brings in new ships that have undergone a major conversion and ships whose conversion is so extensive that the Administration regards them as newly constructed. The answer states the full cohort once, because the Administration's opinion in that third limb is itself examinable.

'Preliminary' and 'final' are the language of the survey and certification guidelines rather than of the Annex. The Annex speaks of an initial survey verifying the attained EEDI. The answer uses the stem's own vocabulary and anchors it to regulation 5.4 so that the relationship is clear.

The calculation formula is deliberately not reproduced. Regulation 22.2 refers the method out and the corpus record states that the corpus cannot state the equation. The answer explains the structure and the inputs instead, which is what limb (a) actually asks for.
No reduction factor, phase date or reference-line parameter is asserted, because each varies by ship type and size band and no single figure would be true generally.

Sections 3 and 4 are limb (a), splitting the file into ship and machinery data, then speed, correction factors and the calculation. Sections 5 and 6 are limb (b): what preliminary verification is and when, then what the verifier interrogates and why it is only preliminary. Sections 7 and 8 are limb (c): the trial with its measurement and correction, then final verification as a numbered sequence ending in the certificate and the reporting duty.

questions.understand_first: The EEDI is a design index - grammes of CO2 per tonne-mile that the ship's design will produce - and it is fixed by what the ship is, not by how she is run. That single fact separates it from the CII, which is operational and moves every year. The question is about verification, and the whole of it falls out of one observation: at the design stage every input to the index is already known except one. Capacity, rated power, specific fuel consumption from the engine's NOx Technical File, the carbon factor, the auxiliary load - all of these exist on paper. The one quantity that cannot be known until the ship exists and runs is her speed at 75 % of rated power, and at design that is a prediction from a tank test. So the file is verified twice: once on the prediction, which is what lets construction and trials proceed on an agreed basis, and again on the measurement, after which the file is revised and the index becomes final. Two other things are worth fixing before writing. The Administration verifies; it does not calculate and it does not approve - the shipbuilder calculates and the technical file is the evidence, and the verification may be done by the Administration or by any organization duly authorized by it. And the Annex is deliberately silent on the detail: regulation 22 prints no formula, no coefficient and no reference line, and it never even defines the EEDI technical file. The method lives in Organization guidelines. Knowing that the regulation refers its own method outward is itself worth a mark, and it is why an answer should explain the structure of the calculation rather than attempt the equation.

steps.title: Where the duty comes from, and why verification is in two stages
points: EEDI is a design index - CO2 per unit of transport work, fixed by what the ship is
MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4, revised Annex adopted by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2023
Regulation 22 - the attained EEDI must be calculated, be ship-specific, be accompanied by the EEDI technical file showing the process of calculation, and be verified on the basis of that file
Regulation 24 - the attained value must not exceed the required EEDI, the reference line reduced by a factor from Table 1 with reference-line parameters in Table 2
Regulation 5.4 - the initial survey verifying the attained EEDI and the SEEMP, and the major-conversion surveys
Regulation 19 - chapter 4 applies from 400 gross tonnage, excludes domestic-only, unpropelled and platforms, and 19.3 disapplies regulations 22 to 25 to non-conventional propulsion
Two stages exist because the reference speed is a prediction at design and a measurement after trial

steps.title: Who does what - and the trap inside it
points: The shipbuilder or owner calculates the attained EEDI, prepares and submits the file, conducts the trial and revises the file
The verifier - the Administration or any organization duly authorized by it - verifies on the basis of the file, attends the trial and confirms the final value
The Administration alone forms the opinion that a converted ship is regarded as newly constructed; that is not delegable
The Administration or its authorized organization reports the required and attained values and relevant information to the Organization within seven months of the regulation 5.4 survey
The trap: the Administration does NOT calculate and does NOT approve the attained EEDI - it verifies it
Regulation 22 imposes no duty on any ship, owner or company; the design obligation bites through regulation 24 and through survey and certification

steps.title: The EEDI Technical File - ship, machinery and capacity data
points: The Annex does not define the file; regulation 22.1 requires it to carry the information necessary for the calculation and to show the process of the calculation
Ship particulars, IMO number, flag, class, ship type and regulation 2.2 category, shipyard and hull number, and the contract, keel and delivery dates that fix the phase
Capacity - deadweight at summer load draught, or gross tonnage for passenger and ro-ro passenger ships - with lightweight, displacement and load line draught
Main engine maker, type, number, rated power and speed, and specific fuel consumption taken from the NOx Technical File; any power limitation arrangement
Auxiliary engine data and specific fuel consumption, likewise from the NOx Technical File
The electrical power table and the derivation of auxiliary power
Fuel type and carbon conversion factor, with dual-fuel and pilot-fuel treatment where relevant, and shaft generator or motor arrangements

steps.title: The EEDI Technical File - speed, correction factors and the calculation
points: The reference speed at 75 % of rated installed power in the maximum design load condition, deep water, calm weather - with the tank test report, model-ship correlation, power curve and the tank's quality-system status as evidence, and stated as an estimate at design stage
Correction factors with their justification - design elements, ice class and capacity limitation, cubic capacity, general cargo cranes, shaft motors, and the weather factor where claimed

Innovative energy efficiency technology - waste heat recovery, wind assistance, solar, air lubrication - described and evidenced, separating power saved from power generated, with the test basis for the claim
The calculation itself: every input with its source, the process set out so it can be reproduced, and the resulting attained EEDI
The required EEDI computed under regulation 24 and the comparison showing the attained value does not exceed it
The description of the intended sea trial and of the correction procedure to be used
No formula is reproduced - regulation 22.2 refers the method out and regulation 22 prints no formula, coefficient or reference line

steps.title: Preliminary verification at the design stage - what it is and when
points: At the design stage, before construction is complete and before delivery, as the first part of the initial survey under regulation 5.4

The owner or builder submits the EEDI technical file with the tank test report and power curve, NOx Technical File extracts, capacity and load-line documentation, the electrical load table, and evidence for every factor and technology claimed
To the verifier - the Administration or an organization duly authorized by it, in practice the recognised organization acting for the flag State
The object is to establish before the ship exists in final form that the design will comply, so a non-compliance is found on paper where it can still be corrected by design change

steps.title: What the verifier interrogates - and why it is only preliminary
points: Applicability and phase - is she within chapter 4 at all, which regulation 2.2 category, and which phase do the contract, keel and delivery dates place her in
Independent recomputation of the required EEDI under regulation 24 with the correct reference line and reduction factor
The calculation method against the current calculation guidelines, including that the correct edition was used

Each input against its source - capacity against load line and stability information, rated power against engine documentation, specific fuel consumption against the NOx Technical File rather than a brochure, carbon factor against the fuel, auxiliary power against a defensible load table

The tank test and power curve behind the speed prediction - test conditions, model scale, extrapolation method and the tank's quality system; the verifier may witness the model test or call for more data
Correction factors and innovative technology claims against their justification; an unsupported factor is removed and the value recalculated
The trial plan - that the proposed condition, measurements and corrections will produce a usable reference speed
Outcome: preliminary verification confirmed. It is preliminary for one reason only - the reference speed is still a prediction

steps.title: The sea trial - conduct, measurement and correction
points: Conducted by the shipbuilder in the presence of the verifier, who examines the conduct as well as the result
At the EEDI reference load condition or close enough to correct back, with draught, trim and displacement measured and hull and propeller confirmed clean
Environment recorded - wind, sea state and swell, water depth, current, water temperature and density; run in deep water where possible because shallow-water correction is large and uncertain
Speed and shaft power measured over runs at several settings spanning the EEDI power point, shaft power from a calibrated torsion meter
Double runs on reciprocal courses at each setting so the effect of current cancels in the mean

Correction to the reference condition by the recognised trial-analysis procedure for wind, waves, current, shallow water, temperature and density, and displacement and trim deviation, giving a corrected power-speed curve from which the speed at 75 % of rated power is read
For a series ship not separately trialled, the lead ship's result may be used where the ships are demonstrably identical and the reliance is justified in the file

steps.title: Final verification - revision, comparison and certification
points: Compare the corrected trial speed with the estimate used in the file
Revise the technical file - replace the estimated speed with the measured corrected value and recalculate the attained EEDI; every other input stands as verified at design stage
The verifier examines the trial procedure, the measured data and the corrections applied, not merely the resulting number

Confirm that the final attained EEDI does not exceed the required EEDI under regulation 24; exceeding it is non-compliance with no tolerance, and the remedy is a design or operational change and re-verification
With the regulation 5.4 initial survey complete, the International Energy Efficiency Certificate is issued under regulation 6 and the verified technical file is retained on board
The Administration or its authorized organization reports the required and attained values and relevant information to the Organization within seven months of completion of the survey
The design is then fixed - operation moves the CII, not the attained EEDI

questions.memory_cue: One sentence carries it - EVERYTHING IS KNOWN ON PAPER EXCEPT THE SPEED, SO VERIFY TWICE (1). Remember who acts: the builder calculates, the verifier VERIFIES (2). Then the three limbs in order - FILE (3, 4), DESIGN (5, 6), TRIAL (7, 8) - and inside the last one the sequence RUN, CORRECT, REVISE, RECALCULATE, COMPARE, CERTIFY (7, 8).

quick_revision.recall_15s: EEDI is a DESIGN index - CO2 per tonne-mile, fixed by the design. MARPOL Annex VI ch.4, MEPC.328(76), in force 1 Nov 2023. Reg 22 - attained EEDI must be calculated, be ship-specific, be accompanied by the EEDI technical file showing the process of calculation, and be verified by the Administration or any organization duly authorized by it. ⚠ The Administration VERIFIES - it does not calculate and does not approve. Reg 24 - attained must not exceed required (reference line reduced by a factor; Table 1 factors, Table 2 parameters). Reg 5.4 - initial survey verifying attained EEDI and SEEMP. Reg 19 - 400 GT and above; 19.3 disapplies regs 22-25 to non-conventional propulsion. Reg 22.2 refers the whole calculation method out to Organization guidelines - the regulation prints no formula. File: particulars, category, dates and phase, capacity, engine MCR and SFC from the NOx Technical File, carbon factor, auxiliary power, estimated Vref from tank test and power curve, correction factors with justification, innovative technology with evidence, the calculation, and the required-EEDI comparison. Preliminary: everything checked, one estimate accepted. Trial: reference condition, double runs on reciprocal courses to cancel current, deep water, calibrated torsion meter, correct to reference condition. Final: revise the file, recalculate, compare, issue the IEEC under reg 6, and report to IMO within seven months. Operation moves the CII, never the attained EEDI.
critical_numbers: Chapter 4 applies to ships of 400 gross tonnage and above - regulation 19
The reference speed is taken at 75 % of the rated installed power, in the maximum design load condition, deep water and calm weather
The attained EEDI must not exceed the required EEDI - the reference line value reduced by the applicable reduction factor from regulation 24 Table 1
The required and attained EEDI values and relevant information are reported to the Organization within seven months of completion of the regulation 5.4 survey
Regulation 19.3 disapplies regulations 22 to 25 to ships with non-conventional propulsion
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 22 read with regulation 24 - regulation 22 creates the attained EEDI, requires the technical file and allocates verification, while regulation 24 supplies the ceiling the verified value must meet. Regulation 22.2 refers the calculation method itself out to Organization guidelines, so the regulation prints no formula at all
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying the Administration calculates or approves the attained EEDI. It does neither - the shipbuilder calculates and the Administration, or any organization duly authorized by it, verifies on the basis of the EEDI technical file. Second trap: treating the EEDI as something that changes with how the ship is operated. It does not - a fouled hull or a slow-steaming voyage moves the CII and leaves the attained EEDI untouched. Third: forgetting that after the trial the technical file must be revised with the measured corrected speed and the attained EEDI recalculated before it can be compared against the required value.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the EEDI verification question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Where the duty comes from and why verification is in two stages. 2 Who does what. 3 The technical file - ship, machinery and capacity data. 4 The technical file - speed, correction factors and the calculation. 5 Preliminary verification, what and when. 6 What the verifier interrogates and why it is preliminary. 7 The sea trial - measurement and correction. 8 Final verification, revision and certification. Sections 3-4 are limb (a), 5-6 limb (b), 7-8 limb (c).
retrieval_cards.why: Two framing sections cost little and set up all three limbs; the trial limb carries the most marks so it gets the sequence treatment.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who calculates the attained EEDI and who verifies it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The shipbuilder or owner calculates it and prepares the EEDI technical file as the evidence. Regulation 22.1 requires the attained EEDI to be verified on the basis of that file, either by the Administration or by any organization duly authorized by it. The Administration does not calculate the value and does not approve it - it verifies it. The one function not delegable is the Administration's opinion that a converted ship is to be regarded as newly constructed.
retrieval_cards.why: Misallocating the calculation to the Administration misstates the whole scheme, and the regulation is precise about it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is EEDI verification carried out in two stages?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because at the design stage every input to the index is already known on paper - capacity, rated power, specific fuel consumption from the NOx Technical File, carbon factor and auxiliary load - except one: the ship's speed at 75 % of rated power, which at design is only a prediction from tank tests. So the file is verified once on the prediction, and again after the trial on the measured, corrected speed, when the file is revised and the index becomes final.
retrieval_cards.why: One unknown quantity explains the entire two-stage architecture, and stating it organises both limbs (b) and (c).

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must the EEDI Technical File contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: Ship particulars, type, category, and the contract, keel and delivery dates that fix the phase; capacity with its basis; engine maker, type, rated power and specific fuel consumption from the NOx Technical File; fuel type and carbon factor; the electrical power table and auxiliary power; the reference speed with its tank test and power curve; each correction factor with its justification; innovative technology claims with their test basis; the calculation process set out so it can be reproduced; and the comparison against the required EEDI.
retrieval_cards.why: Regulation 22.1 requires the file to carry the information necessary for the calculation and to show the process of the calculation - the file is the evidence on which verification rests.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the verifier check at preliminary verification?
retrieval_cards.answer: That the ship is within chapter 4 and not excluded, her category and phase; the required EEDI recomputed independently under regulation 24 with the correct reference line and reduction factor; the calculation method against the current guidelines; every input against its source - capacity, rated power, specific fuel consumption against the NOx Technical File, carbon factor, and auxiliary power against a defensible load table; the tank test and power curve behind the estimated speed; and each correction factor and technology claim against its justification.
retrieval_cards.why: It is where every input except speed is fixed, so a non-compliance is found on paper while a design change can still cure it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does the speed trial use double runs on reciprocal courses?
retrieval_cards.answer: So that the effect of current cancels in the mean. A single run measures speed over ground, which includes any current component; running the same power setting on opposite headings and averaging removes it. Trials are also run in deep water where possible, because the shallow-water correction is large and uncertain, and the results are then corrected for wind, waves, remaining current, water temperature and density and any deviation of displacement and trim from the reference condition.
retrieval_cards.why: An engineer who can explain why reciprocal runs are used has shown understanding rather than recall of a checklist.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens at final verification if the trial speed differs from the prediction?
retrieval_cards.answer: The technical file must be revised: the estimated reference speed is replaced with the measured, corrected value and the attained EEDI is recalculated, every other input standing as verified at design stage. The verifier examines the trial procedure, the measured data and the corrections applied, then confirms that the final attained EEDI does not exceed the required EEDI under regulation 24. If it does exceed it, the ship does not comply and a design or operational change and re-verification are required.
retrieval_cards.why: The revision step is the one most often omitted, and it is the whole reason the design-stage verification is called preliminary.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do EEDI, EEXI and CII differ?
retrieval_cards.answer: EEDI is a design index applied to new ships and to ships converted so extensively that the Administration regards them as newly constructed; it is fixed by the design and does not change with operation. EEXI applies the same style of index once to existing ships. CII is operational, calculated every year from fuel actually consumed and distance actually sailed, so it moves with hull condition, speed and trading pattern.
retrieval_cards.why: Only the CII responds to how the ship is run, and mixing the three is the commonest error in the topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is issued once verification is complete, and what reporting follows?
retrieval_cards.answer: With the initial survey under regulation 5.4 complete, the International Energy Efficiency Certificate is issued under regulation 6, and the verified EEDI technical file is retained on board as the evidence supporting it. For a ship also subject to regulation 24, the Administration or its authorized organization reports the required and attained EEDI values and relevant information to the Organization by electronic communication within seven months of completion of the survey.
retrieval_cards.why: The certificate and the seven-month reporting duty are the two end-points of the process and both are examinable.

blocks.h: 1. What a P&I club is - and the gap it exists to fill

blocks.p: A Protection and Indemnity club is a mutual, non-profit-making association of shipowners, charterers and operators, formed to insure the third-party liabilities that arise from owning and operating ships. It is insurance, but it is not insurance as ordinarily understood - and the differences are the first marks in limb A.

The gap it fills. A ship's hull and machinery policy insures the ship herself. It does not insure what the ship does to other people - and historically it did not even cover the whole of that in collision, because the market's collision liability clause left a proportion of the liability with the owner, and covered nothing at all for cargo, crew, pollution or wreck. Nineteenth-century shipowners created the clubs to carry the liabilities the commercial market would not. That origin still explains the shape of the cover: a club insures liabilities, not property.

blocks.h: 2. How a club is constituted, and what else it gives a member

ul: The rules are the contract. A member's cover is defined by the club rules, and the Certificate of Entry evidences the entry of the ship, the classes of cover and any special terms. There is no policy in the market sense.
The board is the membership. Directors are drawn from member shipowners, and it is the board - not a claims department answering to shareholders - that decides discretionary matters.

The omnibus rule. Most clubs give the board a discretion to meet a claim that falls outside the strict wording but within the spirit of mutuality. That discretion is only possible because there are no shareholders whose money would be given away.

Far more than a payer of claims. A club supplies a worldwide network of correspondents; immediate casualty response; legal and technical advice; condition surveys of older or newly entered ships; loss-prevention work; and - critically for an operating ship - security: a club letter of undertaking given to a claimant will usually secure the release of an arrested ship without cash being put up or a bank guarantee bought.

Certification. A club issues the evidence of insurance - commonly called a blue card - on which a flag State issues the certificates required by the liability conventions: oil pollution under the Civil Liability Convention, bunker pollution under the Bunkers Convention 2001, wreck removal under the Nairobi Convention 2007, passenger liability under the Athens regime, and the financial security for abandonment and for death and long-term disability introduced by the 2014 amendments to the Maritime Labour Convention. Without club cover a ship cannot hold those certificates, and without those certificates she cannot trade.

A note on Indian law. In an Indian examination the governing marine insurance statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 - not the United Kingdom Act of 1906. And under the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, unpaid insurance premium including mutual insurance calls is expressly a maritime claim, so a club is itself a potential arresting party.

blocks.h: 3. The International Group, the Pool and the collective reinsurance

blocks.p: No single club could pay a very large claim from its own resources, and a member needs to know that it could. The answer is a three-tier structure, and understanding it is what makes 'unlimited cover' a credible statement rather than a slogan:

ol: The club's own retention. Each club pays claims up to a retained amount from its own funds.

The Pool. Above that retention, the clubs in the International Group of P&I Clubs share the claim among themselves under the Pooling Agreement, each contributing according to an agreed formula. A single member's disaster is therefore borne by the world fleet.

The collective reinsurance. Above the Pool, the Group buys excess-of-loss reinsurance in the commercial market as one buyer, which secures far greater capacity and a better price than any club could obtain alone.

blocks.p: And above even that sits the overspill call - described in section 4. The Group's clubs between them cover the great majority of the world's ocean-going tonnage, which is why the arrangement works at all.

blocks.h: 4. How the funds are collected - the call system

blocks.p: A club does not charge premiums. It makes calls. The distinction is the whole of mutuality: the members do not buy a product at a fixed price, they share the year's cost between them. The forms of call are these.

ul: The advance call - sometimes the mutual premium. At the start of the policy year, the club estimates its total outgoings for the year - claims, its share of pooled claims, the reinsurance premium and management expenses - and calls that amount from the members in proportion to their assessed share. It is an estimate, and it is collected before the claims are known. Many clubs split the estimated total call into an advance instalment and a deferred instalment, so a member has budget certainty for most of the year.

The supplementary or additional call - and this is the defining feature of a mutual. If the year's claims, reinsurance and expenses exceed the advance calls collected together with investment income, the club calls the difference from the members. A member's cost for a policy year is therefore not finally known until the year is closed. Conversely, a well-run year with good investment returns may see a return of call or a discount at renewal.

The release call. A member leaving the club, or transferring a ship out, may pay a release call to buy itself out of liability for future supplementary calls on the open policy years during which it was a member. Without it the departing member remains exposed to years that have not yet closed.

The overspill call - the top of the whole structure. If a claim exceeds the limit of the Group's collective reinsurance, the excess is met by an overspill call levied on the members of all the Group clubs, assessed by reference to entered tonnage. It is the ultimate expression of mutuality, and it has in practice never had to be levied.

Other elements of a member's cost. The reinsurance element of the call is commonly charged as a separate rate per gross ton by ship type - tankers, dry cargo and passenger ships carrying different rates because they present different pollution and personal-injury exposures. Each claim is also subject to a deductible borne by the member, which keeps small claims out of the mutual system.

Fixed premium entries. Clubs also write some business - smaller craft, and much charterers' cover - on a fixed premium basis with no supplementary calls. The trade-off is that such cover is normally subject to a stated limit rather than being unlimited, so it is not mutual cover in the full sense.

Policy year accounting. Contributions and claims are accounted by policy year, traditionally running from noon on 20 February. A year stays open while claims develop and is closed when the club is satisfied they are settled - which is why supplementary calls can arrive long after the year in question, and why free reserves accumulated over past years are used to smooth them.

blocks.h: 5. What determines a member's contribution, and on what conditions cover rests

ul: Rating factors. The entered tonnage; the ship type and age; the trade and geographical range - a United States trade attracts a very different pollution exposure from a coastal one; the crew nationality and terms of employment, which drive the personal-injury exposure; the member's claims record, which is the largest single influence at renewal; the management standard and its inspection and vetting record; and the classes of cover and deductibles chosen.

Conditions on which cover rests. The ship must be in class with an approved society and hold her statutory certificates; the member must comply with flag State requirements; and the club must be notified of casualties and claims promptly and its directions followed.

The 'pay to be paid' rule. Classically, a club indemnifies - the member must first have discharged the liability before the club reimburses it. That is the historical rule and it is why the club's obligation is an indemnity rather than a promise to a third party; it is displaced in the cases where a convention gives a claimant a direct right of action against the insurer, which the pollution and wreck conventions do.
Cover can be prejudiced by conduct - unapproved contractual terms accepted by the member, unlawful trade, want of due diligence, or a failure to disclose material facts.

blocks.h: 6. 'Protection' - liabilities to persons and to property other than cargo

blocks.p: ⚠ State the division before listing it. The two words are historical, and they still divide the cover accurately in principle even though modern club rules are set out as numbered classes rather than under two headings: 'protection' is the liabilities arising from the ship as a ship - to people, and to property other than the cargo she carries. 'Indemnity' is the liabilities arising from the cargo and the contract of carriage.
Protection risks - people:

ul: Crew - illness, injury and death; hospital, medical and funeral expenses; repatriation and substitute expenses; loss of personal effects; and the financial security for abandonment and for contractual claims for death or long-term disability required by the Maritime Labour Convention.
Passengers - death, injury, delay and loss of or damage to their effects, under the Athens regime.
Others on board or affected - stevedores, pilots, surveyors, supernumeraries and visitors; and persons injured ashore by the ship's operations.
Stowaways, refugees and persons rescued at sea - maintenance, repatriation and the associated diversion expenses.
Life salvage - awards payable for the saving of life.

blocks.p: Protection risks - property other than cargo, and the ship's effect on the world:

ul: Collision liability - the proportion of collision liability to the other ship that is not covered by the hull policy, together with any excess over the hull value, and the cargo and other consequential claims arising out of the collision.

Damage to fixed and floating objects - berths, piers, jetties, dolphins, buoys, locks, bridges, submarine cables and pipelines, and terminal equipment. Commonly the largest routine liability an operating ship generates.

Pollution - liability for oil and other pollutants, the cost of clean-up and preventive measures, and the associated fines and compensation for consequential loss to fisheries and tourism. This is the single largest exposure the system carries.
Wreck removal - the cost of raising, removing, destroying, lighting or marking the wreck of the entered ship where that is compulsory by law, and liability for failing to do so.
Towage liabilities arising under approved towage contracts, and liabilities under other approved contracts and indemnities.
Quarantine and disinfection expenses arising from an outbreak of infectious disease on board.

Fines - for pollution, for customs and immigration infringements including in respect of the crew, for breach of safety or immigration regulations, and for short or over-delivery of cargo. Fines are frequently covered at the board's discretion rather than as of right, and never where the conduct was deliberate.
Enquiry, legal and claims-handling costs, and the cost of sue and labour measures taken to avoid or minimise a liability the club would otherwise have carried.

blocks.h: 7. 'Indemnity' - cargo and the contract of carriage

ul: Loss of, shortage of, damage to, or delay to cargo carried on board the entered ship - the classic indemnity risk, and the reason the second half of the name exists.

Liability arising under the contract of carriage - the bill of lading, waybill or charterparty - where the terms are on a basis the club approves. A member who signs up to liabilities more onerous than the standard regime may find that part of the exposure outside cover.
The ship's proportion of general average that is not recoverable from cargo because of a breach of the contract of carriage - unseaworthiness being the usual reason.
Cargo's proportion of general average or salvage that the member has to bear.
Through-transport liabilities where the ship is part of a combined-transport operation.

Consequences of misdelivery - cargo discharged at the wrong port, over-carried, or delivered without production of the bill of lading, again subject to the club's rules and often to its prior agreement.
The cost of disposing of damaged or unclaimed cargo, and liability for damage to containers and other equipment not owned by the member.

blocks.h: 8. The limits, and what is not covered at all

blocks.p: Cover is unlimited for most risks - but not all, and the exceptions matter. The two principal capped classes are oil pollution and passenger and seamen claims, each subject to a limit per event fixed by the International Group and revised from time to time; the passenger limit sits as a sub-limit within the combined passenger-and-seamen figure. The limits are commercial figures, not statutory ones, so a candidate should give them as such and not as though they were treaty limits.
What a club does not cover:

ul: Damage to the entered ship herself, and her salvage - that is the hull and machinery policy.
Loss of hire or loss of earnings - separate cover, bought if the member wants it.
War risks - separately insured, though clubs write supplementary war-risk P&I cover.
Cargo owned by the member itself.
Crew wages as such - these are a contractual debt, not a liability arising from an incident, although abandonment financial security responds where the Maritime Labour Convention requires it.
Liabilities from deliberate or reckless conduct, unlawful trades, or a want of due diligence.
Liabilities voluntarily assumed under unapproved contracts.

blocks.p: One negative worth stating, because it is examinable: the HNS Convention 2010 is not in force, so there is no HNS certification regime for a club to support - unlike the oil pollution, bunkers, wreck removal and passenger conventions, which are all in force and all certificated.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Two limbs at 8 marks each. Limb A has two distinct demands - what a club is, and how it collects funds - and the second is the specific one, so it needs its own section and its own detail. The comparison table with ordinary insurance is worth writing because it earns several marks in a few lines and frames everything after it. Limb B is a classification question, so the answer must first state the division and then list under each heading; listing risks without saying which word they belong to answers half the question. Ending on the limits and exclusions is what separates a management-level answer from a recitation.

blocks.h: The one idea that organises limb B

blocks.p: Protection is liabilities to persons and to property other than cargo. Indemnity is cargo and the contract of carriage. That single sentence lets a candidate place any risk correctly on the spot without memorising two lists - collision, pollution, wreck, crew, passengers, fixed and floating objects and fines are all protection; cargo loss, damage, delay, misdelivery and the unrecoverable general average contribution are all indemnity. Be honest, too, that the division is historical: modern rulebooks are organised as numbered classes of cover, and the two words survive mainly in the name.

blocks.h: Mutuality is the whole of limb A

blocks.p: Everything distinctive about a club follows from one fact: the members are the insurers. There are no shareholders, so there is no profit motive, so the cover can be sold at cost - and so the club can have an omnibus rule letting the board pay a claim that falls outside the wording but within the spirit of mutuality, which no commercial insurer could offer. It is also why the contribution is a call and not a premium: the members are not buying a product at a price, they are sharing a year's cost, and if the cost turns out higher they pay the difference. Say that once and the four kinds of call become obvious rather than a list to memorise.

blocks.h: Why 'unlimited cover' is credible

blocks.p: A single club could not pay a very large claim, so the credibility rests on four tiers: the club's own retention; then the Pool, in which the International Group clubs share the claim under the Pooling Agreement; then the collective excess-of-loss reinsurance the Group buys in the market as one buyer, which secures capacity no single club could; and finally the overspill call on the members of every Group club, assessed on entered tonnage. A candidate who can name all four has explained why a mutual can promise what a commercial insurer cannot.

blocks.h: Why this matters to a ship, not just to an office

blocks.p: Three practical consequences are worth a line each. Without club cover a ship cannot hold her convention certificates - CLC, Bunkers, Nairobi, Athens and the MLC financial security all rest on the club's evidence of insurance - and without them she cannot trade. A club letter of undertaking is what gets an arrested ship released without cash or a bank guarantee. And in India, unpaid mutual insurance calls are themselves a maritime claim under the Admiralty Act, 2017 - so the club that secures your release for someone else's claim can arrest you for its own.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Calling the contribution a premium. It is a call, and the difference is the whole of mutuality.
Saying cover is always unlimited. Oil pollution and passenger and seamen claims are capped.
Listing risks in limb B without dividing them into protection and indemnity. That is the question.
Putting cargo under protection, or collision under indemnity.
Saying a club covers damage to the entered ship. That is hull and machinery.
Omitting the Pool and the collective reinsurance, and so leaving 'unlimited cover' unexplained.
Forgetting the release call and the overspill call - the two that show real understanding of the call system.
Citing the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 in an Indian examination. The Indian statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Asking why it is called a call rather than a premium.
Asking what happens if a club's claims for a year exceed the advance calls collected.
Asking what a member pays when it leaves the club, expecting the release call.
Asking what happens to a claim that exceeds the reinsurance, expecting the overspill call on all Group members by entered tonnage.
Asking which side of the division fines fall on - protection, and usually at the board's discretion.
Asking whether the club pays before or after the member does, expecting 'pay to be paid' and the convention exceptions giving a direct right of action against the insurer.
Asking what document gets an arrested ship released - a club letter of undertaking.
Asking which liability convention has no certification regime because it is not in force - HNS 2010.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your ship strikes a berth and damages a loading arm. Which policy responds, and under which heading?
A crew member is injured and repatriated. Who pays, and what document proves the cover exists?
You receive a supplementary call three years after the policy year. How is that possible?
Your ship is arrested for a cargo claim in Kochi. How does the club get her released?
What is the difference between your P&I entry and the hull and machinery policy?
Why do tankers pay a different reinsurance rate from dry cargo ships?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb A in three moves - MUTUAL (members are the insurers), TIERS (retention, Pool, collective reinsurance, overspill), CALLS (advance, supplementary, release, overspill). Limb B on one sentence - PROTECTION IS PEOPLE AND EVERYTHING THAT IS NOT CARGO; INDEMNITY IS CARGO AND THE CONTRACT OF CARRIAGE - then run protection in two passes, people then property and pollution, and finish on limits and exclusions.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: Club rules and the Certificate of Entry - the contract of cover; there is no policy in the market sense.
The Pooling Agreement of the International Group, and the Group's collective excess-of-loss reinsurance.
Civil Liability Convention - oil pollution certification; Bunkers Convention 2001 - bunker pollution certification.
Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007, in force 14 April 2015 - wreck removal certification.
Athens Convention regime - passenger liability certification.

Maritime Labour Convention, 2006, as amended - the 2014 amendments requiring financial security for abandonment and for contractual claims for death and long-term disability; the 2022 amendments in force 23 December 2024.
HNS Convention 2010 - NOT in force; no certification regime at this sitting.
Marine Insurance Act, 1963 (India) - the governing marine insurance statute in an Indian examination; not the UK Act of 1906.
Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, section 4 - insurance premium including mutual insurance calls is a maritime claim.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence limits

blocks.p: ⚠ The corpus holds no club rulebook, no Pooling Agreement and no International Group document, and the industry-organisations file classifies the whole area as citation and index only. The description of mutuality, the call system, the Pool, the reinsurance structure and the classes of cover is therefore industry guidance throughout, and it is labelled as such rather than presented as though a rule had been read.

Two figures are handled with particular care. The monetary limits on oil pollution and on passenger and seamen claims are set commercially by the International Group and revised from time to time, and no Group document is held - so they are described as the limits commonly applied, expressly as commercial rather than statutory figures, and flagged for a currency check. The number of clubs in the Group is deliberately not asserted, because it has changed through mergers and no held source establishes it at this sitting. The traditional noon 20 February policy year is likewise given as club practice rather than as a rule.

The division itself is described honestly. Modern club rules are organised as numbered classes of cover and are not divided under the headings 'protection' and 'indemnity'. The two words are historical and survive mainly in the name. The answer says so, and then gives the division - which remains an accurate description of the underlying structure and is exactly what the stem asks for.

The convention-backed elements are on firmer ground and were checked against the sitting. The Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention has been in force since 14 April 2015; the MLC financial-security amendments are in force and the 2022 set entered into force on 23 December 2024, two months before this paper; and the HNS Convention 2010 is not in force, which is recorded as a negative rather than passed over. known_traps.md section 8 is applied: the Indian marine insurance statute cited is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, and the UK Act of 1906 does not appear.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A two-limb commercial question. Limb A asks what P&I clubs are AND how they collect funds from shipowners - two demands, of which the funding mechanism is the specific and less commonly answered one. Limb B asks what risks fall under each of the two words in the name, which is a classification question rather than a list question. The examiner is testing whether the candidate understands MUTUALITY - that the members are the insurers, which is why the contribution is a call and not a premium - and whether they can place any given liability on the correct side of the protection/indemnity division rather than reciting a mixed list.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, set as 8 + 8. Two equal limbs and two equal regions. Within limb A the constitution and the call system share the marks about evenly, and the International Group structure is what makes the funding answer coherent. Within limb B the division must be stated before the lists, because the classification is the question.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For limb A: mutual, non-profit, members are both insurer and insured, no shareholders, board drawn from the membership, the club rules and Certificate of Entry as the contract, unlimited cover for most risks, and the reason for existence - the liabilities the hull and machinery policy does not carry. Then the call system: advance call estimated at the start of the policy year, supplementary call if the year is short, release call on departure, and overspill call on all Group members if a claim exceeds the collective reinsurance - with the Pool and the collective reinsurance explained so 'unlimited' is credible. For limb B: the division stated, then protection risks (crew, passengers, others on board, stowaways, life salvage, collision liability not covered by hull, fixed and floating objects, pollution, wreck removal, quarantine, fines, legal costs) and indemnity risks (cargo loss, damage, shortage and delay, contract of carriage liabilities, unrecoverable general average, misdelivery), closing on limits and exclusions.

The monetary limits and the number of clubs in the Group are commercial and are revised without any entry-into-force machinery - so the limits are flagged and the club count is not asserted at all. decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM, and it is the trap known_traps.md section 8 exists for. technical_ambiguities: The stem's grammar - 'What is P&I clubs' - is as printed and is reproduced without correction.

The protection/indemnity division is historical. Modern club rules are organised as numbered classes of cover and are not divided under those two headings. The answer states that expressly, then gives the division, because the division remains an accurate description of the underlying structure and is what the stem asks for.

'How P&I clubs collect fund from ship-owners' is asking about the call mechanism specifically, not about club finances generally. The answer gives the four kinds of call, plus deductibles, the reinsurance element and policy-year accounting, rather than a discussion of investment income and reserves.

Cover is described as unlimited for most risks with stated exceptions. Saying it is unlimited without qualification would be wrong, and giving the capped classes without saying the limits are commercial rather than statutory would be misleading.

questions.understand_first: Everything distinctive about a P&I club follows from one fact: the members are the insurers. A club is a mutual, non-profit association of shipowners, charterers and operators - there are no shareholders, the board is drawn from the membership, and the cover is provided at cost. That is why the contribution is a call and not a premium: a member is not buying a product at a fixed price, it is sharing the year's cost with the other members, and if the year turns out worse than estimated it pays the difference through a supplementary call. It also explains why a club can afford an omnibus rule, letting the board meet a claim outside the strict wording but within the spirit of mutuality - a commercial insurer would be giving away its shareholders' money. What the club insures is liabilities, not property: the hull and machinery policy covers the ship, and the club covers what the ship does to other people - the gap nineteenth-century owners created the clubs to fill. And 'unlimited cover' is a credible promise only because of a structure worth naming in four tiers: the club's own retention, then the Pool shared among the International Group clubs, then the Group's collective reinsurance bought as one buyer, and finally the overspill call on every Group member. For limb B, one sentence places any risk correctly: protection is liabilities to people and to property other than cargo; indemnity is cargo and the contract of carriage. The two words are historical - modern rulebooks list numbered classes instead - but the division is real, and saying both things is the complete answer.
