steps.title: How a club is constituted, and what else it gives a member
points: The club rules are the contract and the Certificate of Entry evidences the entry - there is no policy in the market sense
The omnibus rule gives the board discretion to meet a claim outside the wording but within the spirit of mutuality
Worldwide correspondents, casualty response, legal and technical advice, condition surveys and loss prevention
A club letter of undertaking secures release of an arrested ship without cash or a bank guarantee
The club's evidence of insurance is what allows a flag State to issue the CLC, Bunkers, Nairobi, Athens and MLC financial-security certificates - without it the ship cannot trade
In India the governing statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, and unpaid mutual insurance calls are a maritime claim under section 4 of the Admiralty Act, 2017

steps.title: The International Group, the Pool and the collective reinsurance
points: No single club could pay a very large claim from its own resources
Tier one - the club's own retention, paid from its own funds
Tier two - the Pool, in which the International Group clubs share the claim under the Pooling Agreement by an agreed formula
Tier three - collective excess-of-loss reinsurance bought by the Group in the market as one buyer, securing capacity and price no single club could obtain
Above that sits the overspill call; the Group's clubs cover the great majority of world ocean-going tonnage, which is why the arrangement works

steps.title: How the funds are collected - the call system
points: Advance call - estimated at the start of the policy year from expected claims, pooled claims, reinsurance and expenses, and called in proportion to each member's assessed share; often split into advance and deferred instalments

Supplementary or additional call - levied if the year's costs exceed the advance calls plus investment income; the defining feature of a mutual, and the reason a year's cost is not final until the year closes
Release call - paid by a member leaving the club to buy out its liability for future supplementary calls on open policy years
Overspill call - levied on the members of all Group clubs by reference to entered tonnage where a claim exceeds the collective reinsurance; never yet levied in practice
The reinsurance element is commonly charged as a separate rate per gross ton by ship type, and each claim carries a deductible
Some business is written on a fixed premium basis with no supplementary calls, but normally subject to a stated limit
Accounting is by policy year, traditionally from noon on 20 February; years stay open while claims develop and free reserves smooth the calls

steps.title: What determines a member's contribution, and on what conditions cover rests
points: Rating factors - entered tonnage, ship type and age, trade and geographical range, crew nationality and terms, claims record, management standard and inspection history, classes of cover and deductibles
Conditions - the ship in class with an approved society, statutory certificates held, flag State requirements complied with, and prompt notification of casualties with the club's directions followed
The 'pay to be paid' rule - classically the member must discharge the liability before the club reimburses, displaced where a convention gives a claimant a direct right of action against the insurer
Cover can be prejudiced by unapproved contractual terms, unlawful trade, want of due diligence or non-disclosure

steps.title: 'Protection' - liabilities to persons and to property other than cargo
points: State the division first: protection is the ship as a ship - people and property other than cargo; indemnity is cargo and the contract of carriage
Crew - illness, injury, death, medical and funeral costs, repatriation and substitute expenses, personal effects, and the MLC financial security for abandonment and for death or long-term disability
Passengers under the Athens regime, and others on board - stevedores, pilots, surveyors, supernumeraries
Stowaways, refugees and persons rescued at sea, and life salvage
Collision liability not covered by the hull policy, and the excess over hull value
Damage to fixed and floating objects - berths, buoys, cables, terminal equipment
Pollution liability, clean-up and preventive measures, and wreck removal including lighting and marking
Towage and other approved contractual liabilities, quarantine and disinfection, fines often at board discretion, and enquiry, legal and sue-and-labour costs

steps.title: 'Indemnity' - cargo and the contract of carriage
points: Loss of, shortage of, damage to or delay to cargo carried on board
Liability under the contract of carriage - bill of lading, waybill or charterparty - on terms the club approves
The ship's proportion of general average not recoverable from cargo because of a breach of the contract of carriage, usually unseaworthiness
Cargo's proportion of general average or salvage that the member has to bear
Through-transport liabilities in a combined-transport operation
Misdelivery - wrong port, over-carriage, or delivery without production of the bill of lading, subject to the rules and often to prior agreement
Cost of disposing of damaged or unclaimed cargo, and damage to containers not owned by the member

steps.title: The limits, and what is not covered at all
points: Cover is unlimited for most risks but oil pollution and passenger and seamen claims are capped per event, the passenger figure being a sub-limit within the combined amount
Those limits are commercial figures fixed by the International Group, not treaty limits
Not covered - damage to and salvage of the entered ship, which is hull and machinery; loss of hire; war risks; the member's own cargo; crew wages as a contractual debt
Not covered - liabilities from deliberate or reckless conduct, unlawful trades, want of due diligence, or unapproved contracts
One examinable negative: the HNS Convention 2010 is not in force, so there is no HNS certification regime for a club to support

questions.memory_cue: Limb A in three moves - MUTUAL (1, 2), TIERS (3), CALLS (4, 5) - with the four calls in order: ADVANCE, SUPPLEMENTARY, RELEASE, OVERSPILL (4). Limb B on one sentence - PROTECTION IS PEOPLE AND EVERYTHING THAT IS NOT CARGO; INDEMNITY IS CARGO AND THE CONTRACT (6, 7) - then finish on LIMITS AND EXCLUSIONS (8).

quick_revision.recall_15s: A P&I club is a MUTUAL, NON-PROFIT association of owners, charterers and operators insuring third-party liabilities - the hull policy insures the ship, the club insures what the ship does to other people. Members are both insurer and insured: no shareholders, board from the membership, club rules and Certificate of Entry are the contract, omnibus rule for discretionary claims, cover unlimited for most risks. Credible because of four tiers: club retention - the Pool (International Group Pooling Agreement) - collective excess-of-loss reinsurance - overspill call. Funds are collected as CALLS, not premiums: advance call estimated at the start of the policy year (traditionally from noon 20 February), often split with a deferred instalment; supplementary call if the year falls short - the essence of mutuality; release call when a member leaves, to close off open years; overspill call on all Group members by entered tonnage above the reinsurance. Plus deductibles and a separate reinsurance rate per gross ton by ship type. Cover conditional on class, certificates, prompt notification and classically 'pay to be paid'. PROTECTION = people and property other than cargo: crew, passengers, stowaways, life salvage, collision liability not covered by hull, fixed and floating objects, pollution, wreck removal, quarantine, fines, legal costs. INDEMNITY = cargo and the contract of carriage: loss, damage, shortage, delay, misdelivery, unrecoverable general average. Capped: oil pollution, and passenger and seamen claims. Not covered: the ship herself, loss of hire, war risks.
critical_numbers: There is no fixed sum insured - cover is unlimited for most risks, with oil pollution and passenger and seamen claims capped per event
Those caps are commercial figures fixed by the International Group and revised from time to time, not treaty limits
Four kinds of call: advance, supplementary, release and overspill
Four tiers of claim payment: the club's retention, the Pool, the collective excess-of-loss reinsurance, and the overspill call assessed on entered tonnage
The policy year traditionally runs from noon on 20 February and stays open while claims develop
quick_revision.critical_regulation: There is no statute governing P&I cover itself - the club rules and the Certificate of Entry are the contract. In an Indian examination the governing marine insurance statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, and unpaid mutual insurance calls are expressly a maritime claim under section 4 of the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017
quick_revision.major_trap: Calling the contribution a premium. It is a call, and the difference is the whole of mutuality - the members are the insurers, so if the year's claims exceed the advance calls they pay the difference through a supplementary call. Second trap: listing risks in limb B without dividing them. The classification is the question - protection is people and property other than cargo; indemnity is cargo and the contract of carriage. Third, and the one that costs marks in an Indian examination: citing the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906. The Indian statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the P&I clubs question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What a club is and the gap it fills. 2 How it is constituted and what else it gives a member. 3 The International Group, the Pool and the collective reinsurance. 4 The call system. 5 Rating factors and conditions of cover. 6 Protection risks. 7 Indemnity risks. 8 Limits and exclusions. Sections 1-5 are limb A, 6-8 limb B.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb A has two demands and the funding one needs its own section; limb B is a classification question, so the division is stated before the lists.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a P&I club differ from an ordinary marine insurer?
retrieval_cards.answer: A club is owned by its members, who are both insurer and insured, and is non-profit - it meets the members' liabilities at cost, directed by a board drawn from the membership. Contributions are calls that can be increased if the year's claims require it, not fixed premiums; there is no fixed sum insured and cover is unlimited for most risks; and it insures liabilities to third parties rather than property.
retrieval_cards.why: Mutuality is the source of every other distinctive feature, including the call system and the omnibus rule.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name and explain the four kinds of call.
retrieval_cards.answer: The advance call, estimated at the start of the policy year from expected claims, pooled claims, reinsurance and expenses and often split with a deferred instalment. The supplementary call, levied if the year's costs exceed the advance calls plus investment income. The release call, paid by a member leaving to buy out its liability for future supplementary calls on open years. And the overspill call, levied on the members of all International Group clubs by reference to entered tonnage where a claim exceeds the collective reinsurance.
retrieval_cards.why: The release and overspill calls are the two that show real understanding of how a mutual actually works.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can a club promise unlimited cover?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because of a four-tier structure. The club pays claims up to its own retention from its own funds; above that the International Group clubs share the claim under the Pooling Agreement; above the Pool the Group buys collective excess-of-loss reinsurance in the market as a single buyer, securing capacity and price no club could obtain alone; and above that an overspill call may be levied on the members of every Group club by entered tonnage.
retrieval_cards.why: Without the Pool and the reinsurance, 'unlimited cover' is an unexplained slogan.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the division between protection risks and indemnity risks.
retrieval_cards.answer: Protection covers liabilities arising from the ship as a ship - to people and to property other than the cargo she carries: crew, passengers, others on board, stowaways, life salvage, collision liability not covered by the hull policy, damage to fixed and floating objects, pollution, wreck removal, quarantine, fines and legal costs. Indemnity covers liabilities arising from the cargo and the contract of carriage: loss, shortage, damage, delay, misdelivery, and general average not recoverable from cargo.
retrieval_cards.why: One sentence places any risk correctly on the spot, which is what limb B is testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is P&I cover unlimited?
retrieval_cards.answer: For most risks yes, but not all. Oil pollution and passenger and seamen claims are each subject to a limit per event, the passenger figure being a sub-limit within the combined passenger-and-seamen amount. Those limits are commercial figures fixed by the International Group and revised from time to time - they are not treaty limits, and should be described as such.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying cover is unlimited without qualification is wrong, and presenting the caps as statutory is a second error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What certificates depend on a club's cover, and what happens without it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The club issues the evidence of insurance on which a flag State issues the certificates required by the Civil Liability Convention for oil pollution, the Bunkers Convention 2001, the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention 2007 and the Athens passenger regime, together with the financial security for abandonment and for death or long-term disability required by the Maritime Labour Convention. Without club cover the ship cannot hold those certificates, and without them she cannot trade.
retrieval_cards.why: It converts P&I from an office matter into an operational prerequisite for the ship.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does 'pay to be paid' mean, and when does it not apply?
retrieval_cards.answer: Classically a club indemnifies: the member must first have discharged the liability before the club reimburses it, which is why the obligation is an indemnity rather than a promise to the third party. It is displaced where a convention gives a claimant a direct right of action against the insurer, as the oil pollution, bunkers and wreck removal conventions do.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why a club's obligation is structured as it is, and the convention exception is the part candidates miss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which marine insurance statute applies in an Indian examination, and how does P&I connect to admiralty?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 - not the United Kingdom Act of 1906, which is easy to cite by mistake because P&I practice is overwhelmingly English-law based. And under section 4 of the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, insurance premium including mutual insurance calls in respect of the vessel is expressly a maritime claim, so unpaid calls can found an arrest.
retrieval_cards.why: Citing the 1906 Act in an Indian paper is a recorded trap, and the admiralty link is a verified statutory connection worth a mark.

blocks.h: 1. Why these devices exist, and where the losses actually are

blocks.p: The stem supplies its own driver and it is worth taking seriously. Emission control from ships is now a design constraint with a number attached: MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 requires a new ship's attained EEDI not to exceed a required EEDI that is the reference line reduced by a factor which tightens by phase; the EEXI applies a comparable index once to existing ships, and the carbon intensity indicator rates a ship on how she is actually operated. Since CO2 is a fixed multiple of fuel burnt, every percentage point of propulsive efficiency is a percentage point of emissions - so a device that was once a fuel-economy option is now, for many designs, what allows the ship to comply at all.
Where the recoverable losses sit. A propeller behind a hull loses energy in four identifiable ways, and each device family attacks one of them:

ul: Axial loss - energy left in the accelerated slipstream. Reduced by a larger, more slowly turning propeller.
Rotational loss - the propeller leaves the water spinning, and that swirl is wasted work. Attacked before the disc by pre-swirl and after it by post-swirl devices.
Frictional and sectional loss - blade drag. Attacked by blade section and area optimisation.
Tip-vortex and hub-vortex loss - concentrated vortices shed from the blade tips and the boss. Attacked by tip-loaded blade designs and by boss cap fins.

blocks.h: 2. The efficiency framework that classifies every device here

blocks.p: Quasi-propulsive efficiency is conventionally written as the product of three terms, and it is the cleanest way to organise the whole answer:
ηD = ηO × ηH × ηR

ul: ηO - open water efficiency. How well the propeller converts delivered power into thrust in uniform flow. Improved by high-efficiency propeller design.
ηH - hull efficiency, the ratio (1 - t) / (1 - w), where t is thrust deduction and w is wake fraction. Improved by changing the flow the hull delivers - which is what a wake equalising device does.

ηR - relative rotative efficiency. The correction for the propeller working in a non-uniform, rotating inflow rather than in open water. Improved by pre-swirl, and its wasted output partly recovered by post-swirl.

blocks.p: The classification the question uses is therefore not arbitrary. Limb (a) works on the flow into the disc, limb (b) puts rotation into the inflow, limb (c) takes rotation out of the outflow, and limb (d) improves the disc itself. Saying that in two sentences before describing anything makes the whole answer read as a system.

blocks.h: 3. Wake Equalizing Devices

blocks.p: The problem. Behind a full-form, single-screw hull the flow into the propeller is strongly non-uniform. There is a pronounced wake peak at the top of the disc where the boundary layer is thickest and the flow slowest, and often separation on the afterbody. The blade therefore sees a violently varying angle of attack and loading once per revolution, which costs efficiency and produces cavitation, pressure pulses, hull vibration and erosion.

The principle. Fit an appendage ahead of the propeller that accelerates and straightens the slow water in the upper disc and suppresses separation, so the inflow is more uniform. Doing so raises hull efficiency by improving the wake fraction, improves the propeller's working environment, and reduces the excitation the hull receives.
Forms:

ul: The wake equalising duct - the classic Schneekluth arrangement: a pair of half-ring nozzles mounted on the afterbody either side of the stern post, ahead of the disc, shaped to accelerate flow into the upper quadrants.
Flow-guiding fins and stern spoilers - fins fitted on the afterbody, angled to redirect flow and suppress the bilge vortex; the Grothues arrangement is the best known.
Stern tunnels and afterbody form changes - a hull-form rather than an appendage solution, available at design stage.

Combined duct-and-fin devices - where a wake-equalising duct carries internal pre-swirl fins, the device belongs to both limb (a) and limb (b). The best-known integrated ducts are of this kind, and saying so is worth a mark because it shows the categories are not watertight.

blocks.p: Gain and limits. Indicatively in the region of a few per cent up to the high single figures, and the vibration and cavitation benefit is often worth as much as the fuel. It works best on full-form, high-block-coefficient, single-screw ships at moderate speed - tankers and bulk carriers. On a fine-form, fast ship with a clean wake there is little non-uniformity to correct, and the added appendage drag can exceed the gain.

blocks.h: 4. Pre-swirl Devices

blocks.p: The problem. A propeller does not only push water aft; it also spins it. The rotational kinetic energy left in the slipstream is pure loss, and on a heavily loaded single-screw ship it is a significant fraction of the delivered power.

The principle. Give the inflow a rotation opposite to the propeller's own direction of rotation, upstream of the disc. The propeller then has to undo that counter-rotation before it can impart any of its own, so less net swirl leaves the disc and more of the delivered power ends up as axial thrust. The effect appears as an improvement in relative rotative efficiency and, through the modified inflow, in hull efficiency too.
Forms:

ul: Pre-swirl stators - a set of fixed radial fins on the hull or stern boss immediately forward of the propeller, each set at an incidence chosen to generate the counter-rotation. They are characteristically asymmetric - more fins, or differently angled fins, on one side - because the wake behind a single-screw hull is itself asymmetric and the rotating propeller meets it differently on the up-going and down-going sides.

Pre-swirl ducts - a duct with internal stator fins, combining the wake-equalising effect of limb (a) with the pre-rotation of limb (b) in one appendage. This is the most widely retrofitted energy-saving device on full-form ships.
Asymmetric or twisted afterbodies - the same effect produced by hull form rather than by an appendage, available only at design stage.

blocks.p: Gain and limits. Indicatively a few per cent. The device is tuned to a design point - a particular draught, speed and propeller loading - so the benefit falls away in ballast or at part load, and a badly matched stator can cost efficiency. The fins add wetted surface and drag, they must be positioned to avoid exciting blade-rate vibration, and they are a fatigue-critical welded appendage in a region of unsteady loading.

blocks.h: 5. Post-swirl Devices

blocks.p: The principle. Whatever swirl the propeller does impart, recover some of it downstream. Post-swirl devices sit in the slipstream and turn its rotation into useful axial thrust, or remove the concentrated hub vortex that carries much of the loss.
Forms:

ul: Propeller boss cap fins - small fins fitted on the boss cap, rotating with the propeller, which break up the hub vortex. Indicatively in the low single figures, and among the cheapest of all retrofits. They also reduce hub-vortex cavitation and the associated rudder erosion, and they can usually be fitted in a routine docking.

Rudder bulb - a bulb on the rudder leading edge, aligned with and streamlining the flow off the propeller boss. It fills the low-pressure hub region, reduces the hub vortex and the drag associated with it, and is commonly combined with the boss cap fins and a twisted rudder as a matched package.

Rudder thrust fins - fins projecting from the rudder into the slipstream, set at an incidence that converts the residual swirl into a forward force. Because the swirl is in opposite senses above and below the shaft line, the fins on each side are angled oppositely.

Twisted and asymmetric rudders - the rudder's leading edge twisted to match the swirl angle of the slipstream above and below the shaft, so the rudder meets the flow at a lower angle of attack. This reduces rudder drag and cavitation erosion and improves manoeuvring - a genuine multiple benefit.

Free-rotating vane wheels - a larger-diameter freely turning wheel astern of the propeller, acting as a turbine on the inner slipstream and a propeller on the outer. Theoretically attractive, but structurally troublesome in service, and not widely adopted.

blocks.p: Gain and limits. Indicatively low single figures individually, and more when the boss cap fins, rudder bulb and twisted rudder are designed as one system. The devices sit in the most hostile flow on the ship - unsteady, cavitating and erosive - so material selection, cathodic protection and inspection matter, and a lost fin is a hazard to the rudder and the propeller behind which it travels.

blocks.h: 6. High-efficiency Propellers

blocks.p: The other three limbs modify the flow around the propeller. This one improves the propeller itself, and it offers the largest gains available.

ul: Larger diameter at lower revolutions. The single most effective measure of all. A larger disc accelerates a greater mass of water to a smaller velocity increase, which reduces the axial loss directly and raises open-water efficiency. It is enabled by long-stroke, low-speed engines and by an afterbody designed with the aperture to accept it - and it aligns naturally with slow steaming, since a de-rated engine at lower revolutions suits a larger propeller.

Tip-loaded and contracted-tip designs. Blades with end plates or winglets at the tip, curved towards the suction side, which obstruct the flow around the tip and weaken the tip vortex. Because the tip loss is reduced, the tip can carry more load, and the effective diameter is used more fully.
Curved-tip designs where the tip is swept smoothly out of the blade plane to the same end, without a discrete plate - a smoother pressure distribution and less cavitation risk.

Contra-rotating propellers. Two coaxial propellers turning in opposite directions, the after one recovering the rotational energy of the forward one. The largest gain of any measure here - it addresses the rotational loss almost completely - but it requires coaxial shafting with concentric shafts and a complex sterntube and bearing arrangement, which is why adoption is limited to specialised ships.

Ducted propellers. An accelerating (Kort) nozzle around a heavily loaded propeller raises efficiency substantially at high thrust loading and low speed - hence its universal use on tugs and trawlers - while a decelerating nozzle is used where cavitation and radiated noise matter more than efficiency.

Blade geometry optimisation - skew to spread the passage through the wake peak over time and so cut pressure pulses and vibration; refined section shape, pitch distribution and blade area ratio chosen for the actual wake field; and, increasingly, a propeller designed for the ship's real operating profile rather than for the contract speed.
Blade number and material - chosen against the hull's vibration response, with high-strength alloys allowing thinner, more efficient sections.

blocks.p: The binding constraints are always the same: cavitation margin, blade strength and fatigue, pressure pulses and hull vibration, aperture clearances, off-design behaviour, and class approval of the design.

blocks.h: 7. Selection, verification and what happens to the gain in service

ul: The devices are not independent, and they are not additive. A pre-swirl stator and a boss cap fin both act on the same rotational energy; fitting both does not add their quoted gains. A matched package must be designed and assessed as one system for the individual hull.

Suitability is hull-specific. The wake and swirl devices reward full-form, high-block, single-screw ships at moderate speed. On fine, fast hulls the added drag can exceed the recovery. The right answer to "which device?" is always "for which ship, at which draught and speed".

Verification. A claim is established by model tests in a towing tank and cavitation tunnel and by computational prediction, and demonstrated by a speed trial - run as double runs on reciprocal courses to cancel current and corrected to a reference condition for wind, waves, depth and displacement. A gain claimed and not measured is a marketing figure.

The regulatory route. Where the benefit is to be credited in the ship's attained EEDI, it must be evidenced in the EEDI technical file, which regulation 22.1 makes the basis on which the attained value is verified. An innovative-technology credit is examined closely for exactly that reason, and it is where an unsupported claim would directly and improperly reduce the attained value.

Retrofit economics. Most of these devices can be fitted in a scheduled docking, which is what makes them attractive as an EEXI or CII measure. The business case is fuel saved against installation and added maintenance, and it improves as fuel price and carbon cost rise.

In service the gain is not permanent. Fouling of the appendage and of the hull erodes it; the device is outside the design point in ballast or at reduced speed; and structural condition matters - cracking of welded fins, cavitation erosion and failure of cathodic protection are all live risks. These appendages belong on the underwater inspection and planned maintenance schedule, and it is entirely appropriate to treat them as identified equipment within the safety management system.

Keep the claim honest. A device improves the attained EEDI, which is a design index and does not change with operation; what improves with a clean hull and a well-chosen speed is the operational carbon intensity. Both matter, and confusing them is the standard error in this subject.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Four printed limbs at 4 marks each means four visible, roughly equal regions and a firm discipline about length - it is easy to write three pages on propellers and leave limb (a) with one line. The two decisions that pay are: put one short framing section at the front giving the efficiency breakdown, because it classifies all four limbs and makes them read as a system rather than a list; and answer each limb in the same internal order - problem, principle, forms, gain and limits - so a marker can find each component instantly and nothing is forgotten under time pressure.

blocks.h: The framework that makes the answer a system

blocks.p: ηD = ηO × ηH × ηR is the whole classification. Limb (a) improves hull efficiency by fixing the flow the hull delivers; limbs (b) and (c) work on rotational loss, one before the disc and one after; limb (d) improves open water efficiency, the propeller itself. Say that in two sentences before describing any device and every subsequent paragraph has a place to sit. It also stops the commonest structural error, which is describing four devices without ever saying what loss each one is recovering.

blocks.h: Where the energy actually goes

blocks.p: Four losses, four families. Axial - water left moving aft, cured by a bigger, slower propeller. Rotational - water left spinning, attacked before the disc by pre-swirl and after it by post-swirl. Frictional and sectional - blade drag, attacked by section and area design. Tip and hub vortex - concentrated vortices, attacked by tip-loaded blades and boss cap fins. An answer that names the loss before naming the device is demonstrating understanding; one that lists trade names is not.

blocks.h: Why the gains are not additive - the point that separates a good answer

blocks.p: A pre-swirl stator and propeller boss cap fins are both trying to recover the same rotational energy: one prevents it being created, the other recovers what was. Fit both and you do not get the sum of the two quoted figures, because the first has already removed part of what the second was going to recover. The correct professional statement is that a package must be designed and assessed as one system for the individual hull - and that is also why the honest answer to "which device is best?" is always "for which ship, at which draught and speed?"

blocks.h: The regulatory link the stem hands you

blocks.p: The stem opens with emission control, so use it. CO2 is a fixed multiple of fuel burnt, so propulsive efficiency and emissions are the same quantity. The attained EEDI must not exceed a required EEDI that tightens by phase; EEXI applies the same idea once to existing ships; CII rates operation. Two further points earn marks: a device's benefit is credited only if it is evidenced in the EEDI technical file, which is what the attained value is verified against; and a device improves the design index, while a clean hull and a sensible speed improve the operational one. Do not stray beyond that into later IMO measures.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Listing trade names without explaining the principle or naming the loss being recovered.
Giving three limbs properly and one in a sentence. Four limbs at 4 marks each.
Confusing pre-swirl and post-swirl. Pre-swirl puts rotation in ahead of the disc; post-swirl takes it out behind.
Treating quoted percentages as fixed properties of a device. They are indicative and depend on hull form, draught, speed and loading.
Adding the gains of several devices together.
Forgetting the penalties - appendage drag, off-design loss, vibration excitation, fatigue and cavitation erosion.
Claiming a device improves the CII directly, or that it changes the attained EEDI after the ship is built. The attained EEDI is fixed at verification.
Omitting larger diameter at lower revolutions from limb (d), which is the single most effective measure of all.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Asking which way a pre-swirl stator turns the flow - opposite to the propeller's rotation.
Asking why pre-swirl stators are asymmetric, expecting the asymmetry of the wake behind a single-screw hull.
Asking what a wake equalising duct does besides save fuel - reduces cavitation, pressure pulses and hull vibration.
Asking why a wake equalising duct would be a poor choice on a fine-form fast ship.
Asking what propeller boss cap fins recover, expecting the hub vortex, and what secondary benefit they give - reduced rudder erosion.
Asking why a Kort nozzle suits a tug but not a container ship - high thrust loading at low speed.
Asking the drawback of contra-rotating propellers - the coaxial shafting, sterntube and bearing complexity.
Asking whether fitting two devices gives the sum of their savings.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your ship has a pre-swirl duct fitted. What would you inspect at the next dry-docking, and what are you looking for?
A stator fin has cracked at its weld. What are the consequences and what do you do?
How would you demonstrate to an owner that a retrofitted device actually saved fuel?
Why does a larger, slower-turning propeller improve efficiency?
Your ship spends most of her time in ballast. How does that affect the case for a pre-swirl device?
What is the difference between the effect of these devices on the EEDI and on the CII?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Four limbs, four positions relative to the disc: BEFORE - STRAIGHTEN (a), BEFORE - TWIST (b), AFTER - UNTWIST (c), THE DISC ITSELF (d). Attach one loss to each: non-uniform wake, rotational loss prevented, rotational loss recovered, axial and tip loss. Run each limb in the same internal order - PROBLEM, PRINCIPLE, FORMS, GAIN AND LIMITS - and close on the three professional points: not additive, hull-specific, and it must be measured.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 22 - attained EEDI, ship-specific, verified on the basis of the EEDI technical file: the route by which a device's benefit is credited.
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 24 - required EEDI, the reference line reduced by a factor that tightens by phase: the ceiling that makes these devices necessary.
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 23 - attained EEXI, extending the pressure to existing ships.
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28 - operational carbon intensity, which responds to how the ship is run rather than how she is built.
Recognised speed-power trial analysis practice - double runs on reciprocal courses, corrected to a reference condition: how a claimed gain is actually demonstrated.

Naval architecture - quasi-propulsive efficiency as the product of open-water, hull and relative-rotative efficiency; wake fraction and thrust deduction; axial, rotational, frictional and tip-vortex losses. Engineering fact, not regulation.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence limits

blocks.p: This question is mostly engineering, and its evidence position differs sharply from the regulatory questions on this paper. The efficiency decomposition, the loss classification, and the working principle of every device family are established naval architecture and marine engineering. They are not IMO inventions, they do not depend on any instrument, and they are stated as engineering fact.

⚠ Every quantified gain is indicative and is labelled as such. The percentage ranges come from reported industry practice and are strongly dependent on hull form, block coefficient, draught, speed, propeller loading and the quality of the baseline being compared against. No figure is asserted as a fixed property of any device, and a candidate should quote them as ranges requiring ship-specific verification. The corpus holds no maker's document, so the named devices are described by working principle only and no maker's performance claim is adopted. The remark that free-rotating vane wheels proved structurally troublesome and were not widely adopted is engineering judgement about industry adoption rather than a cited finding.

The regulatory framing is on firmer ground. It is anchored to the corpus's frozen canonical records for MARPOL Annex VI regulations 22 and 24, which are citation-ready. That is also what makes the innovative-technology point in section 7 verifiable rather than asserted: regulation 22.1 makes the EEDI technical file the basis on which the attained value is verified, so a credited gain must be evidenced there. No reduction factor, phase date or reference-line parameter is asserted anywhere in this answer.

Temporally this question is clean and the one live prohibition is observed. The EEDI, EEXI and CII regulations were all in force and unamended at this sitting. The IMO Net-Zero Framework is post-sitting - approved at MEPC 83 two months after this paper - and is excluded; the two later MIW answers that legitimately carry it were not consulted. The hydrodynamics, of course, do not move at all.

questions.understand_first: The stem hands you the reason these devices exist, so use it: CO2 is a fixed multiple of fuel burnt, so a percentage of propulsive efficiency is a percentage of emissions - and with the required EEDI tightening by phase, and EEXI and CII applying the same pressure to ships already trading, a device that was once an economy option is now often what lets the design comply. Underneath, one framework organises all four limbs. Quasi-propulsive efficiency is ηD = ηO × ηH × ηR, and a propeller behind a hull loses energy in four ways: axially in the slipstream it accelerates, rotationally in the swirl it leaves behind, in blade friction, and in the tip and hub vortices. Each limb of the question attacks one of them from a different position relative to the disc: (a) straightens the flow going in, raising hull efficiency; (b) twists it the wrong way going in, so the propeller's own swirl is partly cancelled before it is created; (c) untwists what comes out, recovering the swirl and the hub vortex; and (d) improves the disc itself, where the largest single gain of all is simply a bigger propeller turning more slowly. Two management-level points separate a good answer from a list. The gains are not additive - a pre-swirl stator and boss cap fins are chasing the same rotational energy - so a package is designed as one system for one hull. And a saving that has not been measured by a corrected speed trial, and evidenced in the EEDI technical file if it is to be credited, is a marketing figure rather than an engineering one.

steps.title: Why these devices exist, and where the losses actually are
points: Emission control is now a design constraint with a number attached - the attained EEDI must not exceed a required EEDI that tightens by phase, EEXI applies the same idea to existing ships and CII rates operation
CO2 is a fixed multiple of fuel burnt, so a percentage of propulsive efficiency is a percentage of emissions
Axial loss - energy left in the accelerated slipstream, reduced by a larger, more slowly turning propeller
Rotational loss - the propeller leaves the water spinning; attacked before the disc by pre-swirl and after it by post-swirl
Frictional and sectional loss - blade drag, attacked by section and area optimisation
Tip and hub vortex loss - attacked by tip-loaded blade designs and by boss cap fins

steps.title: The efficiency framework that classifies every device here
points: Quasi-propulsive efficiency is the product of open-water, hull and relative-rotative efficiency
Open-water efficiency - how well the propeller converts delivered power into thrust in uniform flow; improved by propeller design
Hull efficiency, (1 - t) / (1 - w) - improved by changing the flow the hull delivers, which is what a wake equalising device does
Relative rotative efficiency - the correction for a non-uniform rotating inflow; improved by pre-swirl and its wasted output partly recovered by post-swirl
So limb (a) works on the flow into the disc, (b) puts rotation in, (c) takes rotation out, and (d) improves the disc itself

steps.title: Wake Equalizing Devices
points: Problem - strongly non-uniform inflow behind a full-form single-screw hull, with a wake peak at the top of the disc and afterbody separation, giving cyclic blade loading, cavitation, pressure pulses, vibration and erosion

Principle - an appendage ahead of the propeller that accelerates and straightens the slow water in the upper disc and suppresses separation, raising hull efficiency and improving the propeller's working environment
Forms - the classic wake equalising duct as a pair of half-ring nozzles on the afterbody; flow-guiding fins and stern spoilers; stern tunnels and afterbody form changes at design stage
Combined duct-and-fin devices carry internal pre-swirl fins and belong to both limb (a) and limb (b) - the categories are not watertight

Gain and limits - indicatively a few per cent up to high single figures, with the vibration and cavitation benefit often worth as much as the fuel; best on full-form high-block single-screw ships at moderate speed, and on fine fast hulls the added appendage drag can exceed the gain

steps.title: Pre-swirl Devices
points: Problem - the propeller spins the water as well as pushing it aft, and that rotational kinetic energy in the slipstream is pure loss
Principle - impart rotation opposite to the propeller's own direction upstream of the disc, so the propeller must undo the counter-rotation before imparting its own and less net swirl leaves the disc

Forms - fixed radial pre-swirl stators on the hull or stern boss, characteristically asymmetric because the wake behind a single-screw hull is itself asymmetric; pre-swirl ducts with internal stator fins, the most widely retrofitted device on full-form ships; asymmetric or twisted afterbodies at design stage
Gain and limits - indicatively a few per cent, tuned to a design draught, speed and loading, so the benefit falls away in ballast or at part load and a badly matched stator can cost efficiency
The fins add wetted surface and drag, must avoid exciting blade-rate vibration, and are a fatigue-critical welded appendage in unsteady flow

steps.title: Post-swirl Devices
points: Principle - recover downstream whatever swirl the propeller does impart, turning slipstream rotation into axial thrust or removing the concentrated hub vortex

Propeller boss cap fins - small fins on the boss cap rotating with the propeller, breaking up the hub vortex; low single figures, among the cheapest retrofits, and they also reduce hub-vortex cavitation and rudder erosion

Rudder bulb - aligned with the propeller boss, filling the low-pressure hub region and reducing the hub vortex and its drag; commonly combined with boss cap fins and a twisted rudder as a matched package
Rudder thrust fins - fins in the slipstream converting residual swirl into forward force, angled oppositely above and below the shaft line because the swirl reverses sense
Twisted and asymmetric rudders - leading edge twisted to match the swirl angle, reducing rudder drag and cavitation erosion and improving manoeuvring
Free-rotating vane wheels - theoretically attractive but structurally troublesome in service and not widely adopted

Gain and limits - low single figures individually and more as a designed system; the devices sit in unsteady, cavitating, erosive flow so material, cathodic protection and inspection matter, and a lost fin threatens the rudder and propeller

steps.title: High-efficiency Propellers
points: Larger diameter at lower revolutions - the single most effective measure, accelerating more water to a smaller velocity increase and cutting axial loss; enabled by long-stroke low-speed engines and a suitable aperture, and aligned with slow steaming
Tip-loaded and contracted-tip designs - end plates or winglets at the tip weakening the tip vortex, so the tip can carry more load
Curved-tip designs achieving the same smoothly, with a better pressure distribution and less cavitation risk

Contra-rotating propellers - two coaxial propellers turning oppositely, the after one recovering the rotational energy of the forward; the largest gain available but requiring concentric shafting and a complex sterntube and bearing arrangement
Ducted propellers - an accelerating Kort nozzle for heavily loaded propellers at low speed, hence tugs and trawlers; a decelerating nozzle where cavitation and radiated noise dominate

Blade geometry - skew to spread passage through the wake peak and cut pressure pulses, plus section shape, pitch distribution and blade area ratio matched to the real wake field and the real operating profile
Binding constraints throughout - cavitation margin, blade strength and fatigue, pressure pulses and hull vibration, aperture clearances, off-design behaviour and class approval

steps.title: Selection, verification and what happens to the gain in service
points: The devices are not independent and their gains are not additive - a pre-swirl stator and boss cap fins chase the same rotational energy, so a package is designed and assessed as one system for the individual hull
Suitability is hull-specific: wake and swirl devices reward full-form high-block single-screw ships at moderate speed, and on fine fast hulls added drag can exceed recovery

Verification - model tests in towing tank and cavitation tunnel, computational prediction, then a speed trial run as double runs on reciprocal courses and corrected to a reference condition; a gain claimed and not measured is a marketing figure

Regulatory route - a benefit credited in the attained EEDI must be evidenced in the EEDI technical file, which regulation 22.1 makes the basis of verification, so innovative-technology claims are examined closely
Retrofit economics - most can be fitted in a scheduled docking, which is what makes them attractive as an EEXI or CII measure

In service the gain degrades - fouling of appendage and hull, operation away from the design point in ballast or at reduced speed, cracking of welded fins, cavitation erosion and failure of cathodic protection; these appendages belong on the underwater inspection and planned maintenance schedule
Keep the claim honest - a device improves the attained EEDI, a design index fixed at verification, while a clean hull and a well-chosen speed improve the operational carbon intensity

questions.memory_cue: Four limbs, four positions around the disc: BEFORE - STRAIGHTEN (3), BEFORE - TWIST (4), AFTER - UNTWIST (5), THE DISC ITSELF (6), on the framework that classifies them (2). Same internal order every time - PROBLEM, PRINCIPLE, FORMS, GAIN AND LIMITS. Close on the three professional points: NOT ADDITIVE, HULL-SPECIFIC, MEASURE IT (7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Driver: CO2 is a fixed multiple of fuel, so efficiency = emissions. Attained EEDI must not exceed the required EEDI (tightens by phase); EEXI for existing ships; CII for operation. Framework: ηD = ηO × ηH × ηR. Four losses: axial, rotational, frictional, tip and hub vortex. (a) WED - duct or fins ahead of the propeller accelerating and straightening the slow upper-disc flow; raises hull efficiency; also cuts cavitation, pressure pulses and vibration; best on full-form single-screw, poor on fine fast hulls. (b) Pre-swirl - fixed asymmetric stators or a pre-swirl duct putting rotation opposite to the propeller in, so less net swirl comes out; tuned to a design point, so it fades in ballast. (c) Post-swirl - PBCF break up the hub vortex (and cut rudder erosion), rudder bulb streamlines the boss, thrust fins convert residual swirl to forward force, twisted rudder matches the swirl angle. (d) High-efficiency propellers - larger diameter, lower rpm is the biggest single gain; tip-loaded / contracted-tip blades weaken the tip vortex; contra-rotating recovers rotation but needs coaxial shafting; Kort nozzle for high thrust loading at low speed; skew for pressure pulses. Constraints: cavitation, strength, vibration, clearances. Three closers: gains are NOT additive, suitability is hull-specific, and it must be measured by a corrected trial and evidenced in the EEDI technical file.
critical_numbers: Quasi-propulsive efficiency is the product of three terms - open water, hull and relative rotative efficiency
Hull efficiency is (1 - t) / (1 - w), thrust deduction over wake fraction
Four recoverable loss mechanisms - axial, rotational, frictional and sectional, and tip and hub vortex
All quoted percentage gains are INDICATIVE ranges dependent on hull form, draught, speed and loading - never fixed properties of a device
The gains of several devices are not additive, because more than one may be recovering the same rotational energy
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 24 supplies the tightening required EEDI that makes these devices commercially necessary, and regulation 22 supplies the route by which a device's benefit is credited - the attained EEDI is verified on the basis of the EEDI technical file, so an innovative-technology claim must be evidenced there
quick_revision.major_trap: Confusing pre-swirl with post-swirl. Pre-swirl puts rotation into the flow ahead of the disc, opposite to the propeller's own rotation, so less swirl is ever created; post-swirl recovers the swirl and the hub vortex behind the disc. Second trap: adding the quoted gains together - a pre-swirl stator and boss cap fins are chasing the same rotational energy, so a package must be assessed as one system for one hull. Third: treating the quoted percentages as fixed properties of a device rather than as indicative figures that depend on hull form, draught, speed and loading - and that have to be demonstrated by a corrected speed trial before they mean anything.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the propulsion efficiency devices question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Why they exist and where the losses are. 2 The efficiency framework. 3 Wake equalising devices. 4 Pre-swirl devices. 5 Post-swirl devices. 6 High-efficiency propellers. 7 Selection, verification and in-service degradation. Sections 3 to 6 are the four printed limbs, each written as problem, principle, forms, gain and limits.
retrieval_cards.why: Four limbs at 4 marks each need four equal regions; the framing section is what turns four descriptions into one system.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the efficiency framework classify the four device families?
retrieval_cards.answer: Quasi-propulsive efficiency is the product of open-water, hull and relative-rotative efficiency. Wake equalising devices raise hull efficiency by improving the flow the hull delivers; pre-swirl devices and post-swirl devices both act on rotational loss, one before the disc and one after; and high-efficiency propellers raise open-water efficiency, the performance of the disc itself.
retrieval_cards.why: It classifies every device on the paper and stops the answer becoming a list of trade names.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between a pre-swirl and a post-swirl device?
retrieval_cards.answer: A pre-swirl device imparts rotation to the inflow opposite to the propeller's direction of rotation, upstream of the disc, so the propeller must undo that counter-rotation before imparting its own and less net swirl leaves the disc. A post-swirl device sits in the slipstream downstream and recovers the swirl that was created, or removes the concentrated hub vortex, converting it into axial thrust or reduced drag.
retrieval_cards.why: Prevent the loss or recover it - the two approaches to the same rotational energy, and the commonest confusion in the topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a wake equalising device do, and on which ships does it work?
retrieval_cards.answer: It fits ahead of the propeller and accelerates and straightens the slow water in the upper part of the disc, suppressing afterbody separation and making the inflow more uniform. That raises hull efficiency and also cuts cyclic blade loading, cavitation, pressure pulses and hull vibration. It suits full-form, high-block-coefficient single-screw ships at moderate speed; on a fine, fast hull the wake is already uniform and the added appendage drag can exceed the gain.
retrieval_cards.why: The vibration benefit is often worth as much as the fuel, and the unsuitability case is what shows judgement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What do propeller boss cap fins recover, and what is their secondary benefit?
retrieval_cards.answer: They break up the hub vortex - the concentrated vortex shed from the propeller boss - recovering part of the rotational energy it carries. Their secondary benefit is a reduction in hub-vortex cavitation and the rudder erosion it causes downstream. They are among the cheapest retrofits and can usually be fitted in a routine docking.
retrieval_cards.why: The erosion benefit is often the reason an owner agrees to fit them, and examiners ask for it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is a larger, more slowly turning propeller more efficient?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it accelerates a greater mass of water to a smaller velocity increase, which reduces the axial energy left in the slipstream and raises open-water efficiency directly. It is the single most effective measure of the four families, enabled by long-stroke low-speed engines and an aperture designed to accept the diameter, and it aligns naturally with slow steaming.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the largest single gain available and is the item most often omitted from limb (d).

retrieval_cards.prompt: If you fit a pre-swirl stator and boss cap fins, do their savings add?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Both are acting on the same rotational energy - the stator prevents part of the swirl being created and the fins recover part of what is. Fitting both gives less than the sum of the two quoted figures, so a package must be designed and assessed as one system for the individual hull, at its actual draught and speed.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single point that most distinguishes a management-level answer from a catalogue of devices.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How would you demonstrate that a fitted device actually saved fuel?
retrieval_cards.answer: By model tests in a towing tank and cavitation tunnel and computational prediction before fitting, then by a speed trial - run as double runs on reciprocal courses so current cancels, and corrected to a reference condition for wind, waves, water depth, density and displacement. Where the benefit is to be credited in the attained EEDI it must additionally be evidenced in the EEDI technical file, which is the basis on which the attained value is verified.
retrieval_cards.why: A gain claimed and not measured is a marketing figure, and the technical file is the route by which a real gain becomes a regulatory credit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to a device's saving in service?
retrieval_cards.answer: It degrades. Fouling of the appendage and of the hull erodes it; the ship operates away from the design draught and speed, particularly in ballast, where a tuned device gives much less; and structural condition matters - cracked welds on fins, cavitation erosion and failed cathodic protection all reduce or destroy the benefit and can create a hazard. The appendages belong on the underwater inspection and planned maintenance schedule.
retrieval_cards.why: A device is not a permanent gain but a maintained one, which is the engineer's responsibility rather than the designer's.

blocks.h: 1. The accurate starting point - critical habitat, but not a designated area

blocks.p: The Lakshadweep group and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are without question critical habitat - coral atolls and fringing reefs, seagrass beds, mangrove, turtle nesting beaches and endemic species - and they carry substantial protection under Indian domestic law.

⚠ But neither group is a designated IMO Particularly Sensitive Sea Area. The designations made worldwide are few - fewer than two dozen - and none of them is in Indian waters. No Indian sea area is a MARPOL Special Area either, and none is an Emission Control Area.

That is why limb (a) is written in the conditional - how these islands could be protected - and getting it right is the discrimination the limb rewards. The answer is properly given as a programme: what already protects them under Indian law, what international measures India could seek, and in what order. An answer that assumes a PSSA already exists has misread the question.

blocks.h: 2. The Indian statutory and administrative layer, as it stands at this examination

ul: Ship-source pollution. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the operative Indian merchant shipping statute, carrying the prevention and containment of pollution of the sea by oil and the response to it, with the Merchant Shipping Rules made under it as the working detail. It is the vehicle by which India gives effect to MARPOL, and it is administered by the Directorate General of Shipping.

Coastal and island zoning. The Island Coastal Regulation Zone (ICRZ) Notification, 2019, made under section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, applies specifically to the Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep groups and regulates development, construction and activity in the coastal zone of those islands. It is the instrument that most directly protects the shoreline and the near-shore habitat from land-based and development pressure.

Habitat protection. Marine national parks and wildlife sanctuaries declared under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 - the Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park in the Andamans being the best-known - give the reefs, the turtles and their species statutory protection independent of the shipping regime. This layer would survive whatever happened at IMO.

Jurisdictional reach. The Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 establishes the zones within which India may act, and it is what makes a measure in the exclusive economic zone legally available at all.

Response capability. The Indian Coast Guard, under the Coast Guard Act, 1978, is the central coordinating authority for marine pollution response in Indian waters, and the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan is the framework under which a spill in the islands would actually be fought - with the practical difficulty that these are remote archipelagos and response assets are days rather than hours away.

Port and reception facilities. Adequate reception facilities at the island ports, and port State control inspection of ships calling there, close the loop between a paper discharge requirement and the discharge that actually happens. A regime that forbids discharge and provides nowhere to land the waste does not work.

blocks.h: 3. The international measures India could seek, and the instrument behind each

rows: PSSA designation
PSSA Guidelines, resolution A.982(24) as amended by MEPC.267(68)
Identifies the area to the world as needing care - and, through its Associated Protective Measure, actually regulates shipping
Area to be avoided; traffic separation; no-anchoring area; recommended route
SOLAS regulation V/10 - ships' routeing
Keeps laden tankers and heavy traffic clear of the most sensitive reefs, and stops anchor damage to coral
Mandatory ship reporting
SOLAS regulation V/11
The authorities know which ships are where, which is the precondition for any effective response
MARPOL Special Area under Annexes I, II, IV or V; Emission Control Area under Annex VI
MARPOL
Stricter discharge or emission standards within a defined sea area - but a Special Area's entry into effect depends on adequate reception facilities being provided
Special mandatory measures in the EEZ
UNCLOS article 211(6)
Allows a coastal State, after consultation through the competent international organization, to adopt special mandatory measures in a clearly defined area of its EEZ on recognised technical grounds
Compulsory pilotage in defined approaches
National measure, endorsed as an APM
The mechanism that protects the Torres Strait within the Great Barrier Reef PSSA

blocks.p: The general obligation sits above all of these: UNCLOS article 194(5) requires measures taken under Part XII to include those necessary to protect and preserve rare or fragile ecosystems and the habitat of depleted, threatened or endangered species. That is the treaty basis on which the whole programme rests.

blocks.h: 4. What a coherent programme would look like, in sequence

ol: Establish the science and the traffic picture. Habitat surveys, species and reef condition data, and a study of what shipping actually passes - types, tonnages, cargoes and density. No proposal survives without this, and it is also what identifies which reefs matter most.

Apply the domestic controls already available - the ICRZ Notification, the Wild Life (Protection) Act declarations, and enforcement of the pollution provisions under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and its Rules.

Build the response and reception capability - reception facilities at the island ports, pre-positioned response equipment, and exercised contingency plans under the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan. This must come before or alongside a Special Area proposal, not after it.

Seek the international measures - a PSSA supported by an Area To Be Avoided and mandatory reporting, or Special Area status under the relevant MARPOL Annex, with compulsory pilotage in any confined approach.
Chart, promulgate and enforce. A measure that does not appear on the chart and in the sailing directions does not change what a master does.

blocks.h: 5. What a Particularly Sensitive Sea Area is - and what it is not

blocks.p: A Particularly Sensitive Sea Area is an area that needs special protection through action by IMO because of its significance for recognised ecological, socio-economic or scientific reasons, and because it may be vulnerable to damage by international shipping activities. The governing instrument is the Revised Guidelines for the Identification and Designation of Particularly Sensitive Sea Areas, resolution A.982(24), as amended by resolution MEPC.267(68).
Two features define it, and the second is decisive.

ol: It is a designation by IMO, not a declaration by the coastal State. That is what distinguishes it from a national marine protected area, however well protected the latter may be.

⚠ A PSSA has no legal effect of its own. It is a flag placed on the chart identifying an area as needing care. What actually regulates shipping is the Associated Protective Measure. A PSSA without an APM changes nothing that a ship must do - and understanding that is the single most valuable thing a candidate can say about the concept.

blocks.h: 6. The criteria for identification - three groups, and one is enough

blocks.p: The Guidelines set out the criteria in three groups, and an area must meet at least one of them - not all three.

rows: Ecological
Uniqueness or rarity; critical habitat; dependency; representativeness; diversity; productivity; spawning or breeding grounds; naturalness; integrity; fragility; and bio-geographic importance
Social, cultural and economic

Social or economic dependency - where the area's environmental quality supports fishing, recreation, tourism or subsistence; human dependency, particularly of indigenous and local populations; and cultural heritage
Scientific and educational
Research value; the area's use for baseline and monitoring studies; and its educational value

blocks.p: The Indian islands would satisfy several of these without difficulty - critical habitat, fragility, diversity, productivity, breeding grounds, human dependency of indigenous populations, and research value. Meeting a criterion is not the hard part.

blocks.h: 7. The vulnerability test - separate from the criteria, and where proposals actually fail

blocks.p: Meeting a criterion is necessary but not sufficient. The proposal must also demonstrate that the area is vulnerable to damage by international shipping activities, and that is assessed on two distinct sets of factors:

ul: Vessel traffic characteristics - the operational factors (the kinds of activity conducted there), the types of vessel and their traffic characteristics such as density and routeing, and the harmful substances carried.

Natural factors - the hydrographical conditions such as depth, seabed and confined channels; the meteorological conditions such as prevailing wind, current, visibility and cyclone exposure; and the oceanographic conditions that would determine where a spill went and how fast.

blocks.p: This is where the real work of a proposal lies, and it is the reason a beautiful reef with no shipping near it does not become a PSSA. Conversely, for the Indian islands the argument is available and strong: they lie close to major east-west trade routes, laden tankers pass in quantity, and the combination of remoteness, cyclone exposure and confined reef approaches means a casualty would be difficult to reach and its consequences hard to contain.

blocks.h: 8. The designation procedure, and the Associated Protective Measure

ol: Proposal. Only a Member Government may propose - a non-governmental body or a scientific institution cannot. The proposal goes to the Marine Environment Protection Committee and must describe the area precisely, show that it meets at least one criterion, demonstrate vulnerability to international shipping activities, and propose at least one Associated Protective Measure.

Every APM must have an identified legal basis. It may be a measure already available under an existing IMO instrument - a routeing measure under SOLAS V/10, a ship reporting system under V/11, a discharge restriction or Special Area under MARPOL, or compulsory pilotage - or a measure not yet available, which must then be adopted by IMO in its own right, or a measure under UNCLOS article 211(6).
Designation in principle. MEPC may grant designation in principle once satisfied on the criteria and the vulnerability.

Adoption of the APM. The proposed measure is referred to the appropriate IMO body - routeing and reporting measures to the navigation sub-committee and then the Maritime Safety Committee; discharge measures to MEPC itself.
Final designation. Once the APM has been adopted, MEPC grants final designation.
Charting and promulgation. The area and its measures are charted and promulgated so that mariners can actually see and comply with them - without which the whole exercise is paper.

blocks.p: The designations are few and they are deliberate. The first was the Great Barrier Reef in 1990; later ones include the Wadden Sea, the Galapagos Archipelago, the Baltic Sea Area, the Canary Islands, the Strait of Bonifacio and the Tubbataha Reefs. None is in Indian waters - which is precisely why limb (a) of this question is written as a question about what could be done rather than what has been.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Two limbs at 8 marks each. Limb (a) is a trap disguised as a description: it invites the candidate to assume these islands are already a protected area under some international instrument, and the first mark is for knowing they are not. Answering it as a programme - what exists domestically, what could be sought internationally, and in what order - covers far more ground than a list of good intentions. Limb (b) has two demands, the meaning of the term and the criteria for identification and designation, and the criteria are best given as a three-group table because that is how the Guidelines are structured and it is fast to write.

blocks.h: The one thing to say about a PSSA

blocks.p: A PSSA has no legal effect of its own. It is a designation that identifies an area as needing care; what actually regulates shipping is the Associated Protective Measure attached to it - a routeing measure, a reporting system, a discharge restriction, compulsory pilotage. A PSSA without an APM changes nothing that a ship must do. Say that and the rest of limb (b) follows: it explains why every proposal must propose an APM, why each APM needs an identified legal basis under an existing instrument, and why designation happens in two stages with the APM adopted in between.

blocks.h: Criteria and vulnerability are two different tests

blocks.p: This distinction is worth a clear mark and is regularly missed. The criteria - ecological, socio-economic, scientific - describe why the area is valuable, and only one need be met. The vulnerability test asks something completely different: is it threatened by international shipping?, assessed on vessel traffic characteristics and on natural factors. A pristine, precious, remote reef with no shipping near it fails, and rightly - IMO's jurisdiction is over ships. For the Indian islands both tests are satisfiable, and being able to say why for each is what turns a description into an argument.

blocks.h: The date decides the Indian statute

blocks.p: This examination falls before 15 March 2026, so the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the operative Indian merchant shipping statute and the ship-source pollution limb must be answered on it, with the Merchant Shipping Rules made under it as the working detail. Note carefully, though, that the islands' habitat protection does not come from the shipping statute at all: it comes from the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Island Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019 made under it, and from the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. Attributing the reef and turtle protection to a merchant shipping statute is the mirror-image error, and it is just as wrong.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Assuming the islands are a PSSA. They are not, and neither is any other Indian sea area - nor is any Indian water a MARPOL Special Area or an ECA.
Saying a PSSA by itself restricts shipping. Only the Associated Protective Measure does.
Requiring an area to meet all three criteria groups. One is enough.
Treating the vulnerability requirement as part of the criteria. It is a separate and additional test.
Proposing an APM with no legal basis. Every APM must rest on an identified instrument, or be adopted by IMO in its own right.
Saying anyone can propose a PSSA. Only a Member Government may.
Attributing the islands' habitat protection to the merchant shipping legislation rather than to the Environment (Protection) Act, the ICRZ Notification and the Wild Life (Protection) Act.
Proposing a Special Area without addressing reception facilities, on which its effect depends.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Asking whether the Andamans are a PSSA.
Asking what a PSSA actually prohibits, expecting nothing by itself.
Asking how many criteria must be met - at least one.
Asking who may propose a PSSA - only a Member Government.
Asking for the first PSSA - the Great Barrier Reef, 1990.
Asking which instrument would supply an Area To Be Avoided - SOLAS regulation V/10.
Asking which UNCLOS article lets a coastal State adopt special mandatory measures in its EEZ - article 211(6).
Asking which Indian statute governs ship-source pollution at this date, and which protects the reefs - two different statutes, and the second is not a shipping Act.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your ship is transiting close to the Andamans. What restrictions apply to you today?
How would you know if an Area To Be Avoided existed there?
What would India have to do before proposing a Special Area for these waters?
Who coordinates the response if a tanker grounds on a Lakshadweep reef?
Why is a PSSA designation not enough on its own?
Name an APM and the instrument that gives it legal force.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb (a) as three layers and a sequence: WHAT IS TRUE NOW (not a PSSA) - DOMESTIC LAYER (zoning, wildlife, shipping Act, Coast Guard) - INTERNATIONAL LAYER (PSSA, routeing, reporting, Special Area, UNCLOS 211(6), pilotage) - PROGRAMME (science, domestic, response, propose, chart). Limb (b) as four questions: WHAT IS IT (5) - WHY IS IT VALUABLE, one of three criteria groups (6) - IS SHIPPING THREATENING IT, the separate vulnerability test (7) - HOW IS IT DESIGNATED, propose, in principle, adopt the APM, final, chart (8).

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: Resolution A.982(24), as amended by MEPC.267(68) - the Revised PSSA Guidelines: criteria, vulnerability and designation.
SOLAS regulation V/10 - ships' routeing: areas to be avoided, traffic separation schemes, no-anchoring areas, recommended routes.
SOLAS regulation V/11 - mandatory ship reporting systems.
MARPOL - Special Areas under Annexes I, II, IV and V; Emission Control Areas under Annex VI; and the reception facility requirements on which a Special Area's effect depends.
UNCLOS article 194(5) - the obligation to protect rare or fragile ecosystems and the habitat of threatened species; article 211(6) - special mandatory measures in a clearly defined area of the EEZ.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (India) - the operative statute at this sitting for prevention and containment of pollution of the sea by oil, with the Merchant Shipping Rules made under it.
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, section 3, and the Island Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019 made under it, applying specifically to these two island groups.
Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 - marine national parks and sanctuaries in the island territories.
Coast Guard Act, 1978 and the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan - response coordination.
Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 - the zones in which measures may be taken.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the statute boundary

blocks.p: ⛔ The single most important thing recorded about this answer is what was NOT inherited from its donor. This question has an exact-stem MIW answer at a sitting sixteen months later, on the far side of the Indian merchant shipping statute change. That answer states that the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 is the operative statute and instructs in terms that the 1958 Act must not be cited because it has been repealed. Both statements are correct for June 2026 and prohibited here. At February 2025 the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 governs in full and the 2025 Act does not exist - it was not enacted, not assented and not introduced. The statute reference was reversed, not inherited, and no provision of the 2025 Act appears anywhere in this answer.

The 1958 Act is not held by the corpus either, which holds only its 2025 replacement. Its pollution provisions are therefore named at Part level as authoritative secondary and no section number is asserted - the same discipline the trap register imposes on the 2025 Act, applied in the opposite direction. The non-shipping Indian instruments - the Environment (Protection) Act, the ICRZ Notification, the Wild Life (Protection) Act, the Coast Guard Act and the Maritime Zones Act - were each independently re-derived and each pre-dates this sitting by decades, so none of them turns on the boundary at all.

The worldwide PSSA count is flagged and is deliberately approximate. A count is currency-sensitive, the corpus holds no PSSA register, and the donor is sixteen months later - so the figure was not inherited. The mark-bearing content rests instead on the qualitative facts that do not move: designations are few, the Great Barrier Reef was the first, in 1990, and none is in Indian waters. The related negatives - that no Indian water is a MARPOL Special Area or an Emission Control Area - are carried from the boundary document rather than from a register read this session, and they are stated for February 2025.

The instrument material is stable and was checked. The PSSA Guidelines, resolution A.982(24) as amended by MEPC.267(68), long predate both sittings and did not change between them, so the criteria, the vulnerability test and the designation procedure transfer unchanged. They are not held by the corpus and were not read, so they are authoritative secondary. UNCLOS is held in full by the corpus and its articles are cited by identity.
