questions.understand_first: Limb (a) is a trap wearing the clothes of a description. It names two famously precious island groups and invites you to describe how well protected they are - and the first mark is for knowing that neither is a designated Particularly Sensitive Sea Area. No Indian sea area is; none is a MARPOL Special Area either. That is exactly why the stem says how they could be protected. So answer it as a programme: what already protects them under Indian law, what India could seek at IMO, and in what order. Note where each layer comes from, because the two are easy to swap. Ship-source pollution is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and its Rules - the operative Indian merchant shipping statute at this sitting. But the reefs, the turtles and the shoreline are protected by something else entirely: the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 through the Island Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019, and the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. Then limb (b), where one idea carries everything: a PSSA has no legal effect of its own. It is a flag on the chart saying an area needs care. What actually regulates a ship is the Associated Protective Measure attached to it - a routeing measure under SOLAS V/10, a reporting system under V/11, a MARPOL discharge restriction, compulsory pilotage - and each APM must have an identified legal basis. That single fact explains why every proposal must offer an APM, why designation happens in two stages with the APM adopted in between, and why an undesignated area is not necessarily unprotected. Finally, keep the two tests apart: the criteria ask why is this area valuable, and only one of three groups need be met; the vulnerability test asks is international shipping threatening it, and that is where proposals actually fail.

steps.title: The accurate starting point - critical habitat, but not a designated area
points: Both groups are unquestionably critical habitat - coral atolls and reefs, seagrass, mangrove, turtle nesting beaches and endemic species
But neither is a designated IMO Particularly Sensitive Sea Area, and none of the worldwide designations is in Indian waters
No Indian sea area is a MARPOL Special Area and none is an Emission Control Area
That is why the stem is written in the conditional, and the answer is properly a programme rather than a description of an existing regime

steps.title: The Indian statutory and administrative layer, as it stands at this examination
points: Ship-source pollution - the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, carrying prevention and containment of pollution of the sea by oil, with the Merchant Shipping Rules as the working detail, administered by the Directorate General of Shipping
Coastal and island zoning - the Island Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019, made under section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, applying specifically to these two island groups
Habitat protection - marine national parks and wildlife sanctuaries under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, independent of the shipping regime
Jurisdictional reach - the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976, which makes a measure in the EEZ legally available

Response - the Indian Coast Guard under the Coast Guard Act, 1978 as central coordinating authority, with the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan, and the practical difficulty that these are remote archipelagos
Port and reception facilities, and port State control of ships calling, closing the loop between a paper requirement and the actual discharge

steps.title: The international measures India could seek, and the instrument behind each
points: PSSA designation under the Guidelines, resolution A.982(24) as amended by MEPC.267(68)
Routeing measures under SOLAS regulation V/10 - area to be avoided, traffic separation, no-anchoring area to stop anchor damage to coral, recommended deep-water route
Mandatory ship reporting under SOLAS regulation V/11, the precondition for effective response
MARPOL Special Area under Annexes I, II, IV or V, or an Emission Control Area under Annex VI - with a Special Area's effect depending on adequate reception facilities
UNCLOS article 211(6) - special mandatory measures in a clearly defined area of the EEZ after consultation through the competent international organization
Compulsory pilotage in defined approaches, as protects the Torres Strait within the Great Barrier Reef PSSA
Above all of these sits UNCLOS article 194(5), the obligation to protect rare or fragile ecosystems and the habitat of threatened species

steps.title: What a coherent programme would look like, in sequence
points: Establish the science and the traffic picture - habitat surveys, reef condition, and a study of vessel types, tonnages, cargoes and density
Apply the domestic controls already available under the ICRZ Notification, the Wild Life (Protection) Act, and the pollution provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and its Rules
Build the response and reception capability first - reception facilities at island ports, pre-positioned equipment and exercised plans - because a Special Area depends on it
Seek the international measures - a PSSA supported by an area to be avoided and mandatory reporting, or Special Area status, with compulsory pilotage in confined approaches
Chart, promulgate and enforce - a measure that is not on the chart does not change what a master does

steps.title: What a Particularly Sensitive Sea Area is - and what it is not
points: An area needing special protection through action by IMO because of its ecological, socio-economic or scientific significance, and because it may be vulnerable to damage by international shipping activities
The governing instrument is resolution A.982(24), the Revised PSSA Guidelines, as amended by resolution MEPC.267(68)
It is a designation by IMO, not a declaration by the coastal State - which distinguishes it from a national marine protected area
Decisively, a PSSA has no legal effect of its own; what regulates shipping is the Associated Protective Measure, and a PSSA without an APM changes nothing a ship must do

steps.title: The criteria for identification - three groups, and one is enough
points: The Guidelines set the criteria in three groups and an area must meet at least one, not all three

Ecological - uniqueness or rarity, critical habitat, dependency, representativeness, diversity, productivity, spawning or breeding grounds, naturalness, integrity, fragility and bio-geographic importance
Social, cultural and economic - social or economic dependency, human dependency including of indigenous and local populations, and cultural heritage
Scientific and educational - research value, use for baseline and monitoring studies, and educational value
The Indian islands would satisfy several without difficulty; meeting a criterion is not the hard part

steps.title: The vulnerability test - separate from the criteria, and where proposals actually fail
points: Meeting a criterion is necessary but not sufficient - the proposal must also demonstrate vulnerability to damage by international shipping activities
Vessel traffic characteristics - operational factors, types of vessel, traffic characteristics such as density and routeing, and the harmful substances carried

Natural factors - hydrographical conditions such as depth, seabed and confined channels; meteorological conditions such as wind, current, visibility and cyclone exposure; and oceanographic conditions determining where a spill would go
A precious reef with no shipping near it fails the test, because IMO's jurisdiction is over ships
For the Indian islands the argument is strong - proximity to major east-west trade routes, laden tanker traffic, remoteness, cyclone exposure and confined reef approaches

steps.title: The designation procedure, and the Associated Protective Measure
points: Only a Member Government may propose; the application goes to MEPC and must describe the area, show at least one criterion is met, demonstrate vulnerability to international shipping, and propose at least one Associated Protective Measure

Every APM must have an identified legal basis - a routeing measure under SOLAS V/10, a reporting system under V/11, a discharge restriction or Special Area under MARPOL, compulsory pilotage, a measure adopted by IMO in its own right, or a measure under UNCLOS article 211(6)
MEPC may grant designation in principle once satisfied on criteria and vulnerability
The APM is referred to the appropriate IMO body - routeing and reporting to the navigation sub-committee and the Maritime Safety Committee, discharge measures to MEPC itself
Once the APM is adopted, MEPC grants final designation
The area and its measures are charted and promulgated so mariners can see and comply with them
Designations are few - the Great Barrier Reef was the first, in 1990 - and none is in Indian waters, which is why limb (a) is conditional

questions.memory_cue: Open limb (a) with the negative - NOT A PSSA (1) - then three layers and a sequence: DOMESTIC (2), INTERNATIONAL (3), PROGRAMME (4). Limb (b) as four questions in order: WHAT IS IT (5), WHY IS IT VALUABLE - one of three groups (6), IS SHIPPING THREATENING IT - the separate test (7), HOW IS IT DESIGNATED (8). The line that carries the whole limb: NO APM, NO EFFECT.

quick_revision.recall_15s: ⚠ Neither island group is a designated PSSA - none of the worldwide designations is in Indian waters, and no Indian water is a MARPOL Special Area or ECA. That is why the stem says could. Indian layer at this sitting: ship-source pollution under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and its Rules; coastal zoning under the Island Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019 made under s.3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; habitat under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 (Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park); zones under the Maritime Zones Act, 1976; response by the Indian Coast Guard under the Coast Guard Act, 1978 with the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan. International layer: PSSA; routeing under SOLAS V/10 (ATBA, TSS, no-anchoring); reporting under V/11; MARPOL Special Area; UNCLOS 211(6); compulsory pilotage - over the general duty in UNCLOS 194(5). PSSA = area needing special protection through IMO action for ecological, socio-economic or scientific reasons and vulnerable to damage by international shipping - A.982(24) as amended by MEPC.267(68). ⚠ A PSSA has NO legal effect of its own - the Associated Protective Measure does. Three criteria groups, at least ONE must be met. Then a separate vulnerability test on vessel traffic characteristics and natural factors. Procedure: only a Member Government proposes to MEPC - designation in principle - APM adopted by the appropriate body - final designation - charted and promulgated. First PSSA: Great Barrier Reef, 1990.
critical_numbers: The criteria fall into THREE groups - ecological, social/cultural/economic, and scientific/educational - and at least ONE must be met, not all three
The vulnerability test is a SEPARATE and additional requirement, assessed on vessel traffic characteristics and on natural factors
Designation is a TWO-STAGE process - in principle, then final once the Associated Protective Measure has been adopted
The first PSSA was the Great Barrier Reef, designated in 1990; designations worldwide remain few and none is in Indian waters
Only a Member Government may propose a PSSA
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Resolution A.982(24) as amended by MEPC.267(68) supplies the criteria, the vulnerability test and the procedure - but the measure that actually binds a ship is the Associated Protective Measure, resting on SOLAS regulation V/10 or V/11, on MARPOL, on compulsory pilotage or on UNCLOS article 211(6)
quick_revision.major_trap: Assuming the islands are a Particularly Sensitive Sea Area. They are not, and neither is any other Indian sea area - nor is any Indian water a MARPOL Special Area or an Emission Control Area. That negative is the first mark on limb (a) and the reason the stem is conditional. Second trap: saying a PSSA by itself restricts shipping. It has no legal effect of its own - only the Associated Protective Measure regulates a ship. Third: requiring all three criteria groups to be met when one suffices, or folding the separate vulnerability test into the criteria. Fourth, and specific to the Indian limb: attributing the reef and turtle protection to the merchant shipping legislation. It comes from the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the island protection and PSSA question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The accurate starting point - not a designated area. 2 The Indian statutory and administrative layer. 3 The international measures and the instrument behind each. 4 A coherent programme in sequence. 5 What a PSSA is and is not. 6 The three criteria groups. 7 The separate vulnerability test. 8 Designation and the Associated Protective Measure. Sections 1-4 are limb (a), 5-8 limb (b).
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (a) is a trap answered as a programme; limb (b) splits into four short questions rather than one long description.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are the Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar Islands a Particularly Sensitive Sea Area?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. They are unquestionably critical habitat and are substantially protected under Indian domestic law, but neither group is a designated IMO Particularly Sensitive Sea Area. None of the worldwide designations is in Indian waters, and no Indian sea area is a MARPOL Special Area or an Emission Control Area. That is why the stem asks how they could be protected rather than how they are.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the first mark on limb (a) and the discrimination the question exists to test.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What legal effect does a PSSA designation have?
retrieval_cards.answer: None of its own. A PSSA is a designation identifying an area as needing special protection through IMO action; it is a flag placed on the chart. What actually regulates shipping is the Associated Protective Measure attached to it - a routeing measure under SOLAS V/10, a ship reporting system under V/11, a discharge restriction or Special Area under MARPOL, compulsory pilotage, or a measure under UNCLOS article 211(6). A PSSA without an APM changes nothing a ship must do.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single most valuable thing that can be said about the concept and it explains the whole designation procedure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many of the PSSA criteria must be met, and what are the three groups?
retrieval_cards.answer: At least one, not all three. The groups are ecological - uniqueness or rarity, critical habitat, dependency, representativeness, diversity, productivity, spawning or breeding grounds, naturalness, integrity, fragility and bio-geographic importance; social, cultural and economic - social or economic dependency, human dependency and cultural heritage; and scientific and educational - research value, baseline and monitoring studies, and educational value.
retrieval_cards.why: Requiring all three is a standard error, and the three-group structure is how the Guidelines are actually written.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the vulnerability test differ from the criteria?
retrieval_cards.answer: The criteria ask why the area is valuable, and only one need be met. The vulnerability test asks a different question - whether the area is vulnerable to damage by international shipping activities - and it is a separate, additional requirement. It is assessed on vessel traffic characteristics, meaning operational factors, vessel types, traffic density and routeing and the harmful substances carried, and on natural factors, meaning hydrographical, meteorological and oceanographic conditions.
retrieval_cards.why: A precious reef with no shipping near it fails, because IMO's jurisdiction is over ships - and this is where proposals actually fail.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Set out the PSSA designation procedure.
retrieval_cards.answer: Only a Member Government may propose. It applies to MEPC, describing the area, showing at least one criterion is met, demonstrating vulnerability to international shipping, and proposing at least one Associated Protective Measure with an identified legal basis. MEPC may grant designation in principle. The APM is then referred to the appropriate body for adoption - routeing and reporting to the navigation sub-committee and the Maritime Safety Committee, discharge measures to MEPC. Once adopted, MEPC grants final designation, and the area is charted and promulgated.
retrieval_cards.why: The two-stage structure exists because the APM is what does the work, so designation cannot be final until it is adopted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian statute governs ship-source pollution at this sitting, and which protects the reefs?
retrieval_cards.answer: Ship-source pollution is governed by the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, with the Merchant Shipping Rules made under it as the working detail. The reefs, turtles and shoreline are protected by different legislation entirely - the Island Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019 made under section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and marine national parks and sanctuaries declared under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.
retrieval_cards.why: Two statutory layers doing different work, and attributing habitat protection to the shipping Act is a standard error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name three Associated Protective Measures and the instrument behind each.
retrieval_cards.answer: An area to be avoided, a traffic separation scheme or a no-anchoring area, under SOLAS regulation V/10 on ships' routeing. A mandatory ship reporting system, under SOLAS regulation V/11. A discharge restriction or Special Area designation, under the relevant MARPOL Annex. Compulsory pilotage in defined approaches is a further option, as is a special mandatory measure in the exclusive economic zone under UNCLOS article 211(6).
retrieval_cards.why: Every APM must have an identified legal basis, so naming the instrument is as important as naming the measure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What would India realistically have to do before seeking Special Area status for these waters?
retrieval_cards.answer: Establish the science and the traffic picture through habitat surveys and a study of vessel types, cargoes and density; apply the domestic controls already available; and above all build the reception and response capability - adequate reception facilities at the island ports, pre-positioned response equipment and exercised contingency plans - because a MARPOL Special Area's effect depends on adequate reception facilities being provided. Only then does a proposal to IMO become credible.
retrieval_cards.why: A regime that forbids discharge and provides nowhere to land the waste does not work, and the sequencing is what a management-level answer shows.
